title: Home Nurse
oneLiner: When the serious effects of the covid-19 pandemic set in last year, Mpume Ndabla, a trauma nurse at Netcare quit her job and came up with an initiative that saved many lives
summary:
Mpumi Ndabula is a registered nurse who provides care to frail and vulnerable COVID-19 patients, all this in the comfort of their own homes surrounded by their loved ones. Ndabula worked as a nurse at Netcare’s trauma and emergency department for 11 years before leaving it all at the height of the first wave last year. She says the psychological impact of her experience as a nurse at that hospital affected her immensely and she felt that the hospital didn’t provide the mental health support that she deserved. What made her situation worse was the long hours waiting for people to die, depression, insomnia and isolation.

Amid a global pandemic, when the world needed leadership in healthcare more than ever, registered nurse Mpume Ndabula answered the call and provided home based care to people battling COVID-19. We find out how this young nurse changes lives by bringing ingenuity to the everyday issues impacting her patients and community.
caseStudies: Mpumi Ndabula Lydia Ndabula Janine Meyer

title: Powerless: Eskom
oneLiner: As the lights went out again this week across South Africa, we sit down with Eskom's chief in charge to get answers about the utility's plan to curb power cuts.

a Week before the election, South Africa was left in the dark, again after Eskom announced stage 4 load shedding for the week. We take a look at the reasons why the lights keep going out.

title: Jumping Kids
summary: Ntando Mahlangu, standing high on the podium at 2020 Paralympics with his two gold medals. - Born with fibular hemimelia, a severe congenital condition that affects both legs from the knee down, Ntando spent the first decade of his life in a wheelchair. 16 year-old, Puseletso Mabote performing above expectations, setting a new African record going through to the finals. - In 2010, at the age of five, Puseletso underwent an emergency amputation after a truck crashed into the vehicle transporting him to school. Blade sprinter Tebogo Mofoking showing good progress with another African record. Aged one, Tebogo had both legs amputated below the knee due to severe burns after coming into contact with boiling water. All of them an inspiration to disabled people across South Africa and an example of what is possible for amputees with access to prosthetics and holistic rehabilitative support. With an estimated 20 000 new amputees in South Africa every year, the back story on how they got there is down to the alchemy of two men - Johan Snyders and Michael Stevens - both with their own stories.

title: Rassie VS Goliath
oneLiner: After a leaked video of South Africa's Director of Rugby Rassie Erasmus criticising an international referee went viral, he and the SARU face a disciplinary hearing with World Rugby this weekend.
summary:
Experts agree there is very little doubt that Erasmus would be found guilty according to the code if he is responsible for the leak. But its up to World Rugby to prove that. Erasmus and his lawyer Frikkie Erasmus are confident they will win the case, but have revealed nothing on their strategy to the media. But some of the issues raised by Erasmus in his video point to much bigger problems at World Rugby. The organisation is seen by many to be an "Old Boys Club", with outdated rules and regulations, which often favor them and not the game itself. Berry's condescending tone towards Kolisi during the match is but one example of this. Another is the seemingly absolute protection afforded to referees. International rugby involves hundreds of millions of rands, and decisions made by referees have massive impacts. And while coaches and players have to face the music in endless press conferences after a match, referees never have to. Official complaints against referees are handles behind closed doors, in internal hearings by the very same people who stand accused of running their own old buys club. So while Erasmus may or may not be found in breach of World Rugby's Code of Conduct, perhaps it is time for the organisation to ask itself some very difficult questions about fairness, equality and justice within it's ranks.

Erasmus took on Australian referee Nic Berry in a hour long video after the first test between the Springboks and the British and Irish Lions earlier this year in Cape Town. In the video, he questioned many of Berry's decisions, and notably, suggested that Berry treated Springboks skipper Siya Kolisi differently to British & Irish Lions counterpart Alun Wyn Jones. The issue for world rugby is not so much the contents of the video, but rather the fact that it leaked, which is a breach of their Code of Conduct. Erasmus has denied that he leaked the video, and according to some sources the video leaked social media site Vimeo from Australia, after it was sent to Nic Berry...

title: Corrupt Kidnappings
oneLiner: We expose corruption at the highest levels within the SAPS, as leaked audio recordings implicate the head of a kidnapping taskforce in extorting his already traumatised victims.
summary:
On the 10th of March this year, Amrath Natha was kidnapped for ransom from his business premises in Johannesburg. Amrath had become the latest victim in an ever increasing crime wave that's hit South Africa's Indian communities, where businessmen are often targeted, kidnapped, and huge ransom's demanded from the distraught families for their release. In Natha's case, the kidnappers were demanding R5 million from the family. The family employed a private security company, and contacted the SAPS for help. The security company, Watchdogz, employed a private investigator named Reshaad Ismail, who was well known for dealing with kidnappings, and who had a good relationship with the head of the kidnapping task team, Col "Touch" Moreme. But as Ismail kept upping the amount he wanted for the work, Watchdogz terminated his employment. Soon thereafter, the family spokesperson, Hiren Rama was called by Col Moreme, and asked to be paid an amount to solve the case. Rama told Watchdogz security about the call, and they contacted the Hawks Anti Corruption unit. Rama started recording the phone - calls between himself and Moreme. In two seperate audio recordings, Moreme can be heard negotiating a price of R40 000. At one point he lowers it to R20 000, but later asks for R40 000 again. We also have further conversations where the money and delivery of the money is discussed.

We have access to audio recordings of the head of the Crime Intelligence Hostage Rescue team, or HICR, where he is asking for a R40 000 bribe from a family, to solve the case in which their father, a wealthy businessman, was kidnapped. No one else has what we have, and no other media are onto it yet. We would break the story.

title: Search & Rescue: The art of finding a missing person or criminal
oneLiner: Did you kn0w that a missing person acts a specific way? We take you on a wild ride to find out about the dogs and their handlers searching to find missing people and criminals.
summary:
But there are different versions of search and rescue dogs as well = like an air scenter - which works off leash, and used to cover larger spaces more rapidly to narrow a search area and then mantrailing dogs, which will literally track the air clouds that come off of the missing person directly to where they have gone. These are the new types of dogs that now do search and rescue. We no longer use tracking dogs because they take too long and go along the literal path or every foot print - it takes hours, where as air scenters and mantrailers can take minutes, and mantrailers can track a scent hours and day old. Jackie de Souza is the only person in Africa who been trained in mantrailing by the INBTI - International Bloodhound Training institute. She works in South Africa and Swaziland, but is contracted around Africa to teach. She has been contracted by the Swaziland police to track criminals for them... so much so that criminals often just hand themselves over than be hunted by her team. Amazing video of this! What we have learned is that dogs will track the freshest and most interesting scent, meaning that tricky criminals cant outdo the dogs - whether its going through water, driving off in a car, trying to mask your scent.... the dogs will find them...

Missing Person Behaviour John Traas a scientist and search and rescue expert knows the behaviour of a missing person. So much so that before they even call in the dogs, he's often able to help volunteers locate the person. Through extensive research and in speaking to renowned experts around the world he's now been able to collate his knowledge and has come up with a scientific paper regarding the what a missing person does based on their age, sex, disability etc For example: A 10 year old child will react differently to a 4 year old. A person with Dimentia reacts differently than a person with autism. A middle aged man, reacts different to a teen female. This has become a guide for search and rescue personnel around the world. And is being used as an application in today's missing person's searches right her in South Africa. They are located around the country, a lot in Cape Town obviously.

title: Popping Sports Covid Bio-bubbles
oneLiner: We pop the bio-bubbles that elite sportsmen have been forced to live in
summary:
one of the most topical stories in sports today is the pressure that comes from living in Bio-secure bubbles due to the COVID Pandemic. We look at the mental pressure and the toll taken on elite athletes who've been forced to live inside the bio-bubbles, isolated from family, friends and normal life. The most prominent example currently is the Springbok rugby team. The squad has effectively been isolated from their families, as well as the outside world for the past 4 months. It began in the build-up to the Lions series and lasted 12 weeks when the Boks played their final game of the Rugby Championship. They now come home for a couple of weeks before having to go into another bubble, ahead of their European tour at the end of the year. Cricket is another sport that has to contend with the effects of bubble life. India cancelled the final test of the series against England citing mental fatigue and this year’s Ashes tour in Australia is under threat due to the unwillingness of the England test team to be away from their families for so long. The Proteas are also impacted. They are currently in a bubble, ahead of the T20 World Cup in the UAE and when they return, they will have to go into another bubble, as they prepare to host India this summer. They too face the prospect of several months living in isolation.

We look at the mental pressure and the toll taken on elite athletes who've been forced to live inside the bio-bubbles, isolated from family, friends and normal life.

title: Poaching Pandemic
oneLiner: African wildlife is in deep trouble as the global pandemic has led to another - a poaching pandemic
summary:
In March last year when the world locked down, National Geographic conservationists Beverley and Derek Joubert looked around. They had 660 people working on their Great Plains Safari company in Botswana and absolutely no guests. The 50 billion dollars of revenue that comes into Africa and supports her wildlife dried up overnight and they knew that African wildlife was about to be in deep, deep trouble. Determined to try and keep their staff, the Joubert’s who have 1.2 million hectares under their custodianship -turned chefs and cooks into instant rangers and managed to keep their staff employed and most of their wildlife safe. But the Joubert’s have never been the kind of people to only consider their own needs, and driven by their imperative to conserve African wildlife, they asked how they could help. They spoke to conservationists across Africa, and to their network of wildlife investigators and realized another pandemic was taking place as rangers were furloughed, and organised trans national wildlife criminals moved into the vacuum left behind by the rangers. Says Derek Joubert: “The poaching that is taking place right now is not going to get meat locally – its organised transnational crime. If you consider that there are a billion containers moving around the ocean and about 10% of those have illegal wildlife products in them, so there is an entire industry around this, worth about 27 billion dollars. So the final point of this cycle is that wildlife is collapsing so we are into a second pandemic, a poaching pandemic. The world’s attention and certainly South Africa’s attention needs to focus on keeping rangers employed. It’s our collective duty, and if we don’t do anything, it’s our collective shame,” he says.

Interviews with Derek and Beverly Joubert and unique footage from other african countries

title: Boksburg Tigers

After doing research and visiting social media pages of Matthew and Anneline Kruger, we found that it was not one but actually, two white tigers roaming the grounds of the couple's home. In what sounds like something straight out of popular docuseries Tiger King, a couple in Boksburg is keeping two white tigers in their backyard. We use footage shared by the tiger owners, concerned neighbours and animal groups to paint this bizarre picture for the viewer.

title: Kairos House
oneLiner: A mentally disabled man goes missing form the home where he has been living for 11 years and no-one notices... as the search continues more and more is revealed about Kairos House
summary:
Shane's disappearance and death is suspicious. Kairos House is fenced, with razor wire and there is a security guard on the premises 24/7. There are various reports that a fight broke out between Shane, other patients and management on the day of his disappearance. When Shane was eventually found he was dressed in a different outfit as to what Kairos House said he was wearing on the day. To this day no-one from Kairos House has offered an explanation for what happened. They do not allow anyone access to the premises and they have not returned any of Shane's belongings. But this is just the beginning... On 3 July when Shane's body was discovered on the R513, another patient, Gordon Cloete (48) passed away. Information from Kairos House says he died of natural causes. Autopsy reveal he had a bowel obstruction. On 29 July 48-year old Cornel Grobler committed suicide. She hung herself in the staff quarters of the facility. According to the security guard Frank van der Merwe she had attempted suicide twice before that. Her mother was never informed. In fact, her mom only found out about the death of her daughter from a WhatsApp by another patient. On 6 August, an anonymous patient passed away. She has been identified as Gabriella Hood and her death was confirmed by Bronwyn Engelbrecht DA(Gauteng). Engelbrecht has laid criminal charges with the Cullinan Police and Gauteng Province against the management of Kairos. On 12 August Peet Smith ran away from the centre and was hit by a car. He passed away.

29 year old Shane Jordaan went missing from his place of safety, Kairos House on 4 June 2021. Event hough he had the mental capacity of a 5-year old, the management of Kairos House told no-one. It was only 5 days later that the family were informed by the police who were following up on a report of a missing person filed earlier that day. The family was devastated. Louise Jordaan, mother of 5, had a nervous breakdown and one of her daughters, Christan, took it upon herself to find out what happened to her brother. Numerous search parties were organised along with local security companies and dog units. Sadly the management of Kairos House refused them entry to the facility. Shane had not been allowed a home visit since the start of the Covid Lockdown, so the family had no clothes or items with his scent. They requested clothing from Kairos House to "train the dogs", they were refused. 29 days later, on the 3rd of July Shane's body was found 8kms from Kairos House. The autopsy report reveals devastating injuries, but no-one knows what really happened to Shane Jordaan.

title: Zama-Zamas Go Legit
oneLiner: Klipwal gold mine in KZN was at risk of losing control of their mine to Zama-Zamas. How did they manage to transform the battle into a business?
summary:
So how did Klipwal win this battle and is it a model for other mines to follow suit in South Africa? Klipwal Mine is a relatively high grade mine with significant broken ore and un-mined areas that make it an attractive opportunity for its owners to re-equip the main shaft. Due to the high levels of illegal mining it was decided to utilize the local illegal miners as the main workforce and keep the sophistication of mining at a very low level. This involves mining as it was many years ago – the men manually load ore into bags, it is raised from one level to the next via mono-winches, and then the bags are loaded onto coco-pans and pushed by hand to the adit (mine entrance). The ex-illegals (Zama Zama’s) have been formed into legal entities called Co-ops (of 10 men each) and are remunerated on the basis of each ton lashed and trammed to a collection point. This method has had a profound effect in that it has made management and control relatively easy. The Co-ops are motivated and self-disciplined, and are contractors, not employees. The mine provides full managerial and safety cover using permanent employees that are not induced to take ‘short cuts’, and has to comply with all DMRE regulations. Management now plays a role of planning, leading, organizing and controlling as opposed to pressurizing employees and ultimately having to take disciplinary action.

When people hear the words Zama-Zamas, it instills a sense of fear, lawlessness, within a secretive dog-eat-dog world of thuggery and gangsterism deep in the bowels of mines scattered across South Africa. Existence is treacherous for these illegal miners, living hand to mouth and in danger of losing their lives at any time, whilst venturing into the deep underground with no legitimacy or safety. Now one gold mine in KZN that was at risk of losing control of their mine to these Zama-Zamas, has transformed this battle into a business, by legitimising these so called subterranean gangsters into legal miners. An inspirational story, but still with some challenges.

title: Elections roadshow: Limpopo's community takes their town back
oneLiner: We are going to one of the better municipality's, however, that doesn't mean it's good.
summary:
For a province named after a river – Limpopo sure has a lack of water. It’s their biggest concern speaking to the people on the ground. The communities often go days without water, and it’s also a province that goes well into the 40’s during the summer months. This is a problem not only for the communities, but also for the tourism industry as Limpopo is serves the international tourists who come to the Kruger National Park or the Waterberg Biosphere (which is a UNESCO world heritage site). It consists of 5 districts, and 25 local municipalities. Economically is exports are fruit, cotton, sunflowers, maize, peanuts, avo’s, tea and timber plantations (major forestry industries) and has the largest coal deposit in the country. However, with all this wealth it has a big gap between it’s poor and rich residents, even more so in the rural areas. Agriculturally, it’s known beef cattle country as much of it is bushveld. 80% South Africa’s game hunting industry is found here. This all demands water… and again there is none – so all the private people need to have their own boreholes and private water reservoirs, so that means any business or farm or hotel etc but this is not something that the average person can afford, so they really suffer. In the Waterberg this has been a problem for years, their water issues are well documented, however, in places like Hoedspruit the surrounding community lives without water for 4-5 days on average in a week. Another really important issue throughout the province are roads and road maintenance. Lydenbrug for example has potholes the size of cars, but rural locations are also kept rural because of a lack of infrastructure. We know that there is a lack of service delivery throughout the country and that isn’t any different than in Limpopo. The AGs 2020 report shows this province has the same issues as any other, so I actually want to focus on the differences here. Not the similarities.

https://www.hoedspruit.co.za/history-of-hoedspruit What I liked about the Mopane district, is that 4 of its municipalities are shocking, and maruleng is actually okay… however, that doesn’t mean it’s good. And that’s kind of what I want to focus on. We can focus on the worst, but there you’ll find nothing works, so lets look at a place that works, has issues, but we can work around them. WATER THEME: But just as food security is important, you really can only grow things if you have water. Water is life! But Hoedspruits water is tied up in a municipality deal with the airforce base… So water is bought from the airforce base… and the department of public works often does not pay for it: So they get their water from the Blyde River (cleanest river in the country), however the airforce base are contracted to transport the water from its source (the Blyde river water utility company oversees this)… however without any payment they cannot do this. This happens ALL the time which is why communities are left literally DRY. The airforce base literally put out a message that said the department of public works will have to go fetch the water themselves and deliver it as they hadn’t paid in months. It’s a right to have water, and because of non-payment that is affecting entire areas. HOUSING THEME: Another issue is a lack of housing for workers in the towns where there are jobs… so the community has a project – where the scotia cattle farm was bought for the community, and they’ve decided to turn into affordable housing for those who work in the areas, otherwise the only options are locations. Some people have taken to living under the towns bridge – which is a railway line, and there have been two fires there killing residents. So housing is a big issue around the province. BORDER/MOZAM/ZIMBABWE MINING THEME: I mean Phalaborwa is an hour away and has a place called Mordor which is the centre of the mining industry in the area – a giant phosphate mine that poisoned the river leading into the KNP olifants river. Most towns are so reliant on these mining industries, like Steelpoort, and the Waterberg for coal for Medupi power station. HLOKOMELA CLINIC Just outside of Hoedspruit is Hlokomela clinic, made for the workers of the surrounding community. It focuses specifically on farm workers – as Limpopo is a major exporter nationally and internationally of its produce – this is important for food security. But we need to have healthy workers. And as there are no hospitals in the area, Hlokomela was born. Hlokomela is an award winning HIV and AIDS educational and treatment programme targeting workers, including foreign migrants, in the agriculture, nature conservation and tourism sectors in The Greater Kruger to Canyons area located in Limpopo and Mpumalanga. The programme aims to reduce HIV vulnerability through peer education, raising of awareness, prevention and treatment. The project has been running successfully for the past 11 years and is currently rolled out on 71 sub project sites. An estimated 25 000 people are reached annually through the activities of the programme. In 2008 from 29% to 6%, sex workers are on PREP. title: The Constitutional Court in Crisis
oneLiner: Is a lack of leadership causing instability in the highest court in the land
summary:
Critics argue that The Constitutional Court is in crisis, devoid of leadership and divisions on the bench leading to the Court's unraveling. The leadership vacuum is causing instability within one of the cornerstones of democracy in South Africa. At the end of October, depending on whether the existing vacancies on the Constitutional Court are filled, only six of the Court's 11 judges will be permanent appointees. At present, there are two vacancies occasioned by the retirement of Justices Edwin Cameron and Johan Froneman. In the next month, two more vacancies will arise from the retirement of Justices Sisi Khampepe and Chris Jafta. These developments mark the most significant change to the Court's membership since 2009. Unfortunately, they also coincide with something of a leadership crisis that has befallen the Court. From the leadership point of view, whoever will be the next Chief Justice must treat this as a serious existential problem that must be attended to without delay to avoid the judiciary descending into disrepute and chaos.

The Constitutional Court is the highest court in South Africa. As such it is the protector and custodian of South Africa's constitution and as such, democracy. With Chief Justice Moegeng Moegeng's tenure coming to an end in October and a host of other vacancies due to the retirement of several justices, this is a court in transition. This coincides with a time in which the court itself is under attack from all sides. We ask the question: is this a court in crisis?

title: Elections roadshow: Communities stepping up in the Eastern Cape
oneLiner: The Eastern Cape is South Africa's poorest province, dogged by poverty, poor service provision and lack of development...but some communities are creating solutions to these problems for themselves.
summary:
CASE STUDY 1: ZENZELENI COOPERATIVE We visit Mankozi, where the community has run its own affordable Wi-Fi network since 2012. The Zenzeleni (“Do it yourself”) network has grown from a wireless intranet on analogue phones to a fully licensed internet service provider connected through fibre. It has connected Mankozi to Mthatha and in 2018 expanded to a second cooperative ISP in Zithulele, 56km away. THEMES: Local economic development, and a side-step into education (usually a provincial mandate): local pupils use the network to apply for tertiary education grants and [hopefully] learn under lockdown. CASE STUDY 2: NGQUTHU CLINIC Ngquthu is a village of about 800 people with almost no road access to neighbouring centres. The nearest clinic is at Nqabarah, 8km away across a river that floods in summer – it serves 32 villages and closes in the afternoon. Several women have been raped as they make the 2-hour walk. A mobile clinic that used to visit the village stopped coming years ago. So the community pulled together, donating money towards zinc sheets, and building a clinic. But despite begging government to help them staff and supply the building, healthcare is still unavailable. THEMES: Infrastructure, access to basic healthcare and community safety. CASE STUDY 3: CLEAN QUEENSTOWN The Enoch Mgijima Local Municipality (Queenstown) is tied for last place in the latest Ratings Afrika Index. The municipality is bankrupt, service delivery is nonexistent…residents have had enough. Sean Russell, director of the local funeral parlour, invests his own funds and donations to clear drains and pavements, repair and repaint bridge railings, and install rubbish bins. Two other locals started a similar campaign, Clean Queenstown, in July 2021. THEMES: Service delivery, infrastructure, economic opportunity.

Anyone looking at the political landscape in the years running up to 1994 may understandably have believed that the Eastern Cape would have a bright and favoured future in the era of democracy. The ANC’s birthplace, it was home to many of the independence movement’s brightest stars, and its vast area offers international ports, established industry and large-scale farming. However, today the Eastern Cape is South Africa’s poorest province and in many ways the quality of life for people living there has declined since the advent of democracy. There is an ongoing exodus of the youth and skilled workers who see no future for themselves in their own birthplaces. Much of the population is rural, dependent on subsistence farming and migrant labour. Services in many areas are non-existent: children walk many kilometres to reach schools that are often without teachers or even formal buildings. Many villagers die in their own homes from preventable conditions, unable to reach local clinics that themselves may be without supplies or medical staff. Of its 39 municipalities, 11 are considered dysfunctional, 14 medium risk, 14 low risk and none of them stable, according to an August 2021 report prepared for parliament’s portfolio committee on Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs. We are used to hearing about the decay of infrastructure, the stagnation of innovation, the grind of daily survival. Community projects, when they get attention, are often run by relative outsiders – white doctors at the district hospital, or expats running the local backpackers. Our story will take cognisance of all that, but recognise where people are taking matters into their own hands and creating services for themselves that their government is failing to provide for them.

title: African penguin deaths investigated
oneLiner: In a freak event 63 African penguins died after being attacked by a swarm of Cape Honeybees at their Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town - a blow to the species already in trouble.
summary:
Since the turn of the 20th century the world has lost 99% of the African penguin population. Today there are only 20 000 birds left in South Africa with roughly 2000 of these birds nesting in Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town. Sadly commercial fishing, oil spills and depleted prey populations have been the cause of their rapid decline and scientists predict they could be “functionally extinct” by 2035. The penguins at Boulders Beach are a major attraction for tourists. Up to 60 000 visitors flock to see the birds in their natural habitat in a nature reserve. Co-existing with the penguins are the Cape honey bees who are only found in the Fynbos belt in the southern and western Cape. The freak accident where 63 penguins were killed in a short period of time has been described as unusual by scientists as this is the first time that the African Penguins have been attacked by such a large swarm of Cape honeybees and stung multiple times. The bee stings were found around their eyes and on their flippers where there are no feathers to protect them. Some penguins were stung more than 20 times which would kill a bird of that size.

More than 60 endangered African penguins were killed by a swarm of Cape honey bees, in what conservationists described as an unusual occurrence. The 63 birds were found dead inside the Boulders Beach African penguin colony in Simon’s Town according to the South African National Parks (SANParks). The penguins died sometime between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning in September. A post-mortems revealed that all the penguins had multiple bee stings and many dead bees were found at the site where the birds had died. Samples of the penguins were still being tested for other “toxicity possibilities and diseases'' to rule out other potential causes. The deaths come as a blow to conservation efforts to conserve the endangered species, which the Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) records as having a ‘declining’ population. African penguins have lost around half their population since the late 1970’s.

title: Newlands Bark Stripping

As indigenous forests shrink across the country, about 0.5% of South Africa's total land area is covered by natural forests, the demand far outweighs the supply and the pressure on a forest like Newlands, which is so easily accessible to the public, is enormous. The bark stripping has got completely out of hand and the bark is being shipped across the country to traditional medicine markets in the sack loads.

The centuries old Newlands Forest is under threat from Bark strippers and unless something dramatic is done very soon it will collapse. Newlands Forest is extremely accessible from the M3 highway and bark strippers gain easy access at night, carrying sack loads out of the forest destroying 100's of year old trees. With big winter storms and years of severe drought the old trees are dying off. Assagai and Black Stink wood trees both protected trees are now virtually eradicated in the forest and SANPARKS have very limited resources to fight the scourge. Now volunteer groups like Take Back the Mountain have mounted night patrols to catch the strippers red handed and SANPARK wardens are working in the off times to try and stop this scourge

In addition to the work in various hospitals, the trust has completed several projects in aftercare centres and orphanages, as well as initiating and securing the funding for feeding programmes for our child welfare beneficiaries in Gauteng, the North West province and KwaZulu-Natal.

title: Gauteng’s Deadly Air
oneLiner: In the midst of the Covid 19 pandemic another silent killer continues to attack the people in and around Johannesburg... the deadly air that we breathe.
summary:
In normal times poor air quality kills many people in Gauteng. In 2013, World Health Organization reported that air pollution killed almost 20,000 South Africans with the highest concentration of deadly pollution being in Tshwane and Johannesburg. These days the Covid 19 pandemic exacerbates these conditions for ill health, with the air pollution making Gauteng city dwellers more susceptible to the most acute effects of the coronavirus. It is commonly understood that air pollution kills because of respiratory disease, but sulphur dioxide in the air reacts with other substances in the air forming small deadly particles of mixed chemicals that we breathe, causing not only lung disease, but heart disease and brain disease. This is because these PM2.5 particles are so small they get carried around our bodies within oxygen to all of our organs. The South African Air Quality Information Systems (SAAQIS) recorded twice the annual average of PM2.5 pollution at the end of July this year. In early August levels of pollution exceeded the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) prompting health warnings especially in areas like Diepkloof and Jabavu advising residents to "reduce physical exertion, particularly outdoors." So we're advised to live in well-ventilated areas because of Covid but to close all our windows to keep the hazardous pollution out. What can be done to clean our skies while keeping the wheels of South Africa's economic hub turning?

Take a look online at Johannesburg on IQAir's real time maps of air quality and pollution and the rankings of cities in terms of how hazardous their air is may give you a shock. Seeing Joburg up there with Indian and Chinese industrial cities is pretty scary. It is peculiar to compare the government’s SAAQIS map which uses the same data – indicators are less hazardous than the international IQAir indicators, apparently because South Africa standards are so low. Earlier this year in February the government instigated a probe into unusually high levels of sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide in Mpumalanga and Gauteng and just past, this winter has seen dangerously high levels of pollution. Johannesburg is not helped by its climate or geography. The city is surrounded by petrochemical industries and power generation industries. In winter the long weeks of static high pressure together with the heat of the concrete jungle trap the blanket of coal fired pollution for weeks on end. But the air pollution in Johannesburg, Tshwane and surrounds does not only blow in from Mpumalanga’s coal burning power stations.

Stephenson works on a 50% deposit, and 35% payment on commencement of work basis. Which means that he gets 85% of his quote paid upfront. After receiving a 50% deposit, he'll arrive at his clients house with a few Solar panels - most of these are relatively cheap, and proceed to start installation. This gets his clients to fork over the further 35% of the cost as work has commenced. But once he's done that, Stephenson never returns to complete the Solar installation. He never delivers on the more expensive part of the installation, namely the inverter, batteries and electrical installation needed. Our case studies in short: Alberto Da Silva from JHB paid R171 931 up front in Septemeber 2020. To date he has only received a few solar panels. Da Silva has laid charges of fraud against Stephenson. Maria Singh from JHB paid R161 000 in December 2020. To date she has only received 14 of 18 Solar panels and nothing else. Took Stephenson to court and got default judgement against him, but he has nothing to attach. Charl Du Toit from Capte Town paid R140 000 in Feb 2020. In March received solar panels. In August 2021 went to the cops and laid charges. Stephenson then delivered the inverter. Du Toit is still waiting for the battery, a 10 kilowatt lithium one worth nearly R100 000. Stephenson keeps making promises.

Jonathan Stephenson is the man behind a company called Solar Bay PTY LTD. They offer Solar installations to homes in both Cape Town and Johannesburg. But after getting paid large deposits from his clients, Stephenson simply fails to deliver on his promises.

title: Vaccine Science Rollout

title: Dylan's Journey: From Autism to the Stage
oneLiner: When Dylan Kritzinger was diagnosed with Autism at age 8, doctors said he'd never function independently, never speak a full sentence or even dress himself, but now he's about to graduate matric!
summary:
Tragically at the end of Dylan’s Grade 6 year, his dad passed away in a car accident at the age of 51. A year later, his grandfather who he confided in, and spent may afternoons with, also unexpectedly passed on after having suffered a major heart attack. Dylan’s grandpa Kritzinger also passed away recently, and Dylan was the only person delivering a eulogy at the memorial service – incredibly touching, well prepared and with great confidence. Amidst his personal losses and increasing academic pressure, Dylan however continued to show remarkable progress in his Grade 7 year. His marks improved significantly term-on-term and he gained great confidence in doing so. He was selected as a Leader at the end of the year – an achievement that once again had an amazing effect on his self-esteem. In 2016, during final assembly of junior school, Dylan was given the Headmaster’s Award by the late Mr Nigel Sloane with the following citation:

What it's like to have Autism: Dylan's journey... I have video of him speaking... Dylan turned 19 on November 2029 and is currently completing his final year at Pecanwood College – he is 2 years behind his peers on an academic level due to a host of learning difficulties. It was between the ages 18 months to 2 years when I felt that Dylan was not reaching milestones and was in fact regressing. We consulted with many specialists and experts over the next few years - GP’s, Pediatricians, Neurologists, Psychologists, Psychometrists, AS Specialists, Developmental Delay Experts, Remedial Therapists, Occupational Therapists, Speech & Language Therapists, Headmasters & Teachers, and received various diagnoses from across the globe including Speech Apraxia & Severe Developmental Delay, Petit Mal Seizures, ADD and Dyslexia to name a few. His biological father and I got divorced when Dylan was 3½ years. old. We kept an amicable relationship and Dylan enjoyed visiting his dad every second weekend. Between the ages 4yrs and 10yrs, Dylan attended 8 different schools, all of which were 40+km away from home (and so we spent a large portion of our days traveling backwards and forwards with no social interaction with classmates after school). Most of these schools were not prepared or equipped to educate Dylan and we were asked to leave school and find a place “more suitable” after just a few months in most instances. With virtually no verbal skills still at the age of 7, it was challenging for teachers to communicate with Dylan and vice versa. Dylan was, at this stage, frustrated, unhappy, anxious, and often ran out of his classroom to find a quiet space. Over these 6 years, he was withdrawn and lacked the confidence to leave my side in the mornings – it was heart-breaking dropping him at school. He hardly showed emotion to others and was never excited about his day - always anxious, always sad It was just after Dylan’s 7th birthday that I was referred to yet another paediatric neurologist who came highly recommended. After waiting 8 months for an appointment, Dylan was diagnosed with Classic Autism on the high end of the spectrum within 15 minutes into the appointment. We were advised to place Dylan in a home for Autistic Children ASAP, where we could visit or take him home over the weekends. The specialist stated that - without the help of trained medical professionals & therapists. We were devastated, but putting my son in a home was not an option for me. I had lost my eldest boy to cancer only a few years prior, and couldn’t imagine not having Dylan with me every day – so I discarded the expert advice and set about prioritizing less but more effective therapies and treatments to cope with immediate challenges, making Dylan’s life more comfortable and less anxious. At this point I was fully aware of what Autism was and was not in denial – I simply decided to not use the label and rather focus on one day peaceful and happy day at a time. One day, at the age of 8 yrs. and 4 mos., Dylan spoke a full and clear sentence on our way home from school. It was one of the happiest days of both our lives and the start of a whole new journey. We continued having short but rapidly improving conversations, only in the car, and only when it was just the 2 of us for some time. He then started conversing with more people and at the age of 10 had the vocabulary of a 5-year-old. At this point I met one of the most dedicated and compassionate teachers ever at our local mainstream school, who was incredibly passionate about children with learning difficulties. Dylan was not accepted into the school after completing the standard assessment test, but Mrs. Nadia Prinsloo insisted that she would give Dylan a chance in her bridging class. He thrived from day 1 given the opportunity to be treated like any other learner and of course being at school so close to home, not spending hours on the road and participating in sports for the first time. Dylan started at a Grade 00 level in the bridging class and by the end of the year completed the Grade 2 syllabus. During the same year Dylan went on School Camp for 2 nights, leaving the “safety” of home for the first time ever. He returned happy and relaxed - a different child having made friends (still best friends 10 years later), building confidence and feeling a strong sense of belonging in the school and among his peers. He also attended Speech and Drama lessons at the Barnyard Theatre in Rivonia twice a week and steadily improved his confidence levels. It was during this time I believe Dylan’s love for the stage begun. Expressing himself in front of audiences became a lot easier than having one-on-one conversations, and he continued to participate in any opportunity at school thereafter – from poetry festivals, prepared speeches and school concerts in junior phase to selecting Drama as a subject from Grade 10 onwards. Dylan spent 2 years in the bridging class before he moved on to mainstream Grade 5, and with the assistance of a facilitator, passed his junior school grades each year. He became a proud, dedicated, loyal, independent and responsible boy almost overnight.

title: Chris Bertish - nothing is impossible!
oneLiner: He has surfed death defying waves, paddled 4000 miles across the Atlantic and is now embarking on his next crazy adventure. We visit the man behind these crazy dreams.
summary:
Chris Bertish is no ordinary man. Driven by passion, and powered by purpose this 46 year old Cape Tonian learnt from his late father - an SA ski and canoe champ in his heyday - to brave the elements and take risks from a young age. His father introduced him to every kind of watersport and the love for the ocean. At a young age Bertish became an accomplished waterman beyond the borders of South Africa where he set a number of ‘world first’ records. In 2010 he became the first South African big wave surfer to be invited to the prestigious Mavericks Big Wave event in Half Moon Bay, California in 2010. Surfing some of the biggest waves in history, he won!. In 2013-14 Bertish set three separate Stand Up Paddle World Records, two in Europe and the Open Ocean, 12-hour SUP Guinness World Distance Record. In 2015 he co-directed and released the acclaimed film Ocean Driven and launched the best-selling book Stoked! Both about his life story. In 2017, Bertish redefined adventure by stand up paddling solo and unsupported across the Atlantic Ocean, over 4000 miles from Morocco to the Caribbean in 93 days, raising money for Operation Smile and the support of youth, education and ocean conservation initiatives. The Transatlantic SUP Crossing won Bertish the global “Expedition of the Year Award” at the 2017 US Global SUP Awards and being named one of the Top-100 Genius Icons, by Global Genis 100, Leaders of Innovation and Creativity, by the Einstein Institute in 2018. In June 2021 he planned to cross 2850 miles across the `Pacific Ocean from half Moon Bay, california to Oahu, Hawai in a would be first “solo, wing foil transpacific crossing” but due to technical issues had to put the project on hold till May next year. In August this year he launched his second film, “Last Known Coordinates” about his epic Transatlantic stand up paddle journey.

Chris Bertish, international speaker, author, conservationist and award-winning waterman, is a man driven by passion: passion for the ocean and those in need who he helps through charitable organizations. When he sets his mind to something, there is no stopping Bertish. He relentlessly pushes the boundaries of his own physical and mental strength to achieve what most people will say is impossible! And through this determination has set a number of world first records.

title: Mechanical Hearts saving lives under COVID
summary:
Heart Transplant surgeon Dr Willie Koen says mechanical hearts have many advantages over heart transplants and COVID has impacted the situation further. Heart transplants patients need to be on immunosuppressants and are therefore more vulnerable to developing severe COVID-19 complications. Immunosuppression is not required, however, for implantation of a mechanical heart pump. Transplant patients often die from failing livers and kidneys from long term use of this medication and the transplanted hearts often fail after a few years. The device replaces the function of the failing heart muscle, pumping the blood around the body to provide vital circulation. The heart acts as a reservoir and the LVAD does the work. Previously, LVADs have mainly served as a temporary option to keep a patient alive until a heart transplant could be performed. Technological advances in VADs have increased the longevity of these devices, increasingly supporting their use as a potential long-term solution for heart failure While the LVAD component that pumps the blood is implanted within the patient’s chest, it is connected by a driveline, which protrudes through the abdomen, to a controller and battery pack outside the body. The device records clinical data that the treating specialist needs for monitoring the patient’s condition remotely. Currently the LVAD is powered by two external batteries which weigh about 1kg each and are charged by mains electricity lasting about 8 hours at a time. This is a minor inconvenience for people who before the operation they could not walk and talk at the same time.

A strange impact of COVID in the last 18 months is that it’s stopped the possibilities of heart transplants, there used to be 40 a year. There are no ventilators available to keeping brain-dead people alive to harvest their organs when living COVID patients desperately need to be intubated. So, the pendulum has swung back to develop more effective mechanical hearts. With WiTricity and Nano battery technology gaining momentum, they anticipate that in the near future the batteries required to power the LVAD heart mate will be able to be implanted inside the body and charged by a power vest. Currently the batteries are outside the body and charged on the mains.

title: AMAZON INDIGENOUS LAND DISPUTE
oneLiner: E-commerce giant, Amazon, is in a David vs Goliath battle with South Africa's so-called 'first people' over indigenous land they're now building their R4bn African headquarters on.
summary:
A groundswell of unhappiness has emerged for some of SA's first inhabitants — members of the Khoi and San - over a verdant patch of land in Cape Town that’s now been earmarked for US retail giant Amazon’s R4-billion African headquarters. As development for the project gets underway, the former site of the River Club in Observatory is now a scene of conflict. Cultural activists claim the development will place 150,000m² of concrete on a flood plain of high environmental sensitivity and huge heritage significance for first nation Khoi groups, and infill a sacred river. According to Tauriq Jenkins of the Goringhaicona Khoena Council, a Khoi traditional group opposed to the project, they want the site – “where the land was first stolen by the Dutch (settlers) – to be declared a World Heritage Site. The land, which has been earmarked for a multi-billion rand mixed-use development, comprising hotel, retail offices and residential units, has also faced a backlash from other community leaders, environmentalists and activists. In recent months they have held marches at the site, and are demanding that the development be stopped immediately. But Liesbeek Leisure Properties Trust (LLTP), the structure set up to develop the project, say the development went through an extensive public approval procedure, and that there have only been a “handful of vocal objectors”. He added that the company will also pay tribute to Khoi and San culture and history, by including an indigenous garden and a heritage centre where Khoi and San descendants will work as operators and educators. However, the development is being fiercely opposed by more than 60 indigenous first nation entities, civic associations and environmental NGOs.

Indigenous leaders claim that the land on which Amazon's African HQ is being developed is "a sacred, environmentally-sensitive precinct" which belongs to their ancestors and their shared humanity. It is an epicentre of spirituality and resistance, where occupation and dispossession of the Two Rivers, it’s confluence and embankments occurred in 1657. It is from this site where the First Frontier Wars were fought. And they now want it to be legally recognized and preserved as such.

title: LIFE-SAVING LYMPHOEDEMA SURGERY
oneLiner: In a world first for South African medicine, one Cape Town vascular surgery is bringing long-term relief to sufferers of debilitating lymphoedema
summary:
Imagine beating all the odds and surviving cancer… just to be left with lingering, life and lifestyle-changing side effects which no one talks about. It’s known as “cancer’s dirty little secret”, a condition which can persist for life and leaves the patient with debilitating chronic pain. Lymphoedema is a notoriously progressive condition with currently no known cure. The lymph node disorder results in blockages in the lymphatic system, which causes swelling of the extremities - and excruciating pain. Now a life-altering procedure that brings relief to patients has been brought to South Africa by Cape Town-based vascular surgeon, Dr Laura Redman. Dr Redman trained for this groundbreaking type of debulking surgery in Sweden and the first procedure in Africa was done in 2020. The surgery can improve the quality of life for sufferers, without the potential of a recurrence. It’s the first-of-its-kind to be done by an African doctor, because of how specialised the surgery is - only a handful of surgeons around the world are trained to perform this.

It's the first surgery of its kind to be offered to sufferers of lymphoedema in South Africa. Lymphoedema is a notoriously debilitating progressive condition with currently no known cure that affects people dealing with cancer and HIV??

Dr Sebopetsa believes that as individuals we have to leave a mark on society and by leaving our mark, we can change our circumstance and our environment for the better. He is living proof of this dictum. In one of his previous schools he raised the pass rate from 25% to 75%. At his current Rathaga Primary School the learner enrollment has risen from about 550 to more than 800 in the last 5 years. Dr Sebopetsa has a unique and committed style which is bringing results. So much so that now the Department of Education has asked him to bring some of his learnings and ideas to other schools.

Dr Ngwako Sebopetsa, the Principal of Rathaga Primary school, doesn't believe in limitations, only in opportunities that one creates for oneself and those around one. He is giving us access to himself, his school, parents and teachers to bear witness to an extraordinary story of hope for our children’s educational future. If this Principal can get great outcomes in rural Limpopo during the pandemic, we must learn and be inspired to spread his approach across all of South Africa. A truly inspirational figure, and a feel good story.

title: Driver's license blues
oneLiner: Grace periods to renew Drivers licenses run out at the end of August but Motorists are caught up in a system that doesnt work and politicians who arent offering solutions
summary:
If you live in Gauteng and have an expired driver’s license good luck to you as time is running out and it seems that the backlog will not be cleared any time soon, even as the grace period deadline ends on the 31 August. You can no longer just walk in to renew your license – you have to make a booking online. But try that and see how far you get. It’s an exercise in lost productivity and you may never strike the lucky moment when slots are opened. And go online from Akasia to Alberton, across to Carletonville, Sandton, Randburg, Xavier there is only one number of slots available. ZERO. And the only message you get is the following: No test appointments are available for the license code Recently the Gauteng MEC for Transport Jacob Mamabolo admitted during an unannounced visit to Hammanskraal that it’s unlikely the backlog will be cleared anytime soon and probably not before the deadline. So where does that leave Gauteng motorists – not only exposed on their insurance if they have an accident, but also at the mercy of venal and voracious metro cops – known more for their bribery and corruption than their general concern for traffic flow and motorists well- being. It’s also impossible to hire a car in a different province without a driver’s license. Mamabola says the online system is not the problem – its extreme inefficiencies and different systems that fall under different levels of government. In fact he describes it as Multiple problems into which a technology was thrown that simply wasn’t ready for it. The only option is for national government to extend the deadline once again. But if that doesn’t happen he says – they can only add more testing centres as a solution. He is adamant that they can’t go back to walk ins – especially with Covid. So what do you do? Sit on the system for hours at a time waiting for the moment it opens and lose days of time, or pay someone to help out.

title: Mandatory Vaccinations - The Ethics and The Law
oneLiner: The rights of the individual vs society
summary:
"Mandatory Vaccinations" - a term that is more often used these days as the world scrambles to find ways of keeping people safe while returning to some form of normal. France and Italy have made vaccines mandatory for using indoor facilities like gyms, restaurants and other function venues. Kenya is making Covid vaccinations mandatory for all civil servants. San Francisco has made indoor events for the vaccinated only. CNN fired 3 employees for violating safety protocol and going to the office unvaccinated... The trend continues worldwide. South Africa is no exception. Sasol was one of the first employers to announce that Covid Vaccinations would be compulsory for its staff at the Secunda plant. The plant is set to enter an annual maintenance phase at the end of August and there is an estimated 19,000 people on site during this time. In order to avoid a super spreader event, Sasol decided everyone, including contractors would have to provide proof of vaccinations or a weekly PCR test to the person's own account. Needless to say there has been some pushback. People are adamant that mandatory vaccinations infringe on their personal rights, but how do we balance the right of the individual vs those of society.

Globally there is a move towards shifting the burden of the pandemic on the unvaccinated, meaning that they will be excluded from certain sectors in order to minimise the burden on society at large. By excluding unvaccinated individuals from air travel, certain businesses like restaurants and group gatherings, and even some work situations, one lessens the risk of transmission, and the cost to the state and the individual in terms of testing and treatment. But can one force individuals to give up their personal rights for the greater good?

title: AFRICRYPT CRYPTO HEIST
oneLiner: We investigate how two brothers - barely out of their teens - managed to disappear with billions in investors' monies, in one of the world's largest crypto scams
summary:
How did two Durban brothers - barely out of their teens - manage to scarper as much as an alleged R51.27 billion worth of digital coins from investors off their little-known cryptocurrency platform? That’s the question everyone’s been asking since AfriCrypt founders, Raees (21) and Ameer (18) Cajee, first announced a platform “breach” to their investors in April 2021. They claimed that the company had been hacked, and all its cryptocurrency holdings stolen - to the tune of billions of rand. Since then, the brothers have fled the country - purportedly for fear of their lives - all while a sordid tale of greed, excess and deception has been unfolding back home - in what some experts claim could be one of the biggest crypto scams in history. Africrypt claimed to be a wildly successful cryptocurrency investment platform in which investors would send funds for the Cajee brothers to trade. The platform surged in popularity in 2020 as word spread of the huge gains being made, but in 2021 a familiar pattern began to emerge – there were problems with withdrawals, then communications stalled, and finally the platform collapsed, taking investor funds with it. While it’s now understood a group of about 15 investors who have been pressing for liquidation of AfriCrypt had invested about R100 million in the platform, the total amount invested could run into billions - with some putting the figure at $3.6 billion (R51.27 billion.) If correct, this would far exceed the $588 million netted by Mirror Trading International, rated one of the biggest crypto scams of 2020. And while the Financial Sector Conduct Authority’s (FSCA’s) is investigating Africrypt, a group of some 35 investors have now hired Durban-based PI, Sean Peirce, to track down the brothers, piece together the funds’ disappearance, and bring the pair to book. Now investors say they won’t stop baying for blood, until justice is served.

An international manhunt is underway for two Durban brothers - Ameer and Raees Cajee, the founders of crypto investment firm, Africrypt, who are alleged to have fled the country with an estimated R54 billion worth of crypto assets - all from investors. Thanks to digital forensic evidence and exclusive access to the brothers' bank statements, we go in search of the missing billions, and expose a life of decadence and excess - amassed through lies, fraudulent activities, and selling investors a 'dream'.

title: Adult ADHD
oneLiner: We explore the Personal and Professional costs of Adults living with ADHD, in an already distracted Digital age?
summary:
Described by some, as a life of perpetual failure, Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has received increased scientific, clinical and public attention over the past few decades and is now recognised as a common neurodevelopment disorder, present throughout life, with a chronic, costly and debilitating course if untreated. Unfortunately, many patients suffering from ADHD remain undiagnosed, or if diagnosed, they do not receive optimal treatment. Improved outcomes are possible if patients suffering from ADHD receive a timely and accurate diagnosis, and receive comprehensive care, which would include psychopharmacological interventions, behavioural interventions and support. Previous research established the knowledge gap amongst general practitioners with regard to adult ADHD.

In a slight moment of disorganisation, the phrase often used in social settings is "I might clearly have ADHD." Widely known as a neurological disorder effecting mainly children, Adult ADHD patients, largely go undiagnosed for the better part of their lives. The misconceptions, around Adult ADHD, run far with the stigma of being lazy, disorganised, and unable to complete tasks lay bare the harsher ramifications for adults as the stakes become higher while navigate adult life. Adult Women have been reportedly found to be diagnosed later in life, And in a recent article, found that the Lockdown Pandemic exacerbated symptoms of ADHD in women leading to prevalent diagnosis, due to the breakdown of routine and overwhelming pressures of taking care of the household and work all in the same place. This is something most people without this diagnosis, have gone through. But in a quest to dispel some of the misconceptions about ADHD, this story will investigate the Why ADHD is real and not just a symptom of momentarily lapse of judgement, or inattentiveness.

It’s an age-old tradition but those groups have tended to be pockets of one or two people. But since the virus struck the numbers have surged of both young and old, taking to the icy water off Camps Bay and Clifton and right down to Simon’s Town During the week they meet at dawn, that’s 7am in midwinter you will find the Camps Bay tidal pool full of people who called the “ bobbers” rather disparagingly by the long distance sea swimmers. They just want to immerse themselves in cold water, followers of the Wim Hoff method of deep breathing and cold water immersion which has a host of perported physical and psychological benefits. Swimming to Robben Island used to make the front page of the newspapers, now 30 people are doing the Robben Island swim a month, from the most unlikely people who are really scared of the waves to Tri athletes like Ryan Stramrood who has swum it 116 times, he uses it as a training swim for his more extreme ice swims, because its so challenging.

There has been a global resurgence of cold water or “wild” swimming as people find ways to combat and protect themselves from the impacts of Covid-19. The social and health benefits of cold water swimming have been extolled for decades, a tradition dating back centuries. The ladies private pool on Hampstead Health in the heart of London dates back to the 1930 when the women extolled the benefits of a dip in 1.5 degrees for a quick immersion, turning prawn pink in a matter of minutes. And it’s not only those crazy old ladies in Camps Bay there is the Hot Chocolate club that meets every Sunday morning for a swim and then Hot Chocolate afterwards to warm up. The exhilaration of the shared experience of the icy water fuels the connections as they hang out at a local coffee bar to warm up. For many isolated people it’s broken down barriers and they connect with people they would never have encountered.

title: Succulent Poaching
oneLiner: Succulent Poaching syndicates taking over from Rhino poaching in South Africa
summary:
Sussana Holtz lives on a farm outside Worcester close to the busy N1. When they moved there, they thought they would have to restore the wild animals that had been hunted out by locals hunting dogs, little did they realise they would have to protect the plants as well. To date they have got 12 people arrested and charged for collecting over 3000 conophytum on their little koppie, the street value is estimated to be R1,5 million, and there are signs that the poaching continues. The poaches have been driven as far south as the Robertson/ Worcester area because the policing of the succulent poachers has become more effective up north, and locally farmers are unaware of the scourge, so when they find people on their farms saying they just Rastas collecting muti they get off with a warning not to trespass But what’s great about this story is that because Sussanah was so proactive they have got the local head of the Stock and endangered species protection unit, to return the stolen plants that are not part of any the ongoing case. Specialist succulent botanist Ernst Van Jarsveld who established the Kirstenbosch succulent herbarium and has now done the same at Babylonstoren came to the farm to see if these succulents could be replanted on the mountain where the farmer could keep an eye on them. To their delight they did, and I have filmed them replanting over 500 plants that are over 200 years old, back in their habitat. But this is extremely rare because mostly they are intercepting plants at the airport. After they have to identified them and usually have no idea where they came from, those are likely to die or be cultivated in a nursery, but lost to the wild.

In the last two years there has been a dramatic increase in succulent poaching in South Africa despite their being fewer foreign visitors in the country, but lockdown around the world has in fact driven the demand for exotic succulents for people to cultivate on their windowsills. The Asian market has latched onto conopyhtum succulents as their latest fad which grow in the vast open stretches of the Karoo, the Richtersveld and even as far south as the Robertson in the Western Cape. These wild arid places make easy pickings for poachers. They are harvesting 1000s of plants at a time, and these plants grown is such specific conditions adapted to their unique environment and are extremely localise, their range can be the size of a rugby field. And like all things the more rare the more valuable, these tiny succulents are pound for pound as valuable as drugs and rhino horn

title: Police brutality disciplinary hearing exposed

We have lifted a number of soundbites from the recordings to illustrate instances where this happened. We have now sent right of reply emails to the officer accused, and the discipline official in this case (via SAPS WC spokesperson) and request for interview with National Commissioner Khehla Sitole on the health (or ill-health) of police discipline management, and his proposals for fixing it (which he alluded to in Parliament a couple of weeks ago). We have secured Gareth Newham as an expert to comment on how police discipline management is flawed in South Africa.

Exclusive (and unprecedented) access to police disciplinary hearing recordings show that unpreparedness, omission and bias by SAPS representative / evidence leader facilitated a "not guilty" finding for a police officer implicated in murdering a teenager on the Cape Flats in 2013. Watchdog case data and conflicts of interest / loopholes in police discipline management shows that what happened here is systemic.

title: Clawback Audits

They say Discovery bullies them into signing acknowledgement of debt letters - implying they are unethical and dishonest, and threaten to withhold any further current payments to them unless they co-operate. Many have remained silent – fearing the stigma of Discovery’s accusations. But in April last year when Physiotherapist Karen Gibb’s husband was slapped with a million rand audit. She closed up her own practice for six months, determined to investigate what she believed was Discovery’s unethical practice. She pierced through a veil of fear – found 43 physio’s prepared to relate their experiences to the board and a senior council. Their stories and Karen’s determination changed the board and the structure of their industry body and may well end in a Constitutional court challenge. Discovery have continued to use their tactics which they say are supported in law and protect the scheme.

title: Escargot
oneLiner: Why do French people eat snails? Because they don't like fast food! So they came up with Escargot, a lean source of protein and is now proudly being made at a family farm in South Africa.
summary:
Heliciculture, also known as heliculture, but more commonly known as snails farming is the process by which an individual will reproduce, grow and sell snails for human consumption, as an escargot or to acquire snail gel for the use in cosmetics. Snail eggs have more recently been used as snail caviar or white caviar. When the word ‘escargot’ is mentioned, countries such as France, Spain and Italy come to mind but edible snails have been placed on many menus across the globe. Edible snails have been consumed for thousands of years and surprisingly did not originate from the above-mentioned countries.

When you think protein, you don't think snails. Well a farm in Mossel bay is changing that perception. Escargots is a dish consisting of cooked edible land snails. They are often served as an hors d'oeuvre and consumed by the French people, as well as people in Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Portugal, and Spain. The R260/kg is the breeders price. the retailers sell the 200g can anything from R30 to R50 all the snails on the shelves at the moment are imported from Indonesia, this is where we want to change that and have it all made locally. The cycle is about 6-7 months from egg to harvest size depending on weather. The processing of the snail is that we receive snails in a hibernation state and they are prepared from that state. They never wake up from that state.Size determines when they are harvested. They reach harvest size at 28mm in shell diameter. Goshen Snail farm is a family based snail farm, passionate about producing escargot snails. Goshen Snail farm is located in the heart of Eden, Western Cape. They strive to produce high quality escargot snails. It is their top priority to take good care of their snails from the sorting of eggs to the time they’re ready to leave us.We are proud to deliver an excellent product to their customers with the knowledge that their snails were kept happy and safe while they are with us. Their snails are of premium quality whereby we uphold a strict standard. Their snail bloodline is of that from AfroFarma, Greece. We farm with the Helix Aspersa Muller and the Helix Aspersa Maxima species. The snails have an amazing life her feeding off of greens in a sun shaded special farming area. They are bred there too. The process is quite amazing, and they are about to become national with a future at CHECKERS AND other brands.

title: Telegram Revenge Porn
oneLiner: The Covid-19 pandemic has seen an alarming global increase in image-based abuse on social media.Locally, insidious Telegram groups have been created to share women's intimate images - without consent.
summary:
While some social media and messaging platforms have taken steps in recent years to limit the spread of revenge porn (also known as non-consensual pornography), the problem continues to find new breeding ground in the internet’s shadows, like on encrypted messaging app, Telegram. In recent months, following fears over WhatsApp‘s new privacy policies, hundreds of thousands of South Africans migrated to Telegram, where links to private groups circulate within communities, and joining them as an outsider is simple. One such private group, the “Kinky Kallitz” Telegram account, has around 2000 members, who routinely share pornographic images and videos of young girls and women without their consent. Users here have not only shared images taken without permission, but some have also provided the victims’ personal information, including names and phone numbers. One of the victims, a Durban lingerie model, Jodi Nel, confronted the group’s members and was threatened with rape and physical abuse. Another victim, who has an OnlyFans account, had all her content leaked on the group, and was also threatened with rape. She has now had to flee Cape Town to PE – fearing her life. Research shows that there has been an alarming global increase in image-based abuse during the pandemic. Yet current Cybersecurity laws – which are still being tabled in Parliament – are failing to protect the victims of this new form of technology-facilitated GBV. Faced with legal hurdles and murky regulation, how can victims fight for control of the countless images that are still out there? When a slippery network like Telegram is the locus of this abuse, a course for justice, both online and off, is difficult to chart.

Image-based sexual abuse - Inside the Telegram groups spreading revenge porn Rape videos, revenge porn, and child porn - just some of the content that's being shared on scores of local private Telegram groups which pride themselves at shaming and doxing women, anonymously. Telegram's "revolutionary privacy policy" has made it a safe haven for illegal and lurid activities, including the dissemination of revenge porn.

The implications of this loss is far-reaching as it is not just the beekeepers that are suffering a loss, the large scale destruction of beehives is impacting food production all across the country.

Deliberate beehive destruction and the theft of honey is escalating across South Africa. Brazen thieves are targeting commercial hives placed in remote locations, hacking the structures to pieces, making off with the honey and killing the bees in the process. Videos from beekeepers show the destruction and the aftermath after such an attack. But besides their own livelihoods, loss of income means loss of jobs for farm workers and then there is the impact it has on food production. Most orchards rely on beekeeps for pollination services. Without bees there are no avocados, macadamias, cherries, apples and so much more!

oneLiner: The South African economy is buckling under the stress of load shedding. At the flick of a switch, Eskom is putting the lives and livelihoods of ordinary citizens at risk.
summary:
As we try to live our lives according to Eskom’s load shedding schedule, the dire state of South Africa’s power utility is evident all around the country. I propose we put out a call for viewer submissions of photos/videos of electricity infrastructure in their neighbourhoods – open electricity boxes on the streets, weird cables, substations and how people are living during load shedding events. Nationwide submissions bring home the fact that all South Africans are affected and on the back of the recent Pothole Pandemic story viewers can see that their submissions are valuable to the show. We will visit case studies to go deeper into some of the stories of electric disruption. Like Zarina Loonat from Azaadville, Krugersdorp whose elderly mother is reliant on oxygen to survive, and Jean van Vollenstee from Ekurhuleni whose son, who has asthma, could not use his nebulizer at home during load shedding and had to be rushed to hospital. To get at the structural crisis we interview Mike Rossouw, an electrical engineer and past Eskom troubleshooter, to investigate the reasons behind load shedding and the damage caused materially by power outages and surges. I have also requested an interview with André de Ruyter for Eskom’s side of the story (which Russouw has an experienced take on). Concerning the effect of load shedding on the economy we interview economist Khaya Sithole, with reference to inter-linkages between multidimensional poverty and electricity.

What is the cost of load shedding? In terms of rands and cents, the industry rule of thumb is that the loss to the South African economy is the cost of producing the power, that has been shed from the system, multiplied by 7. In reality, the cost to South Africans of load shedding is far reaching and deep - business are lost and lives are ruined - and for Eskom it’s as easy as flicking a switch on and off … or is it? We try to live by the load shedding schedule – but more often than not a two and a half hour outage disrupts our lives for much longer. Increasingly on turning the power back on substations trip, Eskom, industrial and domestic equipment blow. The consequences to some South Africans are more catastrophic. Unreliable electricity supply can lead to unreliable supply of life-saving oxygen, power surges can electrocute and kill in the home. And in the economy at large fragile electricity supply can cut off much needed investment.
