title: Climate Change Conundrum: Economy v. Environment
oneLiner: South Africa is hoping for a "Just Transition" to a greener future but, in a world turning its back on fossil fuels, will it risk pariah status as a result?
summary:
Last week marked an historic moment in the battle against climate change: for the first time in history a court ruled that a private company must cut its greenhouse gas output. Royal Dutch Shell was told by the Hague District Court to reduce its emissions by a massive 45% by 2030. It’s a ruling that could have implications globally, marking a new era in which not only governments but private companies are forced to cut their emissions. It follows to significant natural gas discoveries off the SA coasts by French firm, Total. It's argued oil and gas production would dramatically reduce South Africa’s current reliance on imports, create employment opportunities and provide an alternative to the current coal dominated energy sector. The Integrated Resource Plan, our energy blueprint, provides for 3000 MW of natural gas by 2030, seeing the commodity as the idea partner for its renewable energy ambitions. The IRP also makes allowance for 1500MW of new "clean" coal-fired power - an indication, say critics, of the lip service being paid to the Just Transition. This insert looks at the global move away from fossil fuels and how – as last week’s court ruling shows – it is no longer being left to the goodwill of even private entities. It also examines the impact of decisions often taken in the developed north on countries yet to fully reap the benefits of their own natural resources. Can a country like South Africa, grappling with some of the highest levels of unemployment in the world and stagnant economy, be expected to commit to “net zero”? And is it right that private companies be compelled to walk away from investments that might help a country like South Africa dig itself out of a large financial hole? Or is there a bigger picture that can’t be ignored? A planet heating at a rate that requires enormous commitment and sacrifice to reverse?

SA's Climate Change Conundrum: What Price Choosing Economy over Environment? A landmark court case in the Netherlands has shone a light on the limitations of companies and governments to determine when and how they move away from fossil fuels. We talk to leading experts in their field to show how South Africa's own ambition for a Just Transition to a greener future, in which job creation and economic growth compete with environmental imperatives, might be stymied by global climate change dictat.

title: Baby Ignus - a medical wonder
oneLiner: When a baby from Heidelberg was born with a rare condition causing a severe breathing problem, a heart and lung machine was his only chance to survive, but the treatment was not without its risks.
summary:
Baby Ignus Greyling was born with a rare conduction of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). This meant part of his diaphragm was missing and his bowls had moved into his chest resulting in his lungs never developing to its full capacity. At birth he was very distressed and could not breath and was rushed to the intensive care unit for life support. The XRays showed the bowel in the left chest and a very small lung. The life support soon starting failing. There was only one option left: put baby Ignus on a heart and lung machine, called Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO). The treatment is not well known in South Africa in neonates as it carries a huge risk and complications for babies. After two weeks, the pediatric surgeon was able to operate on the baby, pushing the intestines back and patching up the missing diaphragm. The lung was still not strong enough; another week of ECMO treatment was needed. It was day 47 when Nadia walked into the hospital and up the stairs to the ICU ward. A miracle awaited her on the other side of the doors. Baby Ignus was off life support and for the first time she held her baby boy. Tears streamed down her cheeks as she looked at the miracle she held in her arms.

For the first time in South Africa a baby born with a rare condition survived thanks to a dangerous and risky treatment he received, which in the end saved his life. It was a medical wonder as the treatment is not widely used in South Africa due to the risks involved, especially for neonates. But baby Ignus responded well and is now on the road of recovery.

We speak to families who lost their loved ones, owners of psychiatric facilities who say they are being let down by the department and parents of children battling mental illnesses. Five years after the mental health care scandal, has the department learnt anything from the tragedy? What should be improved? and we ask whether or not the inquest will yield the desired outcome.

Years after the Life Esidimeni tragedy some psychiatric facilities are struggling to operate due to non-payment of subsidies from the Department of Health. They say they are in financial trouble and will be forced to shut their doors.

title: Me2U MTN Fraud
summary:

They get sent the OTP of the main account holder without their knowledge so they unaware that it is happening until they receive their account at the end of the month. If you call in during the month to see if anyone is spending on your account they can’t tell you, because they only looking at the number you have called in on and you don’t have the OPT of the fraudulent number on your account. Even if you reduce your spend limit to 0 MTN independently sets a credit limit on your account which they do by running a credit check, so the fraudster can spend up to the limit MTN has given you. They are suspending peoples accounts for not paying these fraudulently spent amounts despite customers reporting the fraudulent added numbers.

Me2U is an app on MTN cell phone banking but fraudsters are adding their numbers to MTN accounts without the knowledge of the owner of the account and they only find out that money has been deducted when they get their month end invoice. All calls to the MTN fraud line go unassisted- is this an inside job and if not why is MTN fraud department not assisting their customers?

title: What the Fog

We also offer services in project management, technical advisory and tender document management.” The website details offering “microbial fogs”. Among the claims are that these “prevent the build-up of pathogens … All have been tested and documented by the South African Bureau of Standards.” [There is no list or reference for this claim.] In correspondence project manager Geoffrey Nyathi said the company charged R10.25 per metre and did work for GDID over 27 weeks. The company’s current sole director is registered as 25-year-old Phetogo Molefe. Her name, however, doesn’t appear on the employee list Nyathi provided. The business address is listed as 87 Booysens Road, Booysens, in Johannesburg, and also indicates its address as unit numbers in an “Xspace” storage facility on the same street. If you visist both sites; one appeared to be a tyre workshop and the other a storage unit warehouse. There is only one captioned picture on the website, of a person in a hazmat suit appearing to fog an office. It states “Kempton Park Department of Social Development” and is dated 23 June 2020.

2,300-3000 Gauteng schools were supposedly cleaned when schools went back last year after lockdown level 4 opened. (Thousands of school children and teachers, cleaners etc and unions were concerned about covid – everyone was panicking and so the Gauteng dept of education decided to clean schools – a decision was made to fog them, once they were fogged a "certificate of cleaning" was given to the school by the service provider). Its never been recommended either by our local cleaning industry. We will show these normal cleaning methods... And 6 companies awarded these cleaning tenders worth R431 million just for the schools, and later on some provincial buildings R117 million which took the figure to over half a billion. 95% profit margin in this work according to bath… 40 million – only 2 million doing work…they’ve done costing… THE COMPANIES: The SIU are dealing with three batches – Asset forfeiture for over R40 million – KZN doctors – who were awarded contracts in gauteng… get names listed… main indiv. They find out that it was aid for jewellery, cars, watches, investment policies, paying off bonds. Source: Typically this is for labour, equipment and consumables. Second batch – R20 million 3rd batch – whistle-blower one of them… consulted in general. Work in progress. Only 5% would be actual costs… worse than the PPE one, they had to buy the masks… The Gauteng Exp disclosure report (publicised in daily maverick) was the key document – came out in sometime in early jan. This showed who got the contracts. Mark Heywood… A lot of these companies were est relatively recently, and have no track record. title: Evaluating SA's vaccination rollout
oneLiner: We look at what's really happening on the ground when it comes to SA's slow vaccination rollout
summary: As South Africa sits on the precipice of a dreaded 3rd wave of COVID-19, this county’s vaccination drive remains painfully slow, with just over 1% of the population vaccinated thus far. To date only 1343433 people have received a vaccination shot. The slow rate of vaccination has been blamed on a number for factors, from the glitches with the EVDS system, the ineffectiveness of the Astra Zeneca vaccine against the South African variant, problems with rare blood clots that have forced a pause in the roll out of J&J vaccines, the limited availability of vaccines on the open market and general incompetence by the Department of Health in coordinating the vaccine rollout. With all this in mind, Carte Blanche investigates what’s really happening. We visit vaccination sites being administered by private organisations like Discovery, Dischem & Clicks. We also see what’s going on at vaccine sites being overseen by the Department of Health like the Alexandra Clinic. We send hidden cameras to some of the vaccine sites around Gauteng to reveal what really going on on the ground. We speak to Dr Nicholas Crisp - the man in charge of the government’s Electronic Vaccination Data System, Dr Ryan Noach from Discovery Health, Stavros Nicolau representing Business 4 South Africa, Kwara Kekana from the Gauteng Department of Health To evaluate the success of the Sisonke trial which saw the majority of this country’s healthcare workers vaccinated, we’ve reached out Dr Glenda Gray and Dr Ian Sanne for an interview.

title: Hunting With Dogs
oneLiner: We go inside the inner circle of the dark world of dog poachers and hunters. Blanche investigates...
summary:
We explore the three different types of dog hunting groups: 1. The pot hunters. Economically disadvantaged people who use dogs and traps to hunt for food. 2. Social hunters. People who travel from as far as Johannesburg to hunt with friends using dogs. 3. Gamblers. This is very problematic. Large groups, there can be as much as more than a hundred hunters at a time, gather on a pre-determined farm. Each hunter has between one and five dogs. Every hunter puts a predetermined amount in the kitty. This varies between R1000 and R10 000 per hunter. The rules are also decided. Sometimes the hunter whose dog gets the first antelope will win all the money. Other times it is the owner of the dog that takes down the biggest antelope.

title: Constantia - Life Insurance Cancelled!
oneLiner: We highlight the plight of over 5000 consumers who've had their life insurance policies cancelled by Constantia Insurance
summary:
Between 2010 and 2018, Constantia Insurance Company Ltd sold two short term insurance products to over 5000 customers in the open market. These products were marketed through various media outlets and physical brochures. Beyond this marketing, potential customers were sold the policies telephonically. In 2017, the Short Term Insurance Act 53 of 1998 (STIA) and the Long Term Insurance Act 52 of 1998 (LTIA) were repealed and replaced with the Insurance Act 18 of 2017 (IA), which took effect on 1 July 2018. The IA compelled every insurer to elect whether to operate a life insurance business or a non-life insurance business. To this effect, the IA contained transition provisions which allowed insurers to convert their licenses obtained in terms of STIA or LTIA to whichever mode of insurance they elected to continue selling under the IA. The transition provisions included a lengthy process whereby an insurer could transfer its non-life insurance business to another company if it elected to continue with life insurance business (and vice versa). Constantia elected to conduct a non-life insurance business and it considered transferring the policies to a company in the same holding company. The companies decided that the transfer would not be feasible as it would require an increase in premiums for the take-over to be affordable to it. Consequently, Constantia decided to cancel the policies. It sent SMS notifications to approximately 5348 policyholders cancelling the policies and indicating that an expert would provide an explanation and alternatives in due course.

To provide a platform to showcase the outrageous behaviour of Constantia Insurance who in 2020 cancelled 2 of their Life Insurance products: Prime Living Cover Grow & Living Legacy leaving over 5400 people without life insurance

title: Gun Licencing - Left Defenceless
oneLiner: If the Firearms Control Amendment Bill is passed, citizens of South Africa will no longer be able to possess or apply for a gun licence on the basis of self defense.
summary:
Since the gazetting of the bill, Police Minister Bheki Cele has said that they did not take the decision lightly, and that in fact the bill would help to protect many women who lived in fear of gender based violence. He has repeatedly stated that significant research into the subject has been done, and also that all stakeholders had been consulted. But many groups like Gun Owners SA say they were not consulted, and have in fact been asking for consultations with police for many years. Either way, the minister has not provided any studies/documentation/research to back up his claims that the new bill will make South Africa a safer place.

After it was published in the Government Gazette social media was ablaze with outraged citizens, gun owners associations, civil society and political parties comments on the Bill. In the main, the proposed amendments have been met with harsh criticism, with many questioning why government wants to disarm civilians, when violent crime remains an everyday reality for many people. Meanwhile, the past week has also seen numerous reports on the chaos that exists at the Central Firearms Registry, after a parliamentary oversight committee visited their offices and pictures and videos of firearm license applications literally filling the hallways, tables and chairs of the CFR's offices surfaced. The backlog runs into the tens of thousands.

title: GEKCO SLAPP Suit
oneLiner: Slapped with a R197million lawsuit, simply for for exercising their democratic right to speak out against development
summary:
A R197 million lawsuit by Century Property Developments and Riversand Developments has been filed against GEKCO and their chairperson in her personal capacity. The developers claim that she and her Conservancy have caused them massive loss of income. Especially in a country like South Africa, environmental activism and public participation are essential to keep irresponsible development in check. No-one is saying there should not be any development, but we know that government is not ticking all the boxes when it comes to monitoring things like EIAs and other development regulations. Silencing those looking out for the environment could be disastrous in the long run. And the irony is many developers use the “unspoilt nature”-card to sell their housing estates, while they are effectively decimating nature in the process. Century Property Developments claim that none of GECKO's objections throughout the years have been upheld by COJ, and although Kallesen refutes this claim, one can ask the question.. "How effective is the public participation process, especially if objectors can easily be silenced?"

Gekco - the Greater Kyalami Conservancy and their chairperson, Kristin Kallesen - have been slapped with a R197 million lawsuit by Century Property Developments and Riversand Developments for the income they have allegedly lost because of her continuous objections against their developments in the Kyalami area. This has been labellled as a SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuits against Public Participation) lawsuit... a scare tactic originating from the States and used to scare activists from opposing big corporates... in this case from development.

title: Homeless a growing problem
summary:
Rate paying residents are getting fed up of stepping over human faeces on the pavements, avoiding needles to say not nothing of the increasing public indecency. But not every person living on the streets is a drug addict and a criminal and NGO’s that run shelters are asking is the R744 million spent on this societal challenge could be better spent? R286 million of which is spent on criminal justice costs alone. 7 Street people represented Ndifuna Ukwazi Law Centre launched applications in both the Western Cape High Court and the Equality Court challenging the constitutionality and discriminatory impact of two of the City’s municipal by-laws relating to streets, public places and the prevention of noise nuisances (2007) and the Integrated Waste Management By-law (2009) criminalise homelessness. What these laws highlight is the incredible violence towards the homeless. Their shelters and possessions are considered waste and get confiscated regularly, they also can’t eat, beg, urinate in public yet there are no toilets provided. Uturn report reveals that more money is spent on criminalising the homeless than providing long term solutions, and they not winning the war.

The numbers of people living on the streets has increased globally during the Covid pandemic and the City of Cape Town that survives on its glossy tourism image is looking very shabby. There are 14 300 homeless people in Cape Town and only 2000 beds in homeless shelters. Tent towns have sprung up everywhere – there are tents clinging to the Greenpoint tennis courts fence, homeless people are living under bridges, between the highway and in the parks. There are no doubt more homeless but is it because they are just not having to remove their structures everyday?

title: Westrand Zama Violence
oneLiner: The harsh legacy of mining gone wrong as we meet the small community of West Village where running gunbattles between rival zama groups have residents living like prisoners in their own homes
summary:
The people living in West Village - a once affluent development of residential homes built by the Mintails group, are literally surrounded by abandoned mining land on all sides. And as gunfights between rival zama gangs erupt, they are often caught in the middle. Many zamas, often openly armed with AK 47's and the like, walk through the village to cross between mining sites. Residents say shootings are a weekly occurrence, with bullets flying through gardens as children play. Police are often slow to respond to cries of help, if at all. Residents say their homes have lost all value, and as the sun sets each evening, they lock the doors and hide in their houses.

The liquidation of the massive Mintails gold mining group's operations in and around Krugersdorp and Randfontein has caused what has been called one of South Africa's worst environmental catastrophes. But a darker, more dangerous part of that legacy is once again causing havoc for communities living in the wake of the Mintails disaster - with the mine abandoned and unprotected by private security, and the SAPS unwilling to act as a security force, the land was overrun by large groups of artisanal miners, the Zama zamas. As their turf wars for control of the lucrative minerals heat up, innocent communities are caught in the cross fire.

title: Reconstructing the economy
oneLiner: Following the worst economic decline in centuries due to the pandemic, what will it take resuscitate South Africa’s economy.
summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa inherited a country facing serious economic woes, over the years he has devised various efforts to rekindle economic growth, his annual investment summits, various advisory groups etc. It is imperative especially after the devastation of the pandemic that the heavy lifting to fix the economy must start. One of the interventions outlined by the president in October last year was to 'unlock more than R1 trillion in infrastructure investment over the next four years'. In his budget speech, Finance Minister Tito Mboweni promised an injection of R700 billion into infrastructure development as a means to kick start the economy, both highlighting infrastructure as a cornerstone for the recovery of the economy. Another important focus of the economic reconstruction plan is to revitalise manufacturing in the country, in 1994 manufacturing accounted for 20 percent of the GDP and this has declined to 14 percent currently. Both these sectors are labour intensive and offer long term investment opportunities. However South Africa has a history of being lackadaisical when it comes to implementation of policy and creating plans on top of more plans. Due to the state of the economy, the implementation of this reconstruction plan is urgent for the country.

South Africa’s has seen its economy steadily decline over the past decade, registering a less than one percent growth before the pandemic, it stood no fight chance once COVID 19 hit our shores. Already downgraded to sub-investment grade by all three major ratings agencies, job losses and a contracted GDP due to lockdown, a strong recovery plan became imperative. President Cyril Ramaphosa’s recovery plan has focused on industry as the main driving force to get South Africa back on a growth path. This means manufacturing and infrastructure development are some of the sectors that will be getting both policy and financial support from government with the expectation of more jobs and revenue. The insert will trace South Africa's recovery plan thus far and analyze the possible growth trajectory of manufacturing and infrastructure as economic boosters.

title: Ramaphosa vs Magashule... Extra time
oneLiner: The ANC is going into extra time in the contest between President Cyril Ramaphosa and Secretary General Ace Magashule. Both have ordered the suspension of the other, a tight match is poised at 1-1.
summary:
What next? Magashule insists that there are processes that haven't been followed and that according to the NEC's resolutions he has not been treated fairly. He is going to appeal. His heart, his mind, his soul belongs to the ANC and according to him, nothing will make him leave his beloved party. He openly accused the Ramaphosa team of buying conference votes at Nasrec for Ramaphosa’s election as leader. Magashule says that there are more dominant factions in the ANC who are getting their way. He sees himself as a victim and as a target of those factions who are out to get Ramaphosa a second term. In all this subterfuge and confusion does Ace have a point? What can he do next? Are his governing days over, or can he win through in extra-time? To what lengths will he go and what can he actually do, politically and legally? Outside of the ANC arena, with regards to his court case on the Free State Asbestos charges, Magashule firmly states that he is innocent and has done nothing wrong, that he can't wait for his court case where there will be surprise witnesses. Story Treatment We will tell the story using soccer metaphors, interspersing football terms in the narrative: Goals, own goals, penalties, throw ins, tactics, extra time, injury time, halftime, fulltime whistle, red card, sent off, yellow card, fans, support of the, great save, tackle, foul etc, etc This is also a reference to how Magashule got the name ‘Ace’ – from his nickname in his old soccer playing days/ An idea for on-camera links is to have the presenter speak into a mic, pitch-side and in the stands sitting like a soccer commentator. We need to find a football field for this where we can also shoot atmospheric shots of the football pitch and goal nets.

Ace has set out his game plan with his affidavit lodged at the Gauteng High Court. He is appealing his suspension, citing rule 25.70 of the ANC Constitution, which incorporates the step-aside rule, arguing that it was not implemented in accordance with ANC resolutions - and restates that constitutionally he should be regarded as innocent until proven guilty. Could this prove to be a massive own goal scored by the ANC? Even though he was ordered to stay silent, on 17th May after Former President Zuma’s appearance at the Pietermaritzburg High Court, Magashule went on the attack again - appealing to members (fans) to come en-masse, show their support, on May 26th. Covid-19 restrictions allowing, that day could show if Magashule has actually got the grassroots support, he claims to have, to back up the pressure he is putting on Ramaphosa’s leadership. On the other side, there is pressure on the ANC to show Magashule the red card. After all, he has refused to step aside and to apologise for trying to suspend President Ramaphosa.

title: Liquidating Steinhoff
oneLiner: In 2016, Braam Van Huysteen sold his company Tekkietown to Steinhoff for R3.2 billion paid for in Steinhoff shares a year later they were almost worthless. Now the race is on to liquidate Steinhoff
summary:
Imagine this. You spend a lot of time and money and risk building up your unique company. It starts to do well and gets noticed by Markus Jootse, once South Africa’s darling of the business world. The man who you think, has the Midas touch. Markus makes you and your investors an offer for your company in 2016, and instead of paying you cash he offers you shares in one of the richest companies on the JSE and the Frankfurt stock exchange. You agree, you sign the contracts and you get your shares. You have just sold your company for R3.2 Billion Rand, except you opt for shares in Steinhoff instead of the cash. What could possibly go wrong? A year later you get to answer that question when Markus Jooste’s global fraud is exposed, and the once mighty Steinhoff empire comes tumbling down. This is what happened to Braam Van Huyssteen when he sold Tekkie Town to Steinhoff for R3.2 Billion rand. Braam did his due diligence, he went through the books. The accountants said the financial statements fairly reflected the value of the company. Except they didn’t. Markus Jooste may as well have given Braam Van Huyssteen fake bank notes for Tekkie Town. But it was too late – Jooste had already taken Tekkie Town’s shares and funneled them into Steinhoff. Van Huysteen and his investors had basically given away the asset to Jooste for nothing.

The main players will speak on camera to Carte Blanche. A David and Goliath story in a race against time

title: SAPO's Big Ideas
oneLiner: The Post Office was declared commercially insolvent yet the new CEO plans to turn this state entity into a leader in ecommerce and courier services.
summary:
Despite R8 billion in bailouts since 2014, the South African Post Office is once again staring bankruptcy in the face, with reports of unpaid rentals and desperate suppliers, postal backlogs and broken ICT systems. But the recently appointed CEO, Nomkhita Mona, is optimistic: “we want to grow and build a world-class, commercially viable postal service with no heavy reliance on national fisus”, she says. Mona plans to expand into the highly lucrative e-commerce space as well as having the monopoly on being the only service provider on the market to deliver packages weighing 1kg or less. In April the Post Office announced a strategic partnership with Wish, the largest and fastest growing global ecommerce platform connecting with more than 100 million monthly active users in over 100 countries to over 500,000 merchants around the world. We ask how the commercially insolvent state-entity plans to compete with private courier companies to deliver a reliable service and enter the e-commerce market if it cannot even pay rent, postal agents and deliver parcels on time?

The South African Post Office wants to become a prominent player in the country’s courier industry and ecommerce offering, despite the fact that the Auditor-General has declared it commercially insolvent. How will this struggling state-entity turn around their ‘obsolete business model’ and become financially sustainable when they are unable to pay their long line of creditors and without further bailouts from the National Treasury?

title: Uber bad idea
oneLiner: We investigate how fake Uber drivers trap young women at airports
summary:
Fake Uber drivers are rife at the country’s airports. They wait at the arrivals sections of airports holding up boards indicating that they are drivers for Uber. They are believed to target single travelers, especially young women who may appear not to be travelwise. When the Uber is ordered, fake drivers walk up to their targets and inform that they are the driver that have been hailed/ordered. Unsuspecting victims follow them to their cars and once they are in the car, they cannot get out. When the real Uber drivers who were ordered arrive to pick up the person, it is too late. The fake Uber driver then informs his passenger/target that the other Uber driver is only calling because business is tight, and they fight for passengers. They tell their victims to ignore the calls of the other Uber drivers or to block their numbers. Once they are outside the airport, they spin off and it is only then victims realize, they are being kidnapped. In some cases, the victims are robbed and dropped off next to the road, but in more serious cases, female victims are raped and sometimes killed.

After a young woman took an Uber from OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg, she was never seen again. A couple of days later, her remains were discovered in the Vaal river. We investigate whether a fake uber syndicate may be targeting young women at airports.

title: Mkhondo: The silent war
oneLiner: What happened at Pampoenkraal?
summary:
Small farmers, land beneficiaries, commercial farmers, farmworkers, traditional leaders and the community of Mkhondo are losing the battle against crime in the area. Livestock herders who are tasked with counting stock daily, don’t report the missing numbers to the farmers anymore because they know, they would have to find the missing animals. If they track them, they always track them back to the same area where a syndicate is believed to operate. Criminals here attack the herders for tracking the farmers’ livestock, accusing the herders of siding with the white community. Farmworkers who don’t want to become part of the syndicates are intimidated to the extend where they are too afraid to attend events and social gatherings in the evenings or over weekends, because that is where the criminal await them. That is where they are attacked and killed. Over the last five years, crime has intensified and the community say, it is now completely out of control. And after what happened at Pampoen in April, they see no end in sight. On the contrary, they say, the war has only just begun.

We visit Mkhodo to investigate the events leading up to the tragic incident at the farm Pampoenkraal in Mkhondo during which two brothers were killed.

Not only does our economy need some stimulation, but many agree that South Africa has some of the best water experts and engineers in the world. We have enough engineers and they certainly fall within the government's budget. So why has DWS opted for outside help. On top of that people are sceptical about the Cubans' expertise and training. South Africa has unique challenges and a very unique hydrology.

Last month Minister Sisulu welcomed 24 Cuban engineers to the country, who are said to bring valuable international expertise to our engineers and municipal workers. This is not the first time Cuban experts come to assist the DWS. In 2014/15 we also got help from the country, but many are sceptical that these imports add any real value to our current situation.

title: African Swine Fever - What's the State Doing?
summary:
The GTG Fourie Piggery which has 15 000 pigs got ASF two months ago and the state apart from confirming the infection has done very little to assist. In desperation that took the Dr Mpho Maja as Director of Animal Health for the Department of Agriculture and Land Reform and Rural Development to court with an urgent application to fulfil their obligations under the Animal Diseases Act. The court ruled in GTG’s favour but instead and stepping up they maintain the court ruled they simply had to cover legal costs. The implications of culling 15 000 pigs that have a commercial value of R50 million is massive. Once the infection is detected what do they do? It costs R120 000 a day to feed the pigs, and they now have no commercial value. If they stop feeding them they will eat each other and the farmers charged with cruelty to animals. They only have the facilities to dispose of 10% of the pigs and the Department are doing nothing except to insist the farm must be quarantined.

African Swine Fever is a highly contagious and notifiable disease under the Animal Disease Act requiring the state veterinary services to intervene. The entire herd of pigs needs to be culled and their bodies disposed of and the farm or area quarantined, and then the State is required to compensate the farmer. But this hasn’t been happening. The State is slow to intervene and when they do they simply tests and confirm the presence of the ASF and will oversee the culling. They don’t insist the pigs be culled in order to avoid compensating the farmer. This has massive implications when pigs kept in townships and informal settlements like Mfuleni but also for commercial establishments which can keep up to 15 000 pigs.

title: The Lions are Coming
summary: After months of speculation and rumour, the British and Irish Lions management confirmed that the long-planned for tour of the famous rugby union team to South Africa is on. The four-yearly Lions tours are the blue riband of rugby, the pinnacle of a player’s career and for their opponents, an opportunity to play on a world stage only surpassed for glory by the World Cup. Set to run from 3rd July to 7th August, the tour had been in doubt due to concerns over Covid-19 restrictions and the likely impact of the games being played without spectators. Several contingencies had been under consideration, including accepting an offer by the Australian Rugby Union to move the tour to Australia where sports are now being played to near-full houses. Another option was moving the tour to Britain, which unlike South Africa has an advanced Covid-19 vaccination programme underway and is likely to admit spectators to sporting events by May. The third option was to postpone the tour by a year. All three were rejected after pressure from players and the rugby public mounted to stick to the original plan.

title: Petsitter puppy abuse
oneLiner: When a young couple from Hermanus left their Boxer puppy in the care of pet sitters little did she know what horror would befell her puppy in her absence. Carte Blanche brings you the story.
summary:
A video of a couple abusing a puppy has gone viral. The couple implicated in the abuse scandal are pet sitters who offer their services in Hermanus area. The video, released by the pet owner, shows a man hitting the puppy with an object and a woman complaining. The dog is then grabbed viciously by the flesh of its neck and tossed outside. The owner is very traumatised by the incident and has seeked legal assistance after reporting the case to the SPCA. title: Covid-19 - One year on
oneLiner: We reflect on a year of Covid-19.. How has it changed our lives?
summary:
We look back at the past 12 months of living with a global pandemic, and we revisit some of the people we met along the way. Was it as bad as people had expected? How did their lives change? What are their hopes for the future? We will touch base with Gift of the Givers who spent much time on the forefront of this pandemic, mothers who have had babies in lockdown, couples who found love and navigated relationships. We will also speak to some experts who can summarise how our world has changed over the past year - FEDHASA on on the hospitality industry in SA, economist Duma Gqubule who will convey the impacts on the economy and Francois Venter will speak about the impacts on our healthcare system... Interweaved with updates from case studies as highlighted below.

On 5 March 2020 the first case of Covid-19 was diagnosed in South Africa. Within 3 weeks the country went into hard lockdown and our lives changed forever, but at the same time, life has continued… people have had to carry on without loved ones, learners have had to continue schooling under difficult circumstances, health workers have had to show up for work, sometimes without the correct PPE, during scary times when more than 13,000 Covid-19 patients lay in hospital beds across the country. We don’t know what the future has in store for us, how the virus will continue to alter the world… but we can reflect on everything we’ve been through and perhaps this will give us hope for the future…

title: Long Covid: Lessons from ME/CFS
oneLiner: ME/CFS has long been a source of mystery, but efforts directed at understanding Long Covid might at last reveal the cause of this debilitating syndrome and - possibly - a cure.
summary:
There's ongoing research about what causes ME/CFS, but most experts are of the view that it’s a genetic disease triggered by something that puts stress on the immune system, like a viral infection. Even in its mildest forms, it can leave people exhausted from the most mundane of activities like taking a shower or a short walk. Severe cases are often bed-ridden and unable to talk. ‘Long Covid’ or ‘Post-Covid Syndrome’ is causing similar levels of debate having left a lot of doctors scratching their heads. Because of their similarities scientists are asking whether ‘Long Covid’ that meets certain diagnostic criteria and lasts for longer than 6 months, is in fact ME/CFSs. Professor Ron Davis, a Stanford geneticist whose son has very severe ME/CFS, told CNN recently that some Covid Long Haulers do have ME/CFS. Others are urging more caution and further research. What is clear – and a potential game-changer - is that people living with the chronic symptoms of ME/CFS (for so long ignored and misunderstood, their condition under-researched) will likely benefit from the work going into understanding ‘Long Covid’. This story will examine the link/similarities between ‘Long Covid’ and ME/CFS by re-telling the story of Retha Viviers, founder of the ME/CFS Foundation of South Africa, who continues to fight the cause of those living with ME/CFS. Her advocacy now includes a keen interest in the research on the link with ‘Long Covid’. It will also include an updated interview with Prof Davis and several other researchers currently involved in finding answers to the complex questions: “Is Long Covid actually ME/CFS or a different type of post-infection syndrome?” and “Will global attempts at understanding Long Covid deliver a long-awaited treatment or even cure for ME/CFS?”. ENDS

Long Covid is a new medical phenomenon and is still greeted with cynicism by some in the scientific community. Similarly, those suffering the debilitating effects of ME/CFS struggled to convince doctors that their symptoms - utterly life-changing in most cases - were real. But scientific skepticism isn't the only thing these two syndromes have in common: they also share a remarkable number of symptoms such as brain fog, joint pain and a malaise that follows even slight physical exertion. Is it possible Long Covid could lead to ME/CFS in some patients? And, does their similarity reveal how Long Covid should be treated? With huge resources being poured into understanding Long Covid, could ME/CFS benefit from those studies?

title: Murder In Groblersdal
oneLiner: We investigate a farm murder where all is not what it appears to be.
summary:
After midnight of an early October evening in 2019 three shots rang out on a farm near Groblersdal in Limpopo. There was a moment's pause before seven more gunshots broke the early morning silence. Afterwards, a young farmer, Raymond Papapavlou lay dead. His wife of two years, Simoné was a broken woman. She later told police she had fallen asleep on a couch in the TV room, while her husband was asleep in the bedroom when their dog reacted to a shadow. Suddenly three shots rang out from within the bedroom. Raymond was mortally struck and Simoné, who had a pistol with her, fired seven "warning shots" into the wall. The intruder managed to escape and yet another farm murder was added to the statistics. But all did not seem to be what it appeared to be. The next morning two teams of professional trackers went over the farm with a fine toothed comb. Not a single strange track was found in the area surrounding the house.The window used as an entry point, according to Simoné, seemed suspiciously small. Big enough for a small child to gain silent access, but almost impossible for an adult sized intruder. A month later the small rural community was shocked when a 22-year old friend of Simon's, Patricia Ray-Lee Smith, was arrested and charged with murder and conspiracy to murder. An even greater surprise waited in Smith's charge sheet; Another name - Simoné Papapavlou. Up to date, Papapavlou has never been arrested and Smith was released on bail on 27 November 2020. We will be talking to farmer and road builder, Japie Jonker. He is Raymond Papapavlou's uncle. Jonker also rented the farm for Raymond and his young wife to stay on. Jonker will take CB to the farm and talk us through the events of that horrible night. At the moment our insert will consist of interviews with Jonker, as well as a member of the professional tracking team and also the private detective who traced and arrested Smith, ex-police colonel Gawie Louwrens..

A month after a farmer from Groblersdal was murdered, his widows girlfriend was arrested. Carte Blanche investigates...

Table Mountain, of the iconic tourist sites of the word, is a huge wildness and a favourite amongst hiker. title: Ice Freediver Amber Fillary
oneLiner: We meet a remarkable ice freediver from Cape Town in her pursuit of a world record and what inspired her to go down that path after years of battling with addiction and major depression.
summary:
Technical skills: At high school she received her Western Province swimming school colours and later on became a swimming coach and lifesaver in the UK where she became accustomed to freezing waters during the cold northern winters. She tried scuba diving for a while in Egypt but found the diving and breathing equipment heavy and cumbersome. Freediving was a natural choice for Fillary as she soon proved to have huge capacity for breath hold and staying calm under water. In 2015 Fillary broke three freediving records at the nationals in Port Elizabeth and was awarded her Springbok colours. In 2017 she became the country’s only representative to partake in the under-ice freediving competition in Finland - a sport relatively unknown in South Africa. “My first attempt in Finland was like a practice run; I did not know what to expect and was totally unprepared for the conditions of swimming under a layer of thick ice in sub-zero temperatures,” she says. But it made her more determined to try again. In 2019, she made another attempt - this time with some training from South African coach, Allen Stubbs - but panicked and got entangled in the safety line she was attached to. She fell back into a dark space and with the help of Stubbs, and serious technical training in the pool here in Cape Town, went back in 2020 ready for the biggest challenge ever - to break the Guinness World Record.

On 29 February 2020, forty-seven-year-old Amber Fillary from Cape Town plunged into a hole in a frozen lake near Oslo in Norway to break the record for the longest freedive under ice. She swam a distance of 70meters under 34cm of ice, wearing only a bikini (no fins, no weight to keep her down, no wetsuit) and goggles. She beat the record by 20 meters - all for the sake of mental health. Fillary suffers from severe depression and has battled with addictions all her life. Breaking the world record was a psychological achievement for Fillary where her aim was to give others hope who are suffering from similar problems. Her message was simple: “you can achieve anything if you put your mind to it” and ‘never to give up on your dreams.’

oneLiner: President Ramaphosa has warned that false information about COVID-19 vaccines is putting lives at risk. So what sources can we trust, what is misleading and how do we tell the difference?

These range from alleged miracle cures like Ivermectin to disinformation that sow seeds of doubt about COVID-19 vaccines. Amazingly, a recent public poll revealed that 52% of South Africans would not even take the vaccine if it were available to them. https://www.iol.co.za/personal-finance/insurance/52-of-south-africans-dont-want-covid-vaccine-despite-sa-securing-initial-batch-f45373f0-6199-46ab-8207-fb632706b8e5 Those who doubt the efficacy of the vaccine include Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng (https://www.iol.co.za/pretoria-news/news/covid-19-charges-against-chief-justice-mogoeng-mogoeng-over-devil-666-anti-vaccine-stance-c3fa8c22-bb44-4887-9a03-350492a91044) and amazingly, many primary health care givers: https://www.timeslive.co.za/sunday-times/news/2021-01-24-fear-of-the-vaccine-jab-infects-frontline-health-care-workers/ In this story we look at why there is such scepticism toward the vaccine. Where does it come from and how can it be countered? title: COVID-19 Border Post Chaos: A Day in The Life of A Crosser
oneLiner: From bribing officials to crossing the crocodile infested Limpopo River by foot, these Zimbabwean border jumpers are risking it all for a better life in SA.
summary:
According to reports, thousands of desperate Zimbabwean nationals who were trying to cross into South Africa are no longer camping at the Beitbridge border post. But that doesn’t mean that they have returned to their Zimbabwean homes. Some have resorted to illegal and clandestine ways, like riding on canoes or bribing soldiers, to worm their way back into South Africa via the Limpopo River. This investigation explores how such longstanding issues of border security stand to hamper South Africa's fight against COVID-19.

Images of panic and overcrowding at the Beitbridge border post are familiar enough to anyone who was watching the nightly television news over the festive season. But the reality and pain of such a life is unimaginable for most of us. In this report, we take a closer look at a day in the life of an illegal Zimbabwean border jumper. We take an emotional journey that uncovers who they are, the dangerous and illegal routes they use to cross into SA and how that is expected to affect our country's efforts of fighting COVID-19.

title: The Mystery of the White Lady

summary:
In Namibia, an age-old mystery was painted on rocks in a remote part of the country. It is known as the White Lady of the Brandberg. It is a depiction of a white woman in rock art that seems out of place: when the painting was done there were no white people South of the Equator. So people believed it was a local Shaman, painted white. Now research done by prominent Namibian architect and artist Linus Malherbe indicated that it could be a white woman of Viking origin. An astounding theory. -- hould not be there.

It is a multi-layered story and deals with history archaeology and rock art in Namibia. It can visually be very strong and it is an unusual story -- we seldom get the opportunity to do this kind of story. It is also new research.

title: The Retirement Home Killers.

The retirement home killers. Shaun Oosthuizen (39) and John duPlooy (27) from the Munsieville squattercamp outside Krugersdorp are facing their third murder charge for the death of a female resident of a retirement home. This time however, they will not be facing the court alone. Their fellow Munsieville resident, Maryna Vorster-Lin, will also be in the dock. They are accused of murdering Hetta Potgieter in the Macadamia retirement home in Mbombela on 8 July 2018. Oosthuizen and Du Plooy have already been found guilty of the murders of two women. Their first victim was Engela van Wyk (86), whom they murdered on 24 June 2018 in her unit in the Rus-’n-bietjie-home in Springs. A few weeks after Van Wyk’s murder, the two men (This time allegedly in the company of Vorster-Lin) allegedly struck again and Potgieter was murdered. The three suspects were arrested and were released on bail.

Headliner news. New accused namely Maryna Vorster-Lin, will also be in the dock in connection to these murders.

title: Body Positivity
oneLiner: We share the inspirational stories of women who have challenged societal norms of physical appearance and love the bodies they’re in.
summary:
We share the uplifting stories of women who have, despite discrimination based on their size, come out stronger. Through their journey of self-discovery they have turned their lives around and learnt to embrace their differentness. By celebrating their female form publicly on social media they have attracted many followers and served as an inspiration to others. We go on a journey with four different women of diverse backgrounds and talents who each in their own right have become a body ambassador with a holistic approach to self -love and self-care. We look at the role of healthy living and talk to a dietician who encourages natural weight loss through intuitive eating - an anti-diet approach to eating that focuses on people’s relationship and connectivity to their body’s natural cues for hunger and fullness.

Societal expectations of the perfect body being slim and trim have been the norm for the last hundred years creating barriers for plus size people who feel they don’t fit in. But in the last decade the body positivity movement has changed the landscape to embrace acceptance of all bodies no matter what shape, size or ethnicity. Body positivity is about working towards a world where everyone can live in their bodies as they please while receiving the same respect, representation, and opportunities as everyone else.

summary:
The family of Suraya Deedat may finally get some answers in November after nearly a decade of questions. The inquest into the deaths of Suraya and her four small children will wrap up in the Johannesburg magistrates court. The inquest was opened by private prosecutor Gerrie Nel at the beginning of 2020. Five witnesses have been called to the stand by Nel and the defense team. The last witness who will testify in November is the pathologist who performed the autopsies. She will testify whether there were traces of smoke in the lungs of the family members. title: Land Reform - Expropriation: The Final Act
oneLiner: Emotions recently ran high at a meeting between Police Minister Bheki Cele, farmers, and farm dwellers in Normandien in northern KwaZulu-Natal. Cele met with the farming community over concerns about
summary:
Farmers in KZN blame the department of land reform for the friction in the region. According to farmers of different races, specifically the tenure claimants are a thorn in their flesh. They also lay the spate of stock thefts and farm arson in the area at the door of these claimants. Poor policing and lack of police resources also feature. A person living on a farm can for instance claim tenancy if they can prove their family has lived on that land for longer than a certain amount of time. Yet farmers say, the department requires very little proof before they register a claim. There is also a massive disconnect between the department and SAPS with SAPS “often claiming they can’t arrest.” Ex-rugby player Anton Pitout (43) has tried to register more than ten cases against the Macu-family living on his farm Elandsklip (in the Normandien-area of Northern KZN). “I have tried opening cases for assault, intimidation and contempt of court. SAPS find a different excuse to not register the cases every time.” Of these cases, only one (for assault) is presently open. In one such case, Pitout claims he was assaulted by the Macu-family. He took a video of part of the assault. When he approached his local police, he was told they couldn’t open the case because he couldn’t prove it was him taking the video. Pitout spent R140 000 last year in order to get an interdict to stop the Macu-family chasing their goats into his crops. Since then nothing has changed. Sipho Hadebe (72) bought his farm in the same area with no government assistance. Hadebe says farmers of all races work together, but the tenant claimants and politicians “from outside” make things difficult. “Corruption has eaten all the money. Now they are coming for the farms. This government will turn Normandien into Somalia.”Abu Docrat (32) claims a local politician built a house on a part of his land and gave it to the care taker of a local school. Docrat farms cattle and sheep on just over a 1000 hectares in Normandien

Farmers of all class, race and economic status claim the Dept of Land Reform is driving a wedge between South Africans in rural KZN with the tenure claim system that is not working, leaving residents with more questions than answers.

title: The Borderless War
oneLiner: The border between Lesotho and the Eastern Free State has disintegrated to such an extent that, in places, it no longer exists.
summary:
South Africans living in small towns along the Eastern Free State’s border with Lesotho are under severe pressure resulting from the disappearing border. Farm attacks, stock theft (and at least one kidnapping) are real threats in this almost frontier part of the province. The Free State shares a border of approximately 900km with its mountainous neighbour. How much is compromised? During a recent visit it was noted that some parts of the fence have totally disappeared. ***The fence is non-existent due to part of it being stolen, criminals moving over the border vandalise, break and cut the fence as well. The entire border fence is damaged and entirely gone in some places. In one part, on top of Langberg (Near Boesmanskop) a local farmer has erected a gate in the fence. He claims smugglers of stolen vehicles destroy the fence so often, he was left with no other choice. I spoke to farmers, white and black, last week and the consensus was that the Lesotho border has in fact moved. Citizens of Lesotho are openly moving their animals to grazing in South Africa. In Wepener, the Lesotho-cattle graze up to the main road. Their Lesotho cattle herders wrapped in traditional blankets and armed with cellphones. Locals say some taxi routes lead straight over the border and no passport is ever shown or checked. According to statistics provided by Free State Agriculture, a mere 13 small towns along the border (including 5 in Qwa-Qwa) reported 20% of all the stock theft cases in the entire province for the period of 1 April to 30 June. In the last six weeks, 20 veldfires was allegedly set around the towns, Hobhouse, Vanstadensrus and Zastron. ***The Freestate agriculture association alleges that the Lesotho locals are purposely setting the fires, their motives are unknown.

*We shoot footage of a normal farmgate that was erected in the border fence. *Drone and/or heli footage of the border *Incredible footage of the Eastern Free State landscape. *interviews with victims of violent crimes allegedly perpetrated by citizens of Lesotho.

The five-part documentary series, to be broadcast on M-Net, will debut on Sunday, October 4 (6pm) and conclude on November 1, on the eve of the one-year anniversary. The famous triumph remains a powerful memory, but the story behind the famous win is perhaps even more remarkable. SuperSport was granted unprecedented access to the Springboks both in the build-up and during the tournament which helped produce incredible behind-the-scenes footage that goes to the heart of what it took to claim the Webb Ellis Cup last November. “Chasing the Sun” is no ordinary story. It is a story about changing fortunes and changing mindsets, about pressure and hope, about recognising the power of inspiration, and learning what representation truly means. The moving documentary charts the Boks’ rise from dejection and under-performance to the pinnacle of international rugby, so vividly demonstrated when captain Siya Kolisi lifted the trophy in Tokyo. With unprecedented access and exclusive contributions from coaching staff, players and commentators, the documentary is the story of how a team, a nation and the world came to discover that we are all indeed stronger together. “Chasing the Sun” is infused with humour, technical insights and emotional engagement that will reveal the Springboks like never before.

title: George Bizos Obit
summary: George Bizos Obit George Bizoz passed away on 9th September this week President Cyril Ramaphosa announced the death in a televised news briefing. No cause was given, but he said Mr. Bizos’s health had recently begun to fail. Over a long and combative career, Mr. Bizos was one of only a handful of lawyers who sought redress for victims of racial separation through the very legal system that sanctioned it. While deeply flawed by the pervasive prejudice of the times, South Africa’s legal establishment did offer some slim protection to the accused under a white minority regime that liked to boast of a commitment to Western values. While many of his trials were fought in the glare of publicity, which he often sought to exploit, Mr. Bizos claimed a particular contribution to the destiny of his adoptive land by urging Mr. Mandela to insert three words — “if needs be” — into his oft-cited address from the dock at the so-called Rivonia trial of leaders of the African National Congress in the early 1960s. In his first draft, Mr. Bizos said, Mr. Mandela had written that he was prepared to die for “the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities.” Indeed, from 2012 to 2015 he was among the lawyers who represented the familie of Marikana — bloodletting that he likened to atrocities of the apartheid era. who died in police custody in 1977.

title: It's a baby Pangolin!
oneLiner: A miracle baby pangolin has been born - the first to survive in captivity.
summary:
Niall Beddy and his team has been monitoring Ally’s movements and checking up on her condition since she was released, and part of this process involves setting camera traps outside of her favourite burrows to record movement and behaviour patterns. We are extremely grateful to the Into the Wilderness Podcast series posted by Byron Pace for the kind donation of these expensive trail cams. We are very aware that continuous disturbances from us could have caused her distress and impacted her pregnancy and motherhood or cause her to leave the region. Camera traps are ideal for monitoring her progress without unnecessary disturbance. It was in one of these recordings that we noticed her new-born pup. This is the first time we have a record of an African pangolin successfully giving birth after being retrieved out of the illegal wildlife trade and being released back into the wild. We are a coalition of proud aunts and uncles, with this first in our history - a new pangolin born free! ​ Excellent cooperation between the Johannesburg Wildlife Veterinary Hospital, the African Pangolin Working Group, the South African Police Services Endangered Species Unit, the Limpopo Department of Economic Development, Environment and Tourism, the Department of Environmental, Forestry and Fisheries and private game farm owners have made this truly wonderful and amazing event possible and we are sincerely and truly grateful to this fantastic teamwork and rejoice in celebrating the arrival of a new pangolin pup.

On the 25th of April 2020, a pangolin was retrieved out of the illegal trade in an intelligence-driven operation by the South African Police Service (SAPS) Endangered Species Unit. Pangolins retrieved from the trade are given names of association with their retrieval location or circumstances, and this one was named Ally. In Ally’s case, her name was derived from her rescue location - the Alldays region of Limpopo Province, South Africa. She was transported by the Limpopo Department of Economic Development Environment and Tourism (LEDET) to Dr Xander de Kock, a veterinary surgeon in Polokwane. Dr de Kock phoned the acknowledged expert in the field of pangolin medicine, Dr Karin Lourens from the Johannesburg Wildlife Veterinary Hospital (JWVH). Dr K immediately left for Polokwane and arrived just before 20:00 on that Saturday evening. She has treated more than 100 Temminck’s pangolin and immediately assisted in stabilizing Ally, who was dehydrated and underweight. During an abdominal ultrasound, Dr de Kock established that Ally was pregnant, which made her treatment and recovery even more urgent. Pregnant pangolins are very rarely seen by researchers and vets, and there are no studies or documentation on the stages of development of pangolin foetuses. Because of this, the doctors had no way to determine the age of the foetus, but they could detect a normal, regular heartbeat. Once Ally was stabilized, Dr K transported her back to a secure location in Johannesburg, arriving in the early hours of Sunday morning. Ally’s road to freedom had begun. Pangolins retrieved out of the illegal wildlife trade are all compromised, with the level of compromise varying between individuals. The trauma is both physical and mental and often complicated by hidden conditions like pneumonia. Ally was no different. Not only was she also suffering from pneumonia, but she had an unborn pup to keep healthy. The news of her pregnancy was both happy and sad for the staff at the hospital as a new life is always wonderful, but the risk of Ally aborting due to stress was great. She was slowly nursed back to health, with regular blood tests, CT scans to make sure her lungs were healing as well as ultrasounds to ensure the pup was developing normally. A few days after her arrival she was stable enough to be taken out to forage – Temminck’s pangolins don’t eat in captivity; they only eat live ants and termites that they find by themselves while taken out on supervised foraging excursions. Ally’s improvement over the first week was marked. She became more confident and finally started behaving like a normal, healthy pangolin. Her lungs had cleared, and she had gained sufficient weight for Dr K to clear her for release. Ally was discharged from the JWVH on the 13th of May 2020 and moved up to her selected release site in the Limpopo Valley on the norther border of South Africa with Zimbabwe. Francois Meyer, the African Pangolin Working Group’s Limpopo Field Manager was tasked with managing this delicate release process. All our releases are facilitated processes; designed to slowly introduce retrieved pangolins into their new environments. In Ally’s case it included making certain she had access to sufficient quantities of her desired species of ants and termites and suitable refuge sites. She was fitted with two types of transmitters to ensure efficient post-release monitoring. The first was a VHF transmitter for fine-scaled tracking and the second, a satellite transmitter to locate her should she move out of the 3 km range of the VHF tags. Both tags were attached dorsally to her scales. With these, we will attempt to monitor her well-being for a year or more. Although it was confirmed that Ally was pregnant during veterinary care, we were still unsure on when exactly she would give birth. One thing was certain though, is that we did not want her to give birth during care or during the release protocol, as this would only place additional stress on her and her unborn pup. The release team made sure to adapt all our protocols to maximize a hands-off approach and to ensure that stress on Ally was kept to a minimum. Initially her release had us a bit worried, as she was displaying possible stress behaviour and we were worried that she might not adapt and settle down to the selected release site. Our main concern was the was “fleeing” out of the area, which would be an indication of an extremely stressed animal. Upon observing her behaviour and taking frequent body weight readings, we actually found the opposite. She was definitely foraging effectively and maintaining a constant body weight. With her movement behaviour however, it was clear that she was looking for more familiar habitat, and this is something we had to take into consideration before her final release. After careful consideration on our options we decided to take a risk and move her to a slightly different area upon the reserve, and this risk immediately paid off! Ally showed all the signs we were hoping to see in a successful release. She fed on a high diversity of ant species, she gained body weight, she found sufficient shelter and she was showing typical pangolin settling behaviour. In the following few days, we monitored her behaviour and general signs of health. Once we were satisfied that she was indeed adapting well, we started to reduce our presence within her new territory, only stepping in to collect necessary data for our research. The success of Ally’s release emphasizes the importance of proficient release teams and that of post-release monitoring.

title: Preventing the next pandemic

summary:

Disease X would “have a mortality rate higher than a season flu but [one that] would spread as easily as the flu…. It would shake financial markets even before it achieved pandemic status.” Sound familiar? The last few decades have seen an acceleration in outbreaks of known and new diseases. Zoonotic infections (diseases that 'spill over' from animals to humans) and especially viruses have been identified as a growing threat. 60% of human diseases come from animals and 75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic. There is a 'spill-over' event 1-2 times per year: an increase of 2-3 times what it was 40 years ago. Around the world, virologists have been raising the red flag about the ways in which our overpopulated, environmentally compromised

title: The Death of Soil
oneLiner: It's reported that soil in the U.S and Europe has between 30 and 40 years of fertility left, so how do we ensure we're able to feed ourselves if our farmers no longer can?
summary:
It's hard to keep up with the mounting crises threatening our planet- both present and future. Epidemics, climate change, over-population; has there been another generation that's faced as many existential challenges? Well, it would appear we need to add another to that growing list: the death of soil. It's not a new phenomenon. People have been warning for years that the intense and unrelenting use of cropland associated with industrial-scale farmland is robbing the soil of the nutrients it needs to sustain life. Nor is there consensus on when exactly the earth will say "this far and no further". But the Covid 19 crisis has brought into sharp relief the need to re-evaluate our relationship with the planet and how our actions - shaped as they might be by the noble intention to provide food, for example - are having devastating impacts.

We need to find a different way of producing food if we're to stem some of the damage being done to the planet. The impact of pesticides on insect life and water sources is well-documented, as is the effect on soil fertility of "over-farming". These challenges aren't new, but the current Covid 19 epidemic has, in the minds of those with an eye on the bigger picture, re-emphasised a need to re-evaluate our relationship with the plant and what we demand of it. As difficult as it might be to focus on other crises given the turmoil created by the current one, we have a unique opportunity to reflect on the urgent action required to avoid the worst effects of human behaviour and how many people have already taken on the challenge.

title: Remembering Joseph Shabalala
oneLiner: Carte Blanche celebrates the life of Ladysmith Black Mambazo founder, Joseph Shabalala
summary:
Joseph Shabalala was born on 28 August 1941 in Ladysmith, and grew up on a farm with his six siblings, until he left aged 17 to seek work in Durban. After spending time singing in the Durban Choir and an isicathamiya group called The Highlanders, he formed his own group and named it after his home town. According to the group's webpage, the word 'black' referred to the ox, the strongest of farm animals, and the word 'mambazo' meaning axe referred to the group's vocal strength which won them success. Ladysmith Black Mambazo has always emphasised the preservation of culture through music. Their style is based on isicathamiya, a genre that developed among the migrant workers on South Africa's mines. Their mainstream success has meant that listeners around the world have been exposed to black South African voices and music, and contributed to awareness of the inequality and brutality of apartheid. The group was recognised by Nelson Mandela, who asked them to travel to Oslo with him to receive his Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. They also sang at his inauguration in 1994.

Joseph Shabalala passed away on 11 February 2020 aged 78. He was the founder of the legendary South African male choral group, Ladysmith Black Mambazo, which he established in the early 1960s as a young factory worker. Over the decades until his retirement in 2014, he led the group from strength to strength, recording with international artists at the height of apartheid, winning multiple Grammy Awards, and being declared South Africa's Cultural Ambassadors to the World by Nelson Mandela. We celebrate a musical phenomenon.

title: Dumbo : The Albino Elephant calf
oneLiner: Rescued from a snare trap near Kruger in January this year ( she had been trapped for about 4 days) , Khanyisa is a rare albino elephant calf who is stealing the hearts of people
summary:
Wildlife vets Dr. Peter Rogers of Provet Wildlife Services has continued to assist in attending to Khanyisa’s wounds, check-ups, and fluid and vitamin administrations. 2 With any elephant calf, their delicate nature has proven them to be one of the most difficult wild animals to hand-rear. Our team are facing the additional challenge of Khanyisa’s severe wounds and albinism. So each day her health continues to improve, is a victory. Three weeks have passed since she has been in HERD's care, and Khanyisa continues to improve each day, her wounds are healing, her eyes are bright and she is very alert and inquisitive. She arrived weighing 124KG and her weight on 28 January was 138KG, a welcomed 14KG weight gain. She is an incredibly brave and resilient little elephant, and she has captured our hearts and of many around the world too. The proximity of the neighbouring adult Jabulani Herd have been reassuring to the little one, and once she has fully healed, we will start with the reintegration process with her new family, under the guidance of an expert elephant advisory team.

On 6 January 2020, HERD received a four-month-old female albino elephant that was found trapped in a snare with severe injuries. Her wounds indicated that she had been trying desperately to free herself for a few days. She had severe lacerations around the back of her ears and neck that stretched around her mouth and cheeks. The top section of her right ear had been sliced off. There was no sign of her herd anywhere. The elephant was first taken into the care of the team at Care for Wild Rhino Sanctuary in Mpumalanga. She was stable, but her injuries were extensive. Their veterinary team attended to the calf's wounds as our HERD elephant care team departed immediately to assist in caring for her that vital first night, ahead of transporting her to HERD in Limpopo Province. HERD Founder, Adine Roode and wildlife vet, Ben Muller, joined them the next morning, once all correct permits were in place, to collect the calf and transfer her to HERD. It was a three-hour journey. By the evening of 7 January, the injured calf arrived safely at HERD in the Kapama Private Game Reserve, the elephant settled in quickly, with Lammie, HERD’s resident companion sheep for company. As an albino, the elephant is more visible in the bush, and thus susceptible to attacks by predators. It also means that her eyes are more sensitive to light. However, albino elephants have been known to survive in the wild. Her first morning at HERD, the young calf took her first walk in the early morning light, and Adine decided to name her "Sunshine". Dr. Rogers suggested the closest translation in the local Shona language is "Khanyisa", meaning “Light/Sunshine”.

title: Unleash the hounds
oneLiner: With an outstanding record of 145 arrests and 53 guns confiscated, we meet the K9 team making an incredible difference to the fight against rhino poaching in the Kruger National Park.
summary:
Free-running pack hounds are a new and extremely useful tool in the anti-poaching arena, and the current pilot-program's successes speak for themselves. Except for the fact that the Texas hounds run unleashed, they have also been specifically trained to be aggressive, which normal scent dogs are not trained for. The Texas hounds have been taught to not only track down a poacher, but also attack, disarm and keep them at bay. The thinking is that a poacher, faced with a pack of attacking dogs, will drop his gun and climb a tree, giving law enforcement the chance to go in and make an arrest.

In 2017, Theresa Sowry, CEO of the South African Wildlife College, a wildlife training and management facility based near Kruger, visited dog trainer Joe Braman in Texas, USA. She had heard of his aggressive free-running pack dogs, Texas Coonhounds, used in law enforcement to track down escaped prisoners. While tracking dogs have been used in the Kruger before in the fight against rhino poaching, the animals were leashed and paired with human handlers. They were ultimately too slow to catch the poachers. But the Texas hounds operate very differently - they are sent after poachers unleashed, running in a pack, where they will signal the scent to each other in yips and yelps, and not stop until they've either caught their prey or run themselves into complete exhaustion. The pilot program currently running in the Kruger has had huge success with 145 arrests to date - a massive spike in the number of arrests since the program started running.

title: Dry Ice: In the Belly of the Climate Change Beast.
oneLiner: Carte Blanche ventures to the world's most northerly town, just an hour's flight from the North Pole yet warming at twice the rate of anywhere else on the planet.
summary:
The Norwegian town of Longyearbyen is closer to the North Pole than it is to Oslo. The landscape is icy, unforgiving. For a significant part of the year, the sun never rises. It's home to about 2000 people who live in a state of semi-permanence: it's not an environment conducive to making long-term plans - and that's probably truer now than ever. The impact of climate change is being felt more acutely in the Arctic; it's heating quicker here than anywhere else on the plant. That makes Longyearbyen the planet's fastest warming town. Isolated and unusual, it's a window into our future. We'll film the so-called Doomsday Vault, an initiative aimed at preserving the seeds of most if not all of the world's known plant species in anticipation of a mass extinction event. We'll visit a husky farm to hear how their sleds can no longer be used as effectively because of the shrinking ice, and we'll speak to locals about how their lives are changing with the climate.

It's a well-worn phrase in global warming circles: what happens in the Arctic, doesn't stay in the Arctic. Changes to its climate have an impact on global conditions - yes, even as far away as South Africa. So it should be a concern to all of us that the impacts of climate change are now hard to ignore, particularly in places like Longyearbyen - the most northerly town on the planet. Thawing permafrost, shrinking ice, erratic snowfalls: all are in plain sight in this town where average temperatures have risen four degrees from pre-industrial times.

title: Medical Robots
oneLiner: Would you like to have a robot cut into your bones or perform heart surgery, it's not just science fiction, medical robots are making waves right here in South African operating theatres.
summary:
Robotic surgery first became popular in the 1980s. The first surgery was performed in 1985 when a robot was used to improve precision in neurosurgical biopsies and the da Vinci system was used for prostate surgery. Surgery is the most commonly used robotic application in healthcare. Sadly South Africa has been lagging behind, that is until recently. In December last year Dr Faizel Lorgat at the Christiaan Barnard Memorial hospital in Cape Town, an interventional cardiologist succesfully completed the firsts robotic coronary angioplasties in Africa. In Johannesburg, Dr Chris McCready, performed the first state-of-the-art robotic knee replacement operation. This technology could signal a new era in personalised joint replacement.

Soon autonomous robots could be a regular member of any hospital's medical staff, performing duties from taking a patient's pulse and scanning vital signs, to reading case notes and even performing surgery. Some might say thats just science fiction but doctor controlled-robots already have a massive presence in the medical field, and demand for the less invasive, more patient tailored, doctor controlled procedures are growing. Now, in a first in Africa , two South African doctors are performing robotic-assisted total knee replacements and robotic coronary angioplaties.
