title: Absolute right of inheritance
oneLiner: Private wills will come under the spotlight in a ‘world first’ matter when the ConCourt have to decide on the ‘absolute right of inheritance’ for adopted children and ‘male only’ heirs. We
summary:
The first case involves the inheritance rights of adult adoptees. In the other, five sisters have challenged a “males only” clause in their great-grandfather’s will. Both challenges started in the Cape Town high court, but were unsuccessful. Then the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) failed to come to their aid. But the ConCourt has consolidated the two cases and directed the parties to submit arguments on why it should grant leave to appeal as well as the merits of both matters. There are very few grounds on which to challenge a private will in South Africa (and in fact worldwide). Essentially a person can leave their money and property to whoever they want. Usually challenges are made on allegations that the person was unduly influenced, or was not sane at the time of writing the will. But, as far as we know - and what the papers say in these two matters - the “constitutionality” of a private will has never been tested before. The argument in both these cases is that the right of someone to leave their money to whoever they wish is not “absolute” and should be balanced against equality provisions in the Bill of Rights and the Constitution.

Private wills – as opposed to charitable trusts – are considered sacrosanct, not only in South Africa but the world over. As long as a person is of “sound mind” and not financially responsible for any minor children, they are legally entitled to pass on their assets to whoever they please and can disinherit on a whim. But in a constitutional dispensation this is not an “absolute right” and must be balanced against equality, it has been argued in two matters that will now come before the Constitutional Court in February.

title: Unlawful Arrests
oneLiner: .....what you need to know about unlawful arrests in South Africa
summary:
Unlawful arrest and detention are very common in South Africa. So much so that over the last few years SAPS had to pay out in excess of R1,5 billion rand in claims for this, with another R30 billion in claims pending. It also now transpires that many of these wrongful arrests have been encouraged by illegal instructions from a wide variety of role players within the Police – from divisional commanders to unit commanders. They among other things, set quotas and issued instructions to police on the ground to make arrests which are clearly unlawful. (there are very strict laws governing arrest as it is seen as a measure of last resort). A recent circular by the National Commissioner has now prohibited these instructions (there is a whole list he mentions), and the primary motivation is the recent Constitutional Court ruling that SAPS is responsible for the whole time a person remains in unlawful arrest. This could double or triple the liability of the Minister of Police. The quantum of the claims dwindles into insignificance if the legal costs are added to the picture.

An issue that affect each and everyone in South Africa

title: DISARMING CITIZENS: SA, Lay Down Your Weapons
oneLiner: This week Minister of Police Bheki Cele announced that South Africans should not own firearms. But crime is endemic to every day life in South Africa, is this the solution that will make already defen
summary:
South Africa is rated as 127th out of 163 countries as most violent. In many places the crime and murder rates outstrip some war zones. The amendments to the firearms control act, have far reaching repercussions, which include the security industry, Hunting licences the sporting sector, as well as individual rights. Many South African’s rely on private security companies for safety, and their firearms quotas will also be limited under the proposed amendments, which means that an overburdened police service will be tasked with protecting ordinary people. A leaked version of the draft amended act was circulated, which government has denied is the final version and says it is one of many drafts. How will removing the rights of South African’s to own a weapon for self defence, curb crime? The amendment of the act does not tackle illegal firearms that are in circulation and used to commit many crimes. We challenge Minister Bheki Cele to consider the impact on South Africa’s spiral of crime when there is less armed defence against it.

In his announcement this week Minister Bheki Cele said that legislation was being looked at with regards to amending the Firearms Control Act. The Confederations of Hunting South Africa, says the amendments have been on the cards since 2011 and nothing has happened so far. They also say that limiting or removing a citizen’s rights to defend themselves has sinister overtones.

Over the next year they identified major water leaks and repaired them , in one incident saving 286 000 litres of purified water that was just left to run back into the river which originated at the Municipal officers and they knew about for 9 months but did nothing about. They restored water to the town’s reservoir and bought chemicals to purify the water to the tune of R4.4 million, half of this has been recouped from COGDA . On Thursday and Fridays they remove the rubbish from the town, including the townships and suburbs using private vehicles, paying 15 staff to collect the rubbish and paying for the petrol themselves. Now the residents have bought tar and are beginning to fix the potholes themselves.

Last year Carte Blanche exposed the complete collapse of the Harrismith Municipality or Maluti-A- Phofung due to political corruption. Its been under administration for the last two years and the citizens of Harrismith are desperate, they regularly don’t have water or electricity or refuse removal due to lack of maintenance or funds for chemicals or spare parts to maintain the water supply. Businesses are closing down and residents are leaving because of the shocking state of disrepair and unemployment is on the rise. At the beginning of 2019 a group of Harrismith residents from across town got together and stepped in to try and take back control of basic services. It began with the town’s water supply. Known as the Harrismith Water heroes they describe themselves as a non-political non- racial organization.

title: Eastern Cape Drought
oneLiner: The Eastern Cape is in the grips of one of the worst droughts in living memory...
summary:
The Eastern Cape is said to experience the worst drought in living memory. And although some rain (below average) has fallen in the Eastern part of the province the Western region has had no relief. The Chris Hani District municipality has announced water rationing and many smaller towns and villages are relying on borehole water as dams are drying up. Organisations like Gift of the Givers are working tirelessly to gift water to the desperate regions, but its simply not enough and they cannot keep up with the demand. On top of that Climate and water experts say that there's no real relief on its way. The entire province is just said to become hotter and dryer in the future. The continued use of underground water sources is not sustainable as many farmers have reported their boreholes and windpumps drying up. The biggest concern for the province is that the Eastern Cape has by far the largest numbers of livestock in the country. Without water, agriculture cannot continue as normal, which affects the entire economy of the region, but also has a bigger ripple effect on the country as a whole. According to SA Statistics 2017, 24% of the country’s cattle, 38% of the goats, 29% of all the sheep within South Africa, are farmed in the Eastern Cape. Approximately one third of the Province is extremely/severely dry, with one third being moderately dry and one third being near normal. This drought in these areas is affecting about 1 440 commercial farmers, 8 700 smallholder farmers and about 55 000 subsistence farmers. These farmers collectively support in the region of 405 200 direct dependents, by means of primary agriculture.

We take a trip to the Western parts of the Eastern Cape where the current drought has taken its toll on the humans, the wildlife and agriculture in the region. The area has had no rain for more than 5 years. The Eastern Cape straddles an area of 16 857 million hectares with a population of 6.5 million, mostly rural. This is the poorest of the nine provinces and the knock-on effect of the drought is having disastrous consequences. This week the Chris Hani District Municipality started imposing water rationing as dam levels are simply too low, Many smaller towns like Butterworth have been faced with a Day Zero scenario months ago.

title: Profile: Brad Binder
oneLiner: We meet 24 year old South African Brad Binder, who is about to enter the world's premier motorcycle racing spectacle, the MotoGP series
summary:
Unlike other motorcycle racing classes where riders compete on modified factory spec machines, MotoGP bikes are thoroughbred racing motorcycles that would not be street legal or even available to purchase by the public. The MotoGP is to the motorcycle racing world what Formula 1 is to the car racing scene. Winning the MotoGP world championship literally means you're the fastest racer in the world, and the athletes competing here earn huge money to risk life and limb for the sport's ultimate honour. It's a truly unique achievement to be one of the chosen few to compete in the championship, because only the best of the best ever get anywhere near. For Binder it will not only be the biggest challenge of his racing career, he'll need to adapt fast to the whirlwind world of MotoGP - with millions of fans worldwide, massive television and sponsorship deals and the top manufacturer's expecting only the best from their riders. Will he stand up to the pressure?

The young South African Brad Binder is the first local rider to be offered a spot in the sought after Moto Grand Prix series in the sport's modern era. And judging from his last few years in the junior classes, experts agree that Binder has what it takes to compete against racing legends like Valentino Rossi and Marc Marquez. Before he enters the gruelling 2020 season, which will see riders compete in 20 races in 19 different countries across the globe, he'll be spending a few days in South Africa over the Christmas period, where on the 10th of December we can have two hours out of his busy schedule to interview him.

title: SAA Crash Landing?
oneLiner: SAA could be in business rescue, a first time for a State owned enterprise, but how can it avoid insolvency, when the airline is making a loss of over 500 000 rand a minute?
summary:
According to the Solidarity union, fly South African Airways and lose the country cash. How did we get to such a state that grounding all the SAA flights could actually save us money? Or should we listen to NUMSA that claims that the heart of the recent strike was not pay but a response to a deliberate plan to collapse the company to sell, and cover-up corruption... that management threatens workers with their levels of pay and their future employment, when the management are actually responsible for the collapse. So should the top be cleaned up and refreshed to renegotiate contracts and get the airline back on track? Or should Solidarity’s application for SAA to be placed under business rescue be implemented? But can the country take any view when there is a lack of recent financials coming out of SAA? The issues have mounted up to culminate in political intrigue and manoeuvring. However, all the while the economy of South Africa is being shattered, with the infighting within SAA and other SOEs at large threatening to bring the country and its people to an economic standstill.

With bailout after bailout over the years, Is SAA now the victim of a plot to have it sold off or is it indeed a failed enterprise dogged by corruption and over staffing? After an industrial dispute over pay that was settled with a payment rise in February next year, provided SAA has the money then to afford it, South African Airways has become less about passengers and travel than internal wrangling about where the bailout money went and why the push for privatisation. The blame for SAA’s financial woes is like a tennis match, between procurement corruption on the one hand, and over staffing on the other. Is it time for government to resign itself to privatisation, with the fallout of staff redundancies and the embezzlers of past tender money getting off the hook? Or can the organization be cleaned up under public management to fly the South African flag proudly once more?

title: HELD TO RANSOM - RANSOMWARE AND THE CITY
oneLiner: The shadow kill hackers almost brought the city of Johannesburg to a standstill. How can you protect your data from malicious cyber criminals
summary:
Ever heard of the Shadow Kill hackers? The Best 777 or Sun Pixel? They are all the names of Cyber criminals who take over computers, encrypt your data and demand a ransom normally in Bitcoins to unlock your data. Don’t pay and you could find your information out on the web for all to see and criminals to use. In October the City of Johannesburg was hit by the shadow Kill hackers who demanded R500 000 in Bitcoins to unencrypt the data of the entire city. This was their ransom note: “All your servers and data have been hacked. We have dozens of back doors inside your city. We have control of everything in your city.” The city came to a standstill but they say they did not pay, millions of users data was not compromised, and that international experts had worked around the clock to restore the situation. According to the latest report from Europol, Ransomware maintains its reign as the most widespread and financially damaging form of cyber- attack. Hundreds of businesses around South Africa quietly pay and move on, learn the lesson and keep their back up data off a server far away from the vulnerabilities of the internet.

title: GAUTENG SCHOOL PLACEMENTS
oneLiner: Meant to make school placement convenient and give learners access to schools that they previously could not attend, some parents say the Gauteng online system has failed them and their children.
summary:
Launched in May 2019 for the 2020 school year by the Gauteng Education MEC Panyaza Lesufi, the online system for school placements was meant to allow pupils to attend schools in areas that were previously inaccessible by increasing the feeder radius from a historic 5km distance to 30km. This came after the Constitutional Court ruled in favour of Lesufi's bid to address apartheid spatial planning by expanding the radius in 2016. The department then took the time that followed to determine the feeding zones and eventually launched the online system in May 2019. Some parents complain that they have been placed at schools they did not prefer while others have received no placement offers at all. On the other hand, the department says thousands of parents have not accepted the placement offers. We also speak to key sector players including education specialists and organisations opposed to the system. In fact, on Tuesday, AfriForum launched its petition to remove Panyaza Lesufi as the Gauteng MEC for Education mainly due to Lesufi's handling of the registration process which is reported to have left 14 000 grade 1 and 8 pupils without school placement. What does this mean for unplaced scholars in the coming year? What adjustments will parents and scholars have to make in reaction to being accepted at schools that they did not plan for?

We track the progress of the controversial Gauteng online school placement system from the perspective of parents.

Since it first started sitting in August 2018, there have been so many huge headlines to come out of the Zondo Commission that have shown the extent of State Capture. But this daily drip-drip of news has almost in a way desensitised the average South African citizen from the shocking stories that have come out of the commission. 16 months since it's inception, it's time to take a look back at what has been accomplished thus far. What has been the most important information to have emerged from witness testimony. Who have been the most important people to have made submissions at the commission, from the whistleblowers to the people who’ve been accused in engaging in State Capture. How long before the commission ends and what will be done with the evidence gathered? For the piece we will interview the people such as Thuli Madonsela, journalists who’ve been covering the story, as well as a spokesmen from organisations like Corruption Watch. Finally we will also obtain objective and legal analysis from constitutional law professor Pierre De Vos. We will provide insight into the effectiveness of the commission’s work to date. How long is the commission expected to sit for and when can we expect a final report? Are Commissions of Inquiry effective in South Africa or do they merely whitewash (Seriti & Farlam Commission for example), What will be done with the evidence gathered by the Commission? Will anyone be charged and prosecuted?

The Zondo Commission into State Capture is one of the most important commissions in the history of South Africa's democracy but 16 months since it first started sitting, how effective has it been?

title: Rogue Gas Dealers
oneLiner: We expose and confront the numerous rogue gas dealers putting the lives of the public and their employees at risk in the illicit gas trade in the suburbs of Johannesburg.
summary:
Basically rogue gas dealers fill any cylinders they can get their hands on in the industry. They are not authorised to fill these cylinders. They DO NOT do any safety checks (testing) on the cylinders, yet they fill them up and sell to customers ‘unchecked’ cylinders. Rogues do not do any integrity testing on the cylinders, and why should they, the cylinders do not belong to them, they belong to AFROX, EASIGAS, ORYX, TOTAL, etc etc. It is only these major companies that can do the integrity testing on their cylinders, as they have the proper equipment and trained personnel. There are reputable dealers buying and selling illegal gas. Majority of the public do not know the dangers involved in purchasing these illegally filled cylinders, although plenty people do know the difference and choose to buy it as they are cheap cheap cheap. Private Investigator Johan Myburg has been involved in the industry for the past 24 years - and says that since our last insert the illicit industry has kept growing. This is in part due to a larger demand for gas as the SA market is growing constantly - especially with the current electricity crisis. He also says because of poor enforcement from the authorities, organised crime syndicates have now taken control of much of the illegal trade. And because they don't have their own cylinders to use, the major gas companies are now targets, where armed robbers will break into plants, hold up security guards at gunpoint, and literally steal hundreds and in one case more than a thousand cylinders. (We have obtained footage of a break in at a plant called SIMS Gas) (Legal gas retailers, the small shops in malls etc, are afraid to go on camera because of the syndicates, and threats that some of them have received when outing rogues on social media).

Most members of the public would never realise they are exchanging their home/business gas cylinders for unsafe ones. And while some people will purposely buy illegally filled gas because its cheaper, many other seemingly legit dealers are selling gas they bought on the cheap for the regular retail prices. SO not only is the public being handed a possible ticking time bomb, they are also being ripped off. General retailers, who are buying their gas legally from authorised vendors, are feeling the pinch as they can't compete with rogue gas suppliers.

title: DNA Database
oneLiner: What if you were forced to give your DNA to ensure that South Africa can rid itself of crime?
summary:
Tens of thousands of dangerous convicts are being released from prison each year but not all of their DNA profiles have been recorded. These profiles would enable law enforcement to potentially match their DNA to other crimes they may have committed, cold cases, as well as any crimes committed by the same offender in future. The Department of Correctional Services' figures show that more than 70,000 convicts were released or paroled last year. In addition, many schedule eight offenders — those convicted of murder, culpable homicide, rape, kidnapping, sexual offences against children, human trafficking, assault, robbery and arson — were released without the department collecting their DNA profiles. Cele has failed to sign the Criminal Law (Forensic Procedures) Amendment Bill, drawn up last year, which would allow correctional services officials to take samples of a backlog of 46,727 schedule 8 criminals’ DNA who remain untested. Instead, Cele has declined to sign the amendment bill in favour of moving towards an unprecedented national population DNA database that would require every South African citizen to have a DNA test by way of a buccal (saliva) test. This would then be the mandate of the Department of Home Affairs. Cele's refusal to sign the amendment bill indicates a change of heart since his foreward in the DNA Ethics and Oversight Board's annual report in September last year, in which he wrote that "focus will also be placed on finalising the amendment to the DNA Act which aims to address shortcomings related to the retrospective sampling of offenders serving a sentence for [serious crimes]”. Cele had at that time agreed that the amendment was needed after a two-year "transitional period" expired.

Well this may be South Africa's future and what Police Minister Bheki Cele wants. So what's the problem? They current CRIMINAL DNA database hasn't even completed the testing of Schedule 8 offenders and Cele has suspended that program while he waits to politicize the issue. 1. A backlog of 46,727 Schedule 8 offenders (highest level of danger) who were in jail before the DNA Act (2013) took effect, and therefore have been there for a minimum of 6 years, which shows these were serious crimes because a 6-year or longer sentence is fairly hefty in the SA context. It is not about all offenders - they are being tested when they are arrested or sentenced. It is about the backlog of Schedule 8s who are being paroled or released without being tested. 2. the constitutionality of Cele’s proposed national population DNA database (as opposed to a forensic one, which we have). No country in the world has managed to force every single innocent citizen to submit to DNA testing as it has been ruled unconstitutional. In SA, many experts say it would contravene the Bill of Rights; 3. Why Bheki Cele will not authorise the testing of the convicts while simultaneously exploring the total population DNA database idea; 4. It is about where the money - absolute minimum R5 billion - would come from, AND where is the R20 million that was meant to cover the convict backlog testing? I don’t know the answers re the money. IN the current climate of a veritable war on women and children, and with 58 murders and 114 reported rapes every day, unleashing a violent demographic upon the public without even taking their DNA fingerprint seems irresponsible at best, yet that is precisely what is happening. And the one man - police minister Bheki Cele - who can rectify this has declined to do so.

title: Hitched
oneLiner: Two cousins hitch hike half way around the world to convince Ellen to put them on her show
summary: When Josh and Luke (cousins) where 6 they watched a documentary about a mystical creature that lived in a Congolese jungle. Fast forward 20 odd years and they decided to take 500$ for 100 days and hitch hike to war torn Congo and see if this animal actually exists. Obviously it didn’t but they had the most insane ride regardless. After returning home they decided to do a second trip, this time the mission is to get onto the Ellen show. Again with almost no money they committed to a 7 month trip across Africa and Europe and into LA. They whole trip is being documented and almost become like a daily journal to Ellen. Sadly in 7 months Ellen never replied to all their messages, videos, hashtags. But they made it to LA and are currently camping near the beach still hoping to get onto Ellens couch. Their journey is extreme they do things that seem so insanely unsafe, but they just laugh and take every speed bump in their stride. This trip took them through Sudan, unrest in Ethiopia and subzero temps in a tent in Russia. Luke also got engaged along the way Everyone can learn something about life from the hitched boys. Even if its just that "It ain't about the destination, its about the journey"

title: Vuvuzela Men
oneLiner: In a country drowning under the weight of violence we have to celebrate the people who keep standing up and trying to help
summary: Isaac is 59 years old, 9 years ago he decided enough is enough he couldn’t just sit back and hear the screams of the women in his community, so he started a group of about 20 men to escort women safely to their transport every morning. He is the granddaddy in the group, the OG of the vuvuzela men Every morning at 3:30 Isaac sounds the Vuvuzela to let the community know that the patrol men’s shifts have started and then he collect his first group and safely escorts them to their transport. Armed only with a Taser and a flash light he escorts group after group until well after sunrise then he returns home and has breakfast with his wife and see’s his children off to school. Isaac has three daughters, he worries about their safety and the safety of all women in SA, which is why even if he never gets paid he will keep escorting these women every morning Paul is 45 years old and last year he was escorting his group of women when they intercepted some thugs trying to rob another group of women;. Phillip fought to protect his group and the strangers during the altercation he was shot in the stomach. But this hasn’t stopped him from continuing his service. Every morning once the Vuvuzela has been sounded he leaves his home meet to Isaac and start his shift. Although they are not heavily armed these men are feared in the community, as they have made arrests and brought people to justice. They work in conjunction with the SAPS in the area. title: Hospice
oneLiner: Holistic end-of-life care is about much more than just dispensing the right medication...
summary:
Hospice provides all-round holistic care for the terminally ill and their families. Although most Medical Aids cover palliative care as part of their plans, Hospice relies on donor funding as many of their patients come from previously disadvantaged backgrounds. They don't turn anyone away and offer the same professional high-quality of care to everyone, irrespective of their financial position. But funding is drying up. Hospice only gets about 10% of its funding from Government and for the rest they rely on the public and corporate world. Int he past 2 years 10 in-patient facilities have closed down because of a lack of funding. Hospice Wits (with satellite branch, Soweto) is no different. The Soweto branch's in-patient unit was closed down in 2018, but the effects on the community was devastating. So, this year the unit was re-launched, but it's future is hanging in the balance. Against this backdrop we meet the dedicated nurses and staff of Hospice and the invaluable services they offer. We speak to patients and their families who simply would not have coped without this assistance.

Many people associate Hospice with death, and by saying "yes" to Hospice they feel they're saying "yes" to death, but this is a perception that needs to change. Hospice is about much more than just dispensing medication and keeping the patient comfortable until they die. The organisation wants to be a part of the entire journey of someone being diagnosed with a terminal disease. The Organisation employs doctors, nurses, social workers, psychologists and spiritual councillors that can give holistic care to the patient and the entire family. Patients may be treated at their in-patient facilities or may be supported whilst being cared for in their own homes. Coming to terms with a terminal illness places a lot of stress on the entire family and this is where the emotional en physical support of Hospice staff becomes invaluable.

title: Desmond D'Sa and Kevin Kimwelle
oneLiner: Winner of the internationally prestigious Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014, Desmond D'Sa continues his decades long fight for environmental justice, especially in his South Durban hometown.
summary:
To keep up with what Desmond D’Sa is campaigning on would be a full time job in itself. Only this week he is in the news with The South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) with their appeal against a decision by the Department of Mineral Resources to grant Sasol and Italian multinational oil and gas company ENI environmental authorisation to explore for oil and gas along the North and South coasts of KwaZulu-Natal. Desmond’s bread and butter though is tacking the fallout from local industry waste that is acutely affecting the health of people in the local communities of Durban South. Under President Mandela, an extensive system of monitoring and reporting was set up to keep tags on the situation, but it collapsed and now D’Sa and his organizations have actioned their own systems including the detection of the levels of Benzene and recording and bringing to attention the levels of cancers like leukaemia in the area. Desmond D’Sa is at the forefront of the struggle to ensure a clean environment, for the people living and working in the midst of heavy industry, where environmental regulation is severely absent.

During Apartheid, Desmond and his family were uprooted from their home and dumped in an industry intensive area of South Durban. There he witnessed the environmental damage that can be caused by mishandled waste and embarked on a lifetime of campaigning for the now constitutionally protected right to a safe and clean environment. In 1996, he co-founded the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) which is still highly active today. Through his tireless work Desmond D'Sa came to the attention of the international environmental movement and won the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014 primarily for his unstinting opposition to the hazardous waste fallout from the Bulbul Drive landfill site and his monitoring and actions in "cancer valley", the South Durban basin notorious for its high incidences of leukaemia, asthma and bronchitis, due to toxic waste from the conglomerate of large scale industrial plants in the area. title: UCT and the Skeletons
summary: In the early 1920s, on a farm known as Kruisrivier on the Roggeveld escarpment near Sutherland in the Northern Cape, the landowner and his son dug up the skeletal remains of seven individuals, people who had worked the land. The farmer’s son, a medical student donated these individuals bones to the University of Cape Town for their medical school skeletal collection. In the following years he donated two more bodies. Almost a century later, while doing an archiving audit on the records in the skeletal collection, Dr Victoria Gibbon from UCT’s Division of Clinical Anatomy and Biological Anthropology discovered that a gross injustice had taken place: UCT had unethically obtained the skeletal remains of at least nine individuals, all of whom were San or Khoi. When Dr Victoria Gibbon was appointed curator of the University of Cape Town’s (UCT) skeletal collection in 2016, she never foresaw that the role would pave the way to one of the most extensive, significant and fulfilling projects of her career. Her first year of curatorship – coincided with important national conversations and initiatives around distinguishing between ethically and unethically obtained human remains within university and museum collections – proved to be a remarkable one indeed.

title: Bee Business - The Ethical Removal of Bees
oneLiner: What does it take to ethically relocate a hive of African honey bees?
summary:
It's Summer and honey bees are out in full force to do what they do best - make honey. But often a colony of bees will create a hive in a place that is not suitable according to humans. The African Honey Bee is fairly aggressive, and with the rise in bee allergies, most people do not want a hive on their properties - especially in urban area. Since the African Honey Bee is indigenous to South Africa and threatened, it is advisable to remove the hive and ethically relocate the bees. The problem is that there are a lot of companies out there without the necessary know-how on how to remove bees, so they use the wrong methods and simply dump the removed hive on a plot somewhere. In this case the bees have almost 0% chance of survival. Nico Grobler will show us how to do it the right way. Removing hives at night when most of the bees are in fact in the hive, resting. They make sure they move the queen bee, her nursery apiary and as many of the bees as possible to ensure the survival of the entire hive. Many Bee Removal Companies have a bad reputation. They charge R800 to remove bees, which they do in the day when much of the colony is out scouting for nectar. They often destroy the hive in the process, not taking care to protect the brood and the nursing apiaries. Hives are often just dumped on empty plots.

You have a honey bee hive on your property and would like them ethically relocated. You phone a Bee Removal company, but how sure are you that they know what they are doing? Do they effectively relocate the hive or does the entire colony simply die off because of Bad Bee Removal Practices? We team up with Nico Grobler of the Northern Beekeepers Association to see what some companies are doing wrong, and how it should be done.

summary:
Viagogo is an online event ticket sales platform. Its headquarters are in Switzerland and it operates in more than 160 countries across the globe. Ticket reselling in most countries is allowed if a small volume of tickets are sold and at cost price e.g. if a person has bought a ticket or two to an event they can no longer attend, it is acceptable for that person to resell the ticket. However, what Viagogo does is to go to reliable ticket sellers such as Computicket, buy tickets in bulk and essentially “sell out” the event. Thereafter Viagogo skyrockets the prices and resells the same tickets for exorbitant amounts.

We visit the Viagogo website and show viewers the flaws in the system and how exactly a buyer can end up paying as much as five times the value of an event ticket in some cases.

title: William Kentridge
oneLiner: We meet international acclaimed artist, William Kentridge, famous for his creative work in drawings, films, theatre and opera productions.
summary:
William Kentridge was born on April 28, 1955 in Johannesburg to the parents of prominent apartheid lawyers. Kentridge remembers the sense of indignation and rage at the dinner table that was very formative.“My father was a prominent lawyer with prominent cases. He represented the family of Steve Biko and inquest into his death to the Sharpeville massacre. He was a lawyer in the treason trial of Nelson Mandela and other ANC members”. Kentridge was captured in his own make-believe world as a child where drawing and play-acting was a metaphorical way of dealing with the political landscape and survive. “I did what all children do, and that is drew. And I simply forgot to stop, `` he remembers. Kentridge studied Political Science and African Studies before studying art at the Johannesburg Art Foundation until 1978. There he met South African artists like Dumile Feni, whose works greatly influenced his drawings. Already working as a set designer for film productions, in 1981 Kentridge moved to Paris where he trained under the renowned mime artist, Jacque Lecoq. He then began making his signature hand-drawn animated films, made by filming a drawing, making erasures and changes, then filming it again. He displayed his feelings about the two cities wryly in the title of his first animated film, "Johannesburg - Second Greatest City After Paris." "This is where I've lived for 55 years," he said, explaining how the city inspires him. "It is a city that deconstructs itself the whole time, it's busy erasing itself the way you erase a drawing." He admits to wondering why he has decided to make the city home. "There's certain sections of the city you drive down and think, why on earth do I choose to spend my days in this part of the world," he said. "And there are other days when you see extraordinary things and you think, this is remarkable."

William Kentridge is an artist of black and white, a printmaker first, who uses drawing, animation, film, theatre, sculpture, opera, and even tapestry, to make compelling works that interrogate some of the darkest corners of history and the human psyche. His practice is born out of a cross-fertilisation between mediums and genres and responsd to the legacies of colonialism and apartheid. His aesthetics are drawn from the medium of film’s own history from stop-frame animation to early special effects. Kentridge’s drawings, specifically the dynamism of an erased and redrawn mark, is an integral part of his expanded animation and filmmaking practice.

title: Heatwave Drought
oneLiner: As heat waves hit Gauteng, the water levels of the Vaal dam continue to drop... Will Gauteng have to face DAY ZERO in the near future?
summary:
It's October. It's hot and dusty in Gauteng. "When will the rains come?" is a question Gautengers impatiently ask around this time of year. Traditionally Farmers used President Paul Kruger's birthday (10 October) as the start of the rainy season, but with Climate Change the seasons are shifting and Gauteng's rain comes later and later. Add to that the incredible heatwaves and you would understand that some people are panicking about Gauteng's water supply. The Vaal dam has a very large surface area and water is rapidly evaporating. The levels are currently just above 50% compared to 81% during the same period last year. On top of that the Katse Dam, which feeds water to the Vaal System is alarmingly low - at 13%. And they are doing maintenance on the Lesotho Highlands Pipe networks, which means that additional water can only be pumped to SA from the end of November. In the meantime the weather forecast predicts less than average rainfall for the next few months and hotter temperatures than the average. All this is spelling doom for Gauteng's water supply. The Department of Water and Sanitation states that there is no reason to panic: “When we look at the Integrated Vaal River System, we see a combination of about 14 dams that primarily serve Gauteng and standing at about 73.7%. This is a decline, which is quite huge because about a week ago, we were standing at about 76%.”

The Katse Dam is standing at 13% and the Vaal dam is at about 50% and yet The Department of Water and Sanitation says there is no need to panic. And levels of the Vaal are said to drop further in light of the current heatwave across most of the country. Climate Experts are saying that we should expect below normal rainfall and higher than normal temperatures, which means that our dams will be losing more water, quicker. Yet there seems to be no sense of urgency amongst Government and municipalities. People are watering gardens and washing cars as if there is absolutely nothing to worry about. Spokesperson for the DWS, Sputnik Ratau said the Vaal Dam forms part of an integrated river system, which supplies water to the majority of residents in Gauteng as well as Eskom power stations, and taking all the dams in the system into account.

title: Scented Letters: Chernobyl's Babushkas
oneLiner: We get a glimpse into the daily lives of women who refused to abandon their homes after the world's most catastrophic nuclear disaster.
summary:
This insert takes the viewer inside one of the most contaminated places on the planet. It's an area 2400 square kilometers in size, designated an exclusion zone by the Soviets in 1986 and evacuated of its residents. But, as time has gone by, some people have returned. Some a lot sooner than others. Marusha Ilchenko is one of those people. Forced to leave shortly after the accident, she and her husband returned just a year later. He has since died, but she continues to eke out an existence as one of the ever shrinking number of people who refused to leave forever.

In a South African-tv first, Carte Blanche travels to the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, site of the world's worst nuclear disaster, to interview one of the area's so called self-settlers: a babushka who refused to abandon her home forever.

title: The Morality of Meat
oneLiner: We ask whether the time has come for all of us to give up eating meat to help save the planet.
summary:
This insert will examine one of the clarion calls of the global movement calling for stronger action to halt climate change: that, in order to reduce the levels of greenhouse gasses in our atmosphere, we need to stop eating meat. Granted, not all climate change activists are vegan but it's a lifestyle of world view with increasing influence. Whats-more, far from being easily-dismissed as the rantings of a group of hemp-wearing tree-huggers, they appear to have science on their side. Not only does animal agriculture contribute to mass deforestation and water consumption, but it's claimed it's directly responsible for a significant amount of methane and carbon di-oxide pollution. The vegan perspective is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore; and that's without even considering their arguments in favour of animal welfare. At the same time, the meat and dairy sectors, are fighting their corner. "Yes, there are rogue elements", they say. "But ours is an industry falsely accused of mistreating animals and being unwilling to become more sustainable". One such person is Abi Reader, a dairy farmer in Wales. In response to the onslaught, she is proactively marketing the dairy industry, the good that it does, and the relationship many farmers have with their herd. She's not afraid of controversy and speaks out strongly again militant veganism, an off-shoot of the movement we'll also dwell on in the insert. Along the way, we'll examine the science and ask whether ending meat production will have the impact vegans argue it will, or whether their voices are drowning out more meaningful discussions on the fossil fuel industry.

It's estimated that animal agriculture accounts for around 14% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Protests, increasingly frequent and vocal, are now targeting the sector as vociferously as the fossil fuel industry as they call for greater action on climate change. We take to the streets of London to hear from vegan protesters who've joined ranks with the Extinction Rebellion movement to have their voices heard. We also travel to rural Wales to hear the thoughts of a dairy farmer who feels the sector is misunderstood and - often - unfairly targeted.

title: The NHI Bill - can it deliver universal health care for South Africans?
oneLiner: This month the National Health Insurance Bill was introduced to Parliament, but will NHI be able to address health care provision inequality given the reality of the economic challenges facing SA?
summary:
So, if someone is now paying, say R 3500 for Medical Aid, and they know what they're covered for, what will be the difference under the NHI scheme? What services will they be eligible for, what will the personal cost to them be (eg. personal tax increase) and will there be clarity as to what treatments they're covered for? The current preponderance of private medical aids has, according to industry insiders, led to a milking of the system and their members’ pockets, with over charging and over provision of medication and procedures. On the other hand there has been the well documented culture of widespread state corruption when it comes to state owned enterprises. So is the risk that the latter may replace the former, in reforming the public health apparatus, worth paying?

Whether it be by individuals, insurance schemes or government, over half of South African health care spending is on 16% of the population, a reflection of one glaring aspect of inequality that has been a dripping sore affecting post independence South Africa since 1994. A consensus exists that says this state of affairs is untenable, but what is the solution? The NHI is the ANC government’s solution, the exact form of which is in development even though the Bill has already been tabled in parliament. Even so, the government has announced NHI will be in operation in 2026. There have been localized, so-called pilots that in effect became restricted to limited learning exercises, because the infrastructure of the districts struggled to cope with the demands of the process (eg transport, lack of IT staff and low numbers of participating doctors). A lack of detail on research and the way forward has meant opposition groups have been filling in the gaps and the public have been receiving confused messages. But in reality NHI is already here whatever form it takes. So what happens between now and 2026 for patients, GPs, dentists etc.? Are the plans and timetable for the plans cast in stone? Are there other options being explored? How different might the situation look after the completion of public participation stages? As NHI starts up, we get a grip on the current operations of the project, the fiscal implications for our nation and citizens, and the prospects for the medical industry. Fundamentally, if South Africa is to implement a viable system of fair, universal health care, then it is critical, whatever happens, that the country gets it right.

title: A State of Detransition
oneLiner: we discover that, for some, the difficulty of gender transitioning didn't end in emotional fulfillment but rather more pain and confusion.
summary:
What do you do if, having made the difficult decision to transition from one gender or identity to another, you discover that your're still not happy; that you want to reverse the effects of hormone therapy and - in some instances - surgery? Who do you talk to? How do you begin to deal with the trauma of discovering that the thing you thought would end your misery is making you more depressed? Gender Dysphoria is far better understood than it was just a few years ago, but it is no less controversial. Not least because many countries are making allowance for what's known as surgery by "affirmation" and making hormone therapy available to ever-younger patients. That said, far less is known about what drives the need to detransition beyond the anecdotal and, in some cases, attempts to better understand it have been met with resistance or contempt. But, the figures quoted in places like the UK suggest more research is needed as a matter of urgency. In this story we'll meet an outspoken Irish activist who detransitioned several years ago and is dumbstruck by the resistance to attempts to better understand it - not least from the transgender community itself. We'll interview a British Psychotherapist whose attempt to conduct research on the subject was shot down by his University for being un-PC, and we'll speak to a South African transgender psychologist to examine the issue from a local perspective.

Detransitioning is, in the words of one of our experts, "under reported". That's probably because it's little researched, an unspoken taboo in some circles and downplayed in others. It might also be because, as some activists claim, it isn't that prevalent. But, the fact is that many experts are warning that not enough attention is being paid to the phenomenon, and that charities are filling the vacuum left by a medical fraternity still grappling with elective gender re-alignment surgery. This story will attempt to shed light on this apparently new and controversial element of an already complex issue.

title: Grade 9 Certificate
oneLiner: A General Education Certificate at the end of Grade 9 has educators polarised, highlighting a system that is fundamentally broken at the core. Will this certificate add value to our children’s futur
summary:
A Grade 9 certificate for South African learners is on the horizon. It is meant to create alternative learning streams for pupils not necessarily wanting to follow an academic outcome for their education, as well as providing an early national benchmark making schools accountable in earlier grades. This is modelled on the German schooling system, but South Africa has very different challenges when it comes to education infrastructure and industry participation which forms a large part of the German model. A recent study has outlined fundamental failings within our education system with; 20% absenteeism of teachers on Mondays and Fridays, rising to 33% at every month-end, in schools serving predominantly poor black children only an average of 3.5 hours per school day is spent teaching compared to 6.5 hours in the middle and upper-class schools. According to critics of the new certificate, many challenges across the country, including the observation that Grade 4 children have not yet learned to read with meaning need to be addressed before a grade 9 certificate enters our educational framework. In addition, many educators say that this Grade 9 certificate is going to be costly to implement, in terms of infrastructure, implementation and resources - including supplying teachers who are skilled enough to teach the myriad of new subjects that will be introduced into schools. With the introduction of these subjects it may even be duplicating what the system has currently in place, in terms of the TVET colleges that are supposed to accommodate the non academic stream towards a National Certificate. On the other hand, the Department believes that this certificate will give more credence to the TVET qualifications. Is the new Grade 9 certificate a deflection from the perception that, educationally, South Africa is moving backwards?

By the end of July 2020 the field trial for the general education certificate at the end of Grade 9 is scheduled for completion. Not an exit strategy for learners according to the Department of Education, rather opening the options for non academic streams as well as setting an earlier national benchmark for learners before they get to Grade 12. But can this certificate enhance a failing educational system in dire need of attention?

title: Karoo Drought - Humanitarian Disaster
summary:
In many parts of the country the drought has broken- the horrific images of the Free State KZN that haunted our lives- these farmers have had rain. But the area in the central Karoo around Carnarvon, Sutherland and Williston they are into their 7th year of drought. Sheep numbers decreased by 11 870, and average weaning percentage by 27%. The average feed bill per month is R52 461. The sheep are dying, the ewes are not lambing and the farmers are slaughtering their breeding stock because they can’t afford to feed them. The price of red meat has dropped by R10 kilogram n effect on a 20kg carcass the producer gets nearly R200 less per lamb. 12 000 less sheep from 26 farmers equals R2,4million loss. They have been waiting for over a year to get assistance from the State despite the area having been declared a disaster area in 2018.

The rains came for the rest of the drought stricken country but in the central Karoo, Carnarvon, Williston Sutherland the main sheep producing areas its been 7 long dry years. They got 3 months of drought relief in 2018 but the rains never came and the farmers cant go on. The biggest causality are the farm workers, half have been laid off. Emerging farmers can't afford to employ anyone permanently and rely on causal workers when they have enough money to employ them. People are surviving on SASA grants and soup kitchens. Kids are turning to crime and dropping out of school with drug and alcohol abuse is rife

title: Dusi Disaster
oneLiner: The worst disaster in more than 3 decades -- can the Dusi river recover from a devastating caustic soda and oil spill?
summary:
The Mzunduzi (Dusi) river is famous because of the canoe marathon that is held on the river each year. It is the biggest canoeing event on the African continent, and one of the world’s most popular river marathons, attracting between 1600 and 2000 paddlers each year. But the river has also often been in the news for other reasons. Water quality has often been an issue and high e.coli counts are regularly measured. There are many rural communities who live along the banks of the river between PMB and Durban. On Tuesday 13 Aug there was a large oil and caustic soda spillage in PMB at the Willowton factory. 1.6 million litres of pollutants entered the Bain spruit and flowed into the Dusi river. The pollutants have had a devastating effect on the river, fish and other animals that depend on it. There are reports of dying cattle and massive fish die-offs all the way downstream to the Inanda dam.Provincial Government has issued a warning saying that people and animals should stay clear of the river. No-one should drink from the river, use it for irrigation or even paddle on it. The spill has been labelled the worst in 30 years. The Dusi Marathon organisers are concerned about the long-term effects on the river. The Dusi Umgeni Conservation Trust has stepped in to help monitor the water quality and assist in clean-up operations. Willowton has subcontracted 2 companies to help with the clean-up and government is also "working around the clock" but experts are saying that this kind of spill is very difficult to clean up. The caustic soda mixed with the oil has created a soapy substance that is suffocating all aquatic life in the river. Umgeni Water has tried to flush the river by opening the sluice of Henley Dam and although the water is running clear at some places, the damage has been done. Msunduzi Municipality spokesperson Thobeka Mafumbatha said the city’s environmental health unit was investigating the incident.

At 4am on the 13th of August a storage tank filled with cooking oil crumbled, taking down with it a second container filled with caustic soda. This happened at the Willowton Plant in Pietermaritzburg, KZN. The alkaline mix flowed down the Bain spruit and into the Dusi river. It is estimated that 1.6 million litres of oil and caustic soda ended up in the river and by the weekend the milky polluted water had entered the Inanda dam outside Durban. The liquid is suffocating fish and other aquatic animals. The water is undrinkable for the communities and their animals. According to environmentalists it will take the Dusi several decades to recover.

Filmed during 5 voyages between May 2017 and November 2017, over 4,000 sheep died during these voyages - almost half of them from heat stroke. Australia's Live Animal Export business was flourishing for almost 5 decades until wistleblowers (including the state vet) came out with damning evidence of the treatment and conditions of the animals on board the ships. The industry has been placed in the spotlight and tighter controls were put in place after their expose in 2017/18... Fast Forward to 2019... title: Mass Extinction: Lessons from Chernobyl.
oneLiner: With the world in the grip of its sixth mass extinction, what can we learn from nature's resurgence in one of the most toxic places on the planet?
summary:
We're in the midst of the Sixth Mass Extinction. Animals and insects are dying out at rates up to 1000 times the natural average. Unlike previous mass extinction events, this one is being driven by humans through the destruction of natural habitats, the use of pesticides, poaching and a myriad other unsustainable behaviours. The implications are, potentially, catastrophic. But, a 2600 square kilometre area of forest in northern Ukraine provides a blunt but valuable lesson about our relationship with the remaining biosphere. The massive Exclusion Zone set up around the Chernobyl nuclear facility shortly after the calamitous explosion in its fourth reactor in 1986 has successfully limited human activity in the area. And for good reason: it remains, along with Fukushima in Japan, the most contaminated place on the face of the planet. Extended exposure to ionising radiation in its most toxic areas can lead to serious health issues and death. But, it has also had an unexpected and ironic impact. Animals, birds, fish and flora are thriving. Nature has, over the past three decades, reclaimed the abandoned buildings and quiet roads. Wolves, antelope, moose and bears have returned in numbers not seen since the area was cleared and colonised by humans. The lesson is stark: take man out of the equation, and nature's resilience ensures not just its survival but its proliferation. While not a scientific or even particularly sophisticated argument, there does appear a stark lesson: if you want to ensure nature's survival, simply leave it alone.

In a South African television first, Carte Blanche ventures into one of the most contaminated places in the world to investigate how nature is reclaiming what humans took away. In spite of life-threatening ionising radiation, Chernobyl's wildlife is thriving. We'll venture into the Exclusion Zone and hear from experts who are trying to understand why.

title: ALDICARB DOG POISONING

As many as 1 000 dogs die in SA each week due to poison. Aldicarb is a highly toxic pesticide that is illegal to use and possess in South Africa. However, people from neighbouring countries where the substance is still in use bring it into the country in bulk and sell it on the black market as rat poison. Aldicarb is notoriously known as 'two-step' (because you take 2 steps and you die) and 'aliphirimi' (the sun will not rise – because you will not see the next sunrise if you ingest it). It is deadly to rats, dogs and humans. Criminals often use Aldicarb to kill dogs at a property they wish to rob. The poison is placed inside sausages, wors or viennas, thrown over the fence for the dog to eat and criminals return some time later to rob the home, without the dogs alerting the sleeping owners. That is prevalent in the suburbs whereas in townships, many dogs die after accidentally ingesting Aldicarb which has been laid out in the open for rats. Aldicarb is easily available at most taxi ranks and some spaza shops and is preferred by many as rat poison because it is cheap. It sells for around R10 for a dosage which is enough to deal with rat infestation for the whole house, or kill an adult human.

Dr Verdoorn will illustrate the high toxicity of Aldicarb as well as the poison's effects not only on rats and dogs, but also on humans.

title: Hotting up in the Kalahari
oneLiner: Climate change is threatening our natural heritage and our very survival
summary:
The Kalahari is named for the Tswana “Kgala” (great thirst) or “Kgalagadi” (waterless place). It spans a vast 900 000km2 semi-desert area of South Africa, Botswana and Namibia. It's one of the most extreme habitats in Southern Africa, with daytime temperatures peaking at over 40 degrees C, and plummeting overnight. Its driest areas receive over 4000 hours of sunshine per year. Kalahari and species are adapted to survive on the edge, so it's here that we'll first see the effects of global climate change on ecosystems and communities. Worldwide, hundreds of species are already shifting ranges, breeding and feeding patterns in response to warmer temperatures and unpredictable rainfall. A recent UN study reports that 1 million species are under threat: many will be extinct in decades. In 2018, the UN IPCC said there are 12 years left for action if we are to keep global warming to a maximum of 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial levels. Climate change and biodiversity loss pose an existential threat to human beings, increasing poverty, food insecurity, disease, water scarcity and frequency and severity of natural disasters. Poor communities are most at risk, and Africa is particularly vulnerable. South Africa already experiences 2 degrees warming per century, more than twice global average, and growing evidence suggests species are already being affected. The Kalahari Endangered Ecosystems Project (KEEP) at Tswalu Kalahari Reserve is an ambitious collaboration between 20 biologists undertaking long-term research into the impact of climate change on the whole food system, looking at how changes at grassroots level filter through to the top. It is possibly the first of its kind, and may suggest interventions to help save our wildlife.

Climate change - it's a phrase we hear so often, many of us switch off. But the effects of temperature and rainfall changes are not part of the distant future: they're happening right now in our own backyard. Research in one of the most extreme climates on earth, the Kalahari, demonstrates what the future could look like for all of South Africa - and it's putting our rich biodiversity under threat.

title: KNP Mining

Experts are doubtful whether in fact the Northern Kangwane Coalfield can even yield such volumes. The entire area is approximately 18,000 ha. The Background Information Document (BID) submitted by Singo Consulting states that it will be open cast mining, but the EIA states that it will be a "box-cut" underground mine. Although the underground mine will be less of an eyesore than a large-scale open cast mine, the impact on the environment remains the same. Blasting will affect surrounding communities and wildlife. Increased traffic and noise pollution will spoil the sense of place -- impacting on tourism and the estimated 3,000 jobs in the hospitality industry of the area. Two independent mining experts have pointed out various flaws with the EIA and and the Environmental Consulting Agency that conducted the EIA/EMPr. The EIA came in with a 38% plagiarism count, and the head of Singo Consulting does not have a PHD, although he claims to have one. Singo Consulting is not registered, and has never applied with EAPASA.

Mine application MP 30/5/1/2/2/10216MR by Manzolwandle Mining (Pty) Ltd on the farms Tenbosch, Vyeboom & Turfbult approximately 93kms east of Nelspruit is sending shockwaves through the conservation community and local residents alike. The company has had prospecting rights since 2012 and it is thought that they are pushing to have the mining right approved before the prospecting rights expire. The farms border the Kruger National Park's southern border, i.e. the Crocodile River -- between Marloth Park and Ngwenya Lodge. The concerns about the mine range from the obvious ecological and hydrological impact, to the impact on business and tourism, and well as the way in which the application process has been handled.

People pointed fingers to a small bakery run by Natasha Mandiringa who sells products labeled as gluten-free. Natasha claims that she found a unique way to ferment gluten-free flours to bake goods that look and taste like wheat products. The City of Cape Town’s Health directorate, as well as TOPIC, a non-profit organisation, went to investigate. They found Natasha very open and willing to get to the root of the problem. It seemed there were some misunderstandings and honest mistakes that she corrected and removed gluten-free labels from her products. The City of Cape Town was satisfied that Natasha now complied with the regulations. But new allegations surfaced that Natasha was using wheat in her baking, without listing it as an ingredient. Staff at the bakery also informed clients verbally that the products did not contain gluten. Dr Harris Steinman of FACTS (Food and Allergy Consulting Services) lab in Stellenbosch tested the products and found high levels of both gluten and wheat in the goods. Natasha responded that people were running a vendetta against her and that the allegations were false. She does not have the resources to continually test all her products, but went to great lengths to ensure that she complied to all regulations. Now, a health shop in Centurion is also selling gluten-free products that shows high levels of gluten in lab tests. What is the truth? Are these business owners unscrupulous frauds taking advantage of health-conscious consumers or are they innovative entrepreneurs suffering a vendetta by competitors? Is it possible that gluten can be picked up in lab tests, even though the ingredients contain no gluten? Is the City of Cape Town shirking its responsibility by not properly investigating claims that could have serious consequences for its citizens?

A real-life drama of accusations and claims of victimization that not only affects every health-conscious consumer, but can potentially have severe health implications. Only deep investigation will help us solve this puzzle.

Almost 8 million of the country's young people under the age of 34 will not be employed nor will they be enrolled in any from of education or training leaving them destitute with no hope for the future. Sixty percent of those who enter the employment market without a matric are jobless and many of these young people now believe that there's no hope that they will ever find a job.Youth aged 15-24 are the most vulnerable group in the labour market. There existence is eked out on a day-to day basis. We will tell the story of 3 unemployed youths and the daily challenges that they face.

title: Submarine: SAS 'Manthatisi
oneLiner: We are going on a submarine!!!
summary:
So what do they use them for? Well that’s part of national security and it’s a strategic key point, the presidency has given the SA navy and carte blanche exclusive access (cos ive hounded them for years) to let us board and submerge in the S102 (that’s the designation for the boat (a submarine is a boat NOT a ship: ships carry boats; that is to say, a sea-going vessel that can be carried, launched, and/or tended by another sea-going vessel is a 'boat', and a ship cannot be carried by another ship; since it is a historical holdover, it reflects the time it came to be, when submarines were actually boats) However, they will tell us past missions – they have been a part of helping catch pirates in the Mozambican Channel and other missions off of the West coast of South Africa. Submarines are made to be non-detectable – so their missions require stealth – they safe guard our waters daily submerged – sometimes for weeks. https://www.iol.co.za/dailynews/crackdown-on-sea-pirates-yielding-results-18130909 They act as part of our national security ensuring people are not illegally fishing in False Bay or doing other illegal activities, all along our coastline. The main advantage of submarines is that once they sail from Simon's Town, they can watch over our sea lanes without anyone noticing them. And should it ever come to a war situation, one submarine has the capability to sink a number of enemy ships - as was illustrated by the SAS MANTHATHISI when she sank an entire NATO fleet in September 2007. (http://www.armsdeal-vpo.co.za/articles11/sinks.html).

So we’ve all seen the headlines that say we aren’t taking care of our submarines from the arms deal, and that we’ve spent billions on what? The SA Navy say this is all wrong – and are going to take Carte Blanche aboard the SAS 'Manthatisi (Manthatisi was 19th century known as “queen of the Wild Cat,” leader of the Tlokwa people – she was a strong, brave and a capable leader after her son and husband died, both in times of peace and war.) There are 3 submarines that form part of the Heroine Class – the SAS Charlotte Maxeke and the SAS Queen Modjadji I. They were bought from Germany –and are still serving the country. The way in which our Navy uses them is in line with international best practises of other Navies. One of the submarines must be operational, meaning it must be ready to conduct missions for the SA Navy. Of the two remaining submarines one will have minor maintenance issues, whilst the third will be in a deep maintenance cycle - requiring some time and money to get operational again. The three submarines are then cycling through this process to ensure that they can serve our country for upwards of 30 years.

title: RX Radio: Broadcasting for Children by Children
oneLiner: We hear the young voices behind the microphone of the first radio station in the world to live-stream from a children’s hospital: presented by children they share their life stories.
summary:
The Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital is dedicated entirely to children. The hospital treats more than 250 000 children annually from those with life-threatening diseases to day-patients, many of whom are from marginalised communities. When RX Radio began broadcasting in November 2016 under the wing of the Red Cross Children’s Hospital, its aim was to to bring a little sunshine into these young lives, to put a smile on these children’s faces. RX Radio is the brainchild of Dr Gabriel Urgoiti, RX Station Manager and Child Health Care Specialist at the hospital. “RX Radio has created a platform for children to voice their own issues and holding the mic gives them the power to engage not only with other children, but also with adults, asking questions and sharing their opinions,” says Urgoiti. Pre-recorded and live shows are streamed via the internet 24/7. From music to podcasts and radio diaries, the station transmits audio and images through the hospital’s internal television system to all wards and public spaces. “Children in the hospital form part of the show as they can request songs, dedications and live games by calling us or interacting through social media,” says Content Producer Noluyolo Ngomani. Our radio presenters are children as young as five and the oldest ones are 18. We also allow siblings of patients to co-host shows,” says Ngomani. “Those who are interested in becoming presenters attend a 5-day workshop where they learn about storytelling, radio reporting and production skills. We also send them out to live events where they interview people and come back to do a podcas.” “The microphone gives them a voice; it changes the conversation around their illness and they are able to express what is going on deep inside themselves with their doctor and parents,” says Ngomani. “Their experience at the hospital becomes easier when they understand exactly what is wrong with them and how to cope.”

RX Radio at the Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital in Cape Town is presented by children who share their stories of hope and understanding their chronic health conditions they live with. Talking about their experiences in hospital helps them to cope better and teaches them valuable life skills.

Agri SA claims that if NERSA had their house in order sooner Level 1 load shedding could have been prevented. NERSA claimed that they needed to establish a suitable registration tariff. title: Sleep - The New Wonder Drug
summary: Scientists have discovered a revolutionary new treatment that makes you live longer. It enhances your memory, makes you more attractive. It keeps you slim and lowers food cravings. It protects you from cancer and dementia. It wards off colds and flu. It lowers your risk of heart attacks and stroke, not to mention diabetes. You’ll even feel happier, less depressed, and less anxious. Its called sleep, what we don’t have enough of, Chronic sleep deprivation has been called ‘the disease of our time’. A century ago, people slept for an average of nine hours a night, today it is closer to seven hours. Strict schedules of full work or school days, early mornings for exercise, late nights for television or emails all disrupt our circadian rhythms. Sleep is the thing we regularly sacrifice for ‘more important’ activities. The effects of insufficient sleep are horrifying: poor memory, weight gain, low mood, higher anxiety, lower libido, shorter life expectancy. It makes you more likely to get cancer, dementia, Alzheimer’s, diabetes, flu or a cold. You’re more likely to suffer a heart attack or stroke and more likely to die in a car crash. Regularly getting less than seven hours a night is as harmful as smoking or drinking to excess. There is serious evidence that lack of sleep is a factor in the onset of depression and schizophrenia, and is even associated with the symptoms of ADHD.

title: Crude Oil - Call to Ban Palm Oil
oneLiner: We examine the impact of a product that has decimated huge tracts of virgin forest in south east Asia and ask "is there merit to calls to ban Palm Oil?"
summary:
Cultivating Palm Oil makes economic sense. It's 10 times more productive than soya, and does just about everything you demand of a tasteless vegetable oil. Ironically, it also makes environmental sense because - given its outstanding yields - you need less land to produce more oil than would be the case with other species. But, here's the rub: it only makes environmental sense if you're not slashing-and-burning virgin forest to make way for more palm trees. If you do, not only are you creating more pollution and destroying a vital carbon sink, you're decimating the habitat of dozens of animals including tigers, monkeys and orangutans. For a very long time, that's precisely what happened. Swathes of forest were cleared in Malaysia and Indonesia in particular as the global demand for Palm Oil continued to rocket. The result was a massive pay-day for the suppliers and millers, and social and environmental misery for just about everybody else. Thanks to the efforts of international organisations like Mighty Earth, the industry was pressured into adopting measures aimed at limiting its environmental impact, including a pledge not to chop down any more forests. That, for some, has been enough: many suppliers peg their reputations on this certification process and consumers who care about such things are able to buy guilt-free butter and hair gel. For others, though, it's a charade. They argue that forests continue to burn, animals continue to die and local villagers continue to be fleeced of their land. Leaning on the experience of international campaigners, we look into the local Palm Oil supply chain to gauge its commitment to sustainability and ask whether we as consumers can trust the certification process or whether what we're buying is the fruit of a now devastated landscape.

Social media is driving a growing international campaign to ban Palm Oil because of its devastating impact on forest biodiversity, including endangered species like the Orangutan. It's a vegetable oil that is found in a range of products from ice-creams to pies and mascara. The industry has responded to the mounting criticism by establishing a body that certifies sustainable Palm Oil, but that hasn't satisfied some lobbyists. They say rogue suppliers continue to operate, and that the certified standards are too vague. All of which makes for an unsurprising stand-off between environmentalists and big business. But, this is a complex issue and, sadly, the debate rarely takes that into account. Ours aims to be a more nuanced insert that explains the impact of Palm Oil, takes a closer look at attempts to re-package the industry as one committed to sustainability and the efforts of rogue suppliers to prioritise profits over the environment.

title: Cyclone Idai - Mozambique
oneLiner: On 15 March the devastating cyclone Idai hit the Mozambique coast, killing more than a thousand people and leaving hundreds of thousands destitute.
summary:
Winds of up to 170 kph (105 mph) and flooding swept across southeastern Africa, including Zimbabwe and Mozambique, affecting more than 2.6 million people, United Nations officials said on Tuesday. Eye-witnesses have said that it looked like the town of Beira was hit by a Tsunami. There are reports of pets being swept away by the strong winds, and people killed by flying debris. Official numbers from the Red Cross is more than 400,000 homeless, although people on the ground says it's more than double that.

The city of Beira is said to be 90% destroyed and rescue efforts continue to help people affected by the intense storm that hit the coast on 15 March. title: Middle Ear 3-D Transplant - A World First!

The procedure carries less risk than known prostheses and their associated surgical procedures. Titanium is used which is biocompatible. An endoscope is used to do the replacement and the scarring is minimal. The surgery also aims to simplify the reconstruction of bones during middle ear procedures. The procedure reduces the chance of facial nerve paralysis, which can occur if the facial nerve that passes through the middle ear space is damaged during traditional surgery.

A pioneering surgical procedure using 3D-printed middle ear bones, developed by Professor Mashudu Tshifularo and his team at the University of Pretoria Faculty of Health, may be the answer to conductive hearing loss, a middle ear problem caused by congenital birth defects, infection, trauma or metabolic loss.

title: HOPE FOR MND PATIENTS - EDARAVONE
oneLiner: An intensive therapy, initially developed for stroke patients and approved by the FDA for MND, now gives hope to Andre Swartz and others suffering from the neurodegenerative disease with no cure
summary:
The well-known entertainer Andre Swartz has recently started a therapy that he is hopeful will slow down the progression of MND that he was diagnosed with in 2018. The therapy, Radicava/Endaravone was approved by the FDA in 2017; the first treatment that they have approved for MND diseases in twenty years. The therapy had proved in three human trials in China to have 30% effectiveness in the slowing down progression of this dibilitating, life-threatening disease with no cure. Motor Neuron Disease is a neurodegenerative disease that affect the nerves (motor neurones) in the brain and spinal cord that tell your muscles what to do. With MND, messages from these nerves gradually stop reaching the muscles, leading them to weaken, stiffen and waste. This treatment, that is still new in SA, is now giving hope to the many sufferers of MND.

Andre Swartz, one of our countries leading and best known entertainers, was diagnosed in 2018 with MND, similar to Joost vd Westhuizen, while starring as Captain von Trapp in the theatre production of The Sound of Music. Andre recently started using Edaravone, the generic of Radicava, that was initially developed for stroke patients. After three human trails on MND related diseases with a 30% improvement of degeneration, the FDA for the first time in twenty years approved the treatment in 2017 for MND patients. The treatment is new in SA and not many people are aware of the option. Andre is positive and hopeful that the treatment will slow down the progression of the disease but has no illusions as to what might be lying ahead for him.
