title: Homeschooling under threat
oneLiner: Homeschooling was legalised in 1996. But a new bill is about to change the face of home education giving the state the power to dictate how homeschooling should be done. We have the story.
summary:
Education in South Africa is the responsibility of the Department of Basic Education. Its vision statement is “to ensure learners from Grade R to Grade 12 have access to lifelong learning, education and training which will contribute towards improving the quality of life and building a peaceful, prosperous and democratic South Africa”. But the stats tells another story: Only a third of learners starting Grade 1 each year make it to their final matric exams. The department is simply not equipped to handle the growing number of learners annually resulting in overcrowded classrooms, poor quality of teaching and discipline problems. These are some of the reasons many parents in South Africa have chosen to go the homeschooling route. With home education, parents take ownership over their children’s learning process and create an environment where each child is given the best opportunity to grow according to his or her needs and personality.

Since 1996, more than 54 000 families have provided home education for their children. The movement to homeschooling has been the result of parents being dissatisfied with the quality of teaching and feeling that public education does not prepare their children for professional careers. Prior to 2017, homeschooling was not regulated by the state. Then in 2017, the Department of Basic Education or DBE made a sudden announcement proposing drastic changes to the homeschooling policy. His motivation for the changes, he said, was to regulate the environment, provide guidelines and make sure that homeschooling is legislated. The nuts and bolts of this new legislation, however, will remove parents’ freedom of choice and make the state co-parents of home education. The key changes as outlined in the Basic Education Laws Amendment (BELA) Bill are: parents have to apply to homeschool and go through a stringent process, an official will visit the home to check that the environment is similar to a classroom situation, only government-approved curriculums will be accepted; a child’s progress will be assessed annually by a government assessor at huge additional cost to the parent, and parents must keep a register of their child’s attendance. There was an immediate backlash from parents. Why is the state interfering with a process that has been successful over the last 22 years, they wanted to know. Why is the state taking away parents’ constitutional right to decide what type of education their child should receive by becoming the co-parents of their children’s education at home? They contend that the amendment outlined in the Bill defeats the purpose of homeschooling in the first place. It will also place an extra financial burden on the state, which means the taxpayers, as well as the parents, who are already footing the bill of homeschooling in that one parent may be forfeiting a salary to stay at home and teach and homeschoolers need to buy the study material. From the 13th of October 2017, when the announcement was made by the department, less than a month’s grace period was given for public comment. Despite many emails and public lobbying by the Pestalozzi Trust, acting on behalf of homeschooling families, comment closed on November, the 10th. The Bill is in the process of becoming an Act.

title: Matric to University
summary:
The matric pass rate of 2018 has been celebrated as a great success across the country, with a 78% pass rate, up from 2017’s 75% pass rate, but despite the heartfelt stories of students achieving matric passes against all odds, the reality behind the headlines remains dire. The real pass rate is closer to 50% if one accounts for all the students who started in grade one in 2007 and dropped out at Grade 10 or earlier. The number of bachelor passes has risen with more black matriculants achieving them, but for tertiary educators, the 2019 intake that arrives on their doorstep is as ill-equipped as in previous years. A bachelor’s pass which gives students access to university and technicons requires 40% in their home language, only 50% in four other subjects, and 30% in two other subjects. A matric doesn’t mean much any more. The burden of the failure of the schooling system has been transferred onto tertiary institutions. Government has long recognised the need for bridging/development courses to help students cope with the demands of tertiary education - massive amounts of money are spent every year, but it’s still not enough. The through-put of students through tertiary institutions remains very low, either with high levels of dropouts or extended periods to obtain a basic degree – a three year degree plus one year often takes five or six years.

The 2018 national matric pass rate of 78% makes for fabulous headlines, but the reality is that the standard of matric has dropped, and the burden of the failure of the Basic and Higher Education system has simply been transferred to tertiary institutions. Matriculants now have access to free higher education, with all subjects now qualifying for a Bachelor’s pass, and expectations are running high. In an election year, tertiary education remains under enormous pressure to fulfil the dreams of the youth, and to address the massive unemployment rate. Already parties like the EFF are threatening disruption of the academic programme. The focus will be on students’ struggles and aspirations, and the reality of what tertiary educators have to accommodate.

title: Death Matters
oneLiner: Space for traditional burials is fast running out, but besides cremation, what are the alternatives?
summary:
In South Africa, a new trend of eco burials is emerging. This means that the body is not embalmed, often wrapped in cloth and buried in a wicker or paper mache coffin. This makes the actual burial a lot more environmental friendly, but it does not solve the space problem. Cremation solves the space problem, but it has a huge environmental footprint. It takes about 15KWH of electricity to cremate one body. Besides the smoke pumped into the atmosphere, greenhouse gases are also released, not to mention toxic formaldehyde from the embalming process and other chemicals used in the making and varnishing of the coffin. Every body is cremated in a wood coffin, once again using a great deal of wood. Internationally there are some alternatives emerging...

It is estimated that there are about 25,000 burials in Johannesburg per annum, and space is fast running out. Not only do burials take up space, but cemeteries are often dead space and costly to maintain. On top of that is the environmental footprint of a traditional burial. Bodies are embalmed with formaldehyde and coffins are made of wood (a precious resource) and often lacquered and glued that end up leaching into the soil. Coffins are also very often lined with plastic which slows down the decomposition of the body. But what are the alternatives and are they viable options for the future?

title: THE BABY TRADE - JOURNEYMAN SPECIAL

summary: The Baby Trade Wild orangutans are expected to face extinction within 50 years. Despite this, the multi-million dollar poaching industry thrives as baby orangutans are captured and smuggled from their rain-forest homes. “Every time she hopped on a tree we’d cut that tree down. We’d catch the mother in a net and either hit her or shoot her. Once she was dying we’d take the baby”, says an ex-smuggler, describing the brutal capture of a baby orangutan. Intelligent yet relatively passive primates, orangutans are desirable pets, as they can be taught tricks and dressed up. Most are trafficked from the rainforests of Indonesia to Thailand, where they are sold for thousands of dollars. Edwin Wiek runs rescue facilities for these stolen animals, but with little government support he faces significant challenges; “the illegal wildlife trade is very lucrative, a lot of people make lots of money including some politicians or government officials in some cases". For the rescued orangutans, rehabilitation and re-release into the wild is a complex process. Oki, newly released after 15 years in captivity, struggled to adjust to life in the wild according to veterinarian Rian Winardi. “The release didn’t go according to plan. We hoped he wouldn’t turn around and look at people. But he did. He’s an ex-rehab orangutan after all.”

Anton, is an ex pro boxer, trainer and promoter, with over 20 years first-hand experience of the impact that boxing has in the lives of youth in the Southern Suburbs of Rosettenville. Luke has 25 years experience in the child protection and development field and works with many Non Profit Organisations. Anton and Luke are supported by Sheri Errington, a Research Psychologist with more than 10 years Non -Profit Monitoring and Evaluation experience. In 2014 Fight with Insight launched an open access boxing gym in the inner city of Johannesburg, in response to the needs of children living there. Fight with Insight was established with the vision of creating a safe place for the children of Johannesburg, using boxing to teach them life skills that assist them in taking responsibility for claiming their rights. They aim to contribute positively to healthy lifestyles and sustainable communities for children.

Ten years on from the first insert on FIGHT WITH INSIGHT, we revisit Luke Lamprecht and the young men whose lives have been saved through the discipline of boxing at the Fight with Insight gym on the outskirts of the roughest parts of Johannesburg. Taking a glimpse behind the scenes of these young men's lives, we discover where they might have been if it hadn't been for the programme that teaches them the values of teamwork, consideration, self-control and healthy competition.

title: Bo-Kaap Gentrification
summary: The residents of Cape Town’s Bo Kaap have been fighting developers for years, the latest is against an apartment/office block in Lion Street when a crane was prevented from entering and some protesters hauled off to jail. About 50 protesters gathered at the corner of Buiten and Buitengracht Street on Tuesday. Their aim was to prevent a crane from entering Bo-Kaap and making its way to a development on 40 Lion Street. On at least two occasions, riot police officers forced them out of the street using shields and stun grenades. According to SAPS, four people were arrested. We look at this age old and historic area of Cape Town and it’s process of gentrification, what does this mean to the people whose families have lived hear. for decades. They are seeing their ancestors mowed down, their communities broken apart as firstly trendy South Africans and tourists bought these quaint houses often at steal - to now developers coming in with multi storey apartment blocks aimed at a lifestyle of people who see the City Bowl and specifically Bo-kaap the place to live. “These developers don’t care about our people, they don’t care about the culture. The fact that more than 17 generations have lived in some of these houses,” Bo-Kaap dates back to the 1760s, when rental houses were built and leased to slaves. According to the Heritage Portal, liberated slaves moved into the area after 1834 and with them Malay people who had been living in the town. The community was one of the few inner-city areas where people were not forcibly removed under the Group Areas Act during apartheid.

title: Vault 2120
oneLiner: Never before has a time capsule project on this scale been undertaken...
summary:
The world is set to change dramatically over the next 100 years. Futurists predict that our world will be unrecognisable by the year 2100. With that in mind Eugene Botha has set out to create the Vault 2120 project. The Vault will be built and sealed in 2019 -- a airtight, watertight concrete vault will be buried underground at a location in Maropeng - the cradle of humankind. Eugene has a representation of what the vault will look like. It will consist of two chambers. One chamber will be the actual vault with "treasures" from our world today -- including never-seen-before works of art and literature, scientific and historic contributions, as well as contributions from individuals and societies. The other chamber will house a yearly time capsule added to the cache. The time capsule will contain some artefacts from the specific year. Together with Eugene and Piet Muller, the presenter will be involved in packing/preparing the time capsule for 2018. So in effect every year something will be added to the vault. A Trust has been established to oversee the process until 2120 when the Vault will be opened.

Vault 2120 South Africa is an international social/historical/scientific experiment to create a secure, airtight and watertight underground vault in South Africa where individuals, companies and institutions will be able to securely deposit artefacts, documents, art works, information, music, technologies, personal/family items and the like in individual containers also known as time capsules. Carte Blanche will have an exclusive look at how the vault will be built, what will be put inside and how this bit of history will be safe-guarded for generations to come.

title: Ugly Food: Want not, waste not.
oneLiner: Why are we wasting one-third of all our food... because it's not aesthetically pleasing? We explore how perfectly nutritious food can be given a second life and what viewers can do to curb food waste
summary:
Climate conference: Ban-ki Moon -panel commission on adaptation - to help especially poor and vulnerable countries - food security - climate. (Bangladesh). Every year in the US, 20-40% (that’s at least 1 in 5) of fresh produce is discarded even before it gets into stores because it is ‘ugly’. Like a misshapen tomato, a too curved cucumber or a lumpy potato. The ‘Ugly Fruit & Veg Campaign‘ encourages us to buy ugly and focuses not on what is on the outside, but what is on the inside – the taste and nutritional goodness of fruits and vegetables that are not visually perfect. It is not just that there are ridiculous marketing standards that specify sizes, diameter, consistency and colour of produce (interestingly, standards don’t specify ripeness or taste); we are also the problem. We’ve been trained to shop with our eyes and to go for perfect apples, tomatoes and carrots – those that are ideally shaped, coloured and blemish-free. Pressure from shoppers, supermarkets and farmers sees rules being shed in the US and Europe and more ugly produce is being sold alongside aesthetically appealing versions. In the US and Europe, there are now grocery stores and home delivery services that sell ugly produce that is perfectly good to eat – and cheaper. These are ideal outlets for farmers to sell produce that is less visually appealing at a good price. Once fruit and veg are chopped up and tossed into a salad, baking dish, juice, stew or soup, does it really matter that it was misshapen when you bought it? Another bonus – children are delighted by the strange forms of wonky carrots and other misshapen veg. Buying ugly is a win-win.

14 Million South African's go hungry everyday, and Statistics by the World Wide Fund have shown that almost one-third of all food produced in South Africa - totalling 10million tons of edible food - is wasted every year. We will go out with FoodForwardSA and explore how their 4 projects are saving "UGLY" food and supplying it to those who are hungry. About them: 50% of edible agricultural production is wasted due to specification requirements, cold-chain and processing inadequacies as well as access to markets. FoodForward SA is launching Second Harvest, a programme that sources and collects surplus fruit and vegetables from commercial farmers across South Africa and redistributes this fresh produce to the 600 beneficiary organisations in their network. Established in 2009 to address widespread hunger in South Africa, FoodForward SA connects a world of excess to a world of need by recovering surplus food from the consumer goods supply chain. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EwaxmKIIU2g The organisation reaches up to 250 000 daily at the cost of R0.79 per meal. Beneficiary organisations include orphanages, places of safety, creche’s, disability care, aged care, skills and youth development. The Second Harvest allows farmers to donate their post-harvest surpluses while they are harvesting, to ensure the food does not go to waste. FoodForward SA is working with a network of farmers located in the Western Cape, Gauteng, and Durban to improve the nutrition level of the groceries provided to beneficiaries. According to Managing Director of FoodForward SA, Mr Andy Du Plessis, “Dedicated refrigerated vehicles go directly to our farmers to collect fresh fruit and vegetables while they are harvesting. This fresh produce meaningfully increases the nutritional value of the food distributed, as well as volume, which significantly increases the number of people FoodForward SA are able to reach.” Foodbanking is the most effective solution at present to reducing hunger, and reducing food waste is the third most effective solution in fighting climate change. An independent study by WWF and Green House reflects that recovering food saved 17,400 tons of green house gas emissions, which is equivalent to 3,600 cars driven every day for a whole year. The launch of Second Harvest will ensure that more agricultural production is redistributed to the hungry. FoodForward SA encourages farmers, growers, food processors, and other supply chain stakeholders to partner with them and join the food recovery revolution. We will have chef Jenny Morris cook with "Ugly food" and "Left overs" and potentially do a blog.

title: #Rhodes War
oneLiner: Does the Punishment fit the crime
summary:
Their crime- they were part of a crowd of some 200 students both men and women who were protesting the inaction of Rhodes University to deal with the extremely high levels of rape on campus. A spontaneous protest happen when a list of 11 men were named as sexual predators, 3 of who lived in residences and were rounded up to account for their actions. One man spent the night with a dwindling crowd of angry women. Humiliating and no doubt scary, but the charge of kidnapping is debateable and the source of an on-going legal battle between the University and the legal representatives of the two women. These women have never had criminal charges laid against them by any of the 3 men that were removed from their residences on the night in question. The man accusing them of kidnapping did have a rape charged laid against him the following morning by a women which the NPA failed to prosecute. In the context of student protest and Fees Must Fall in particular no students have had their academic record stripped even when they have had faced criminal charges and convicted of various crimes. They have been suspended from Universities, but have been able to continue their studies in one form or another. Why has Rhodes reacted in such a draconian manner? It smacks of Russia in the 80’s when academics had their entire academic achievements stripped because they were gay. Even men found guilty of rape at Rhodes that have been expelled have not been banned from any further study.

Two Rhodes University students, Dominique Mc Fall and Yolanda Dyantyi have had their entire academic achievements stripped and are banned for life from Rhodes University. The impact is they are unable to study at ANY University in South Africa, including UNISA. Even criminals spending life sentences are able to study. Both 3rd year students- Mc Fall was on the Dean’s list and both would have completed their first degrees. Their academic record states they are guilty of kidnapping and insubordination (acting in common purpose) and in the case of Yolanda Dyanyti also assault and Defamation. Was the sanction of a life time ban and the destruction of the academic careers appropriate for the mass action of removing 3 men from their residences and holding one of them overnight? This protest took place soon after the “Me Too campaign” began and still holds relevance in the current the international outcry of the rape and sexual assault of women as seen in Justice Kavanaugh case. The crowd were angry and challenging these men who had taken part in what is known as “serenading or seal clubbing” a humiliating practice at Rhodes Residences. The men in turn shouted back at the women calling them “cock blockers” because they were being publicaly named and shamed. No doubt the ousting was humiliating and scary, and some on the reference list have declared their innocence but and even if we accept the charges are the sanctions appropriate?

title: Lariam Lament
oneLiner: Could an unprecedented court battle reveal why 12 Irish soldiers killed themselves? The answer might just open Pandora's Box in South Africa.
summary:
These 350 former soldiers all claim to have suffered damaging side-effects from Lariam. They were prescribed the drug while serving as peace-keepers in sub-Saharan Africa, and say their health hasn't been the same since. Their symptoms include mood swings, hallucinations, depression and what's known as "suicidal idealisation". 12 of their comrades, they say, killed themselves rather than deal with the debilitating mental damage wrought by the drug. One of the complainants in the case, Mark O'Sullivan, has built up a library of documents he believes points to Lariam as the reason for the suicides. The paper trail, he adds, implicates the Irish state in knowingly poisoning its soldiers: the drug continues to be prescribed by that country's military despite its manufacturer, Roche, having withdrawn it from the general Irish market in 2016. To channel their outrage and help highlight their concerns around Lariam, they've formed a victims' support group, and have approached a lawyer to take the case to the Irish High Court. If they win, it'll be the biggest personal injury award in Ireland's history. More significantly, though, in the same way that the Round Up ruling is threatening Monsanto's financial prospects, a win for the alleged victims could open the legal floodgates against Roche as well a global medical fraternity apparently indifferent to the psychological welfare of its patients.

Lariam is still widely prescribed in South Africa in spite of mounting evidence of its damaging side-effects. But, in a case not unlike the one which dealt a hammer blow to the cancer-causing pesticide, Round Up, the Irish government is being taken to court for ignoring those side-effects and knowingly endangering the lives of soldiers. In essence, this case, involving more than 350 soldiers, could have international repercussions including in South Africa.

title: The Climate Threshold
oneLiner: New climate research confirms what many experts have long been warning about: the earth might be on an irreversible path to a scorching future. How can humanity prepare for living in a hothouse?
summary:
New research conducted by a group of respected global scientists has found that there exists a climate threshold that, if crossed, would make the effects of climate change irreversible. Worryingly, they suggest, we may already have crossed that line. In other words, even if we cut our greenhouse gas emissions to zero, the impact of the damage already done combined with a number of knock-on effects, means the earth will continue to warm. The net result? A planet that heats up well beyond the 2 degrees set as the limit by global treaties. We will be living in a hothouse. Among the knock-on effects is the thawing of what's known as the Permafrost - a layer of once continually frozen vegetation found in areas around the poles. Rising temperatures are casing the Permafrost to "unfreeze" releasing carbon di-oxide - previously trapped within frozen vegetation - into the atmosphere. The consequence is what in sporting parlance would be known as a "double whammy": the Permafrost thaws because of higher temperatures, greenhouse gas is emitted as a result, increasing the rate at which atmospheric temperatures rise. Ellen Dorrepaal is a scientist based at the Abisko Research Centre in the Arctic Circle. She's researching the impact of global warming on the permafrost in a series of fascinating experiments and, crucially, looking at how the impact can be mitigated. We will spend a day at the centre with Ellen - filming mostly outdoors - as she explains her research, and describes a future shaped by dramatically altered climate.

The Abisko Research Centre is 200km north of the Arctic Circle and provides a unique opportunity to research the effects of global warming on colder climates. Carte Blanche has been offered a unique opportunity to venture to this remote area in the far north of Sweden to speak to some of Europe's leading climate scientists.

title: CB30: Three decades of history
oneLiner: unimaginable changes have taken place in South Africa and internationally since you first heard our signature tune way back in 1988
summary:
In 1988 South Africa was a very different country. President PW Botha was state president, Nelson Mandela was behind bars, townships were on fire, and activists resisted a repressive state of emergency. The idea of Nelson Mandela as president six years later, was as alien to some as the idea of a black president of the United States. There was no internet, cell phones or even email and we had no idea that a young man from South Africa would make himself a billionaire and fund his way into space.

Carte Blanche has covered many of history's triumphs and tragedies. At a time when populists are trying to rewrite our history we go back to show you how your wolrld has changed

title: CB30: Adventure
summary: From the start of Carte Blanche 30 years ago adventuring was always a big part of our stories. From 1996 when we flew to Katmandu, to interview the first South African Everest Expedition. Their team member Bruce Herrod had fell to his death and South Africans wanted answers. From Sean Wisedale the first South African to conquer all Seven Summits to Eveline Tshabala. who despite her HIV positive status was - together with friends Zuki and Nomawethu preparing to climb all seven of the summits around the world. We have captured extreme moments be it on land, sea or air and over the years we have met brave and intrepid men and woman who have pushed the boundaries of modern day adventure from Mike Horn and his Arctic adventure to Joey Evans who after recovering from a major bike accident finished the Dakar Rally. Riaan Mansers has had many extraordinary adventures - possibly the most frightening - was when he rowed with his then partner, now wife, Vasti, from Africa to the USA. Vasti became the only woman from the African continent to have rowed across any of the worlds oceans

title: Cyclists at risk
oneLiner: A high-profile attack on a cyclist has raised public awareness of increasing violent crime
summary:
Bike jacking and bike theft have become quite commonplace as more and more South Africans take part in this expensive and increasingly popular sport, and criminals realise the potential for a quick buck. Many speculate that the thieves are organised by syndicates selling bikes outside the country. With little real data on the size of the problem, cyclists rely on social media to find stolen bikes and raise community awareness about their vulnerability. Forums are littered with reports of stolen bicycles and awareness campaigns seek to educate both cyclists and motorists. But on a regular basis the stakes are raised by stories of escalating violence. In the latest such story, which has made news headlines, 'Jim' was accosted while riding alone in the Cradle on Saturday morning (11 August) and shot twice by men who then took his bike and shoes and escaped in a bakkie. Mere minutes later, hobbyist hiker Jon Jon Pietersen and his friend came across Jim lying on the side of the road. Pietersen had been out scouting for new locations for his hiking club, and they had decided to drive past the spot to see the white tiger kept at the Rhino and Lion park. It was pure chance that Jon Jon heard Jim's call for help. They immediately stopped and with the help of a second motorist, Jon Jon tried to stop Jim's bleeding using a single surgical glove, a towel and some tape. Miraculously, he managed to keep Jim alive until the ambulance arrived 20 minutes later. Jim is now recovering at home.

The latest and one of the most violent attacks on a cyclist took place in the Cradle of Humankind last Saturday. An unidentified cyclist (Jim) was shot twice by men who then drove away with his bicycle. In an act of heroism that has captured the imagination of the country, passerby Jon Jon Pietersen stopped to help and with nothing more than a single glove, a towel and some tape, stopped the bleeding long enough for Jim to be airlifted to hospital. Pietersen's heroism might restore faith in humanity - but the dark truth is that cyclists are increasingly at risk on our roads and off them. And it seems police and society alike are powerless to stop the escalating violence.

title: Centurion is sinking
oneLiner: Centurion south of Pretoria has shown rapid growth over the past few years.But the area is prone to huge sinkholes resulting in loss of property, jobs and livelihood..
summary:
The greater part of land in the area south of Pretoria is underlain by dolomite from the Chuniespoort Group of the Transvaal Supergroup. In South Africa dolomite rock has a notorious reputation for the formation of sinkholes and subsidences. Thousands of people reside and work in the Centurion area, where numerous sinkholes have occurred causing damage and in some instances loss of property. Centurion has rapidly densified over the last 40 years.

The City of Tshwane is plagued by 31 sinkholes as certain areas in Centurion and Pretoria East are prone to sinkholes. The City is making headway in repairing two giant sinkholes, in Centurion and Laudium, with most major repairs expected to be completed by the end of August. Parts of Jean Avenue that were swallowed by a large sinkhole last year will finally be opened to traffic, with phase one soon to be completed. The massive sinkhole affected businesses around the area, as the intersection of Jean Avenue and Gerhard Street was closed to traffic. “Geological investigations and repair methods are done. The repair of the sinkhole started in April after the rainy season and is 90% complete, with planned completion at the end of August. At least 460 square meters of the city is on dolomitic land, meaning certain areas in Centurion, Pretoria East and Laudium are prone to sinkholes. Not much can be done to prevent these disasters as they are largely caused by burst water pipes and storm water. The capital is now plagued by 31 sinkholes, with R27.5 million allocated in the previous financial year to repair five of the highest ranked. Two of them were repaired, while the remaining three were earmarked for completion in the first quarter of this year. R25 million has been set aside to repair three additional sinkholes. One of the main causes of sinkholes was aging infrastructure, especially in the Centurion and Laudium areas, MMC for corporate and shared services Cilliers Brink said. Business owners around Jean Avenue have felt the impact of the sinkhole in their pockets as many have lost revenue, and even staff, due to the large obstruction on the main road. But the city would not compensate businesses for loss of income unless it could be proven that it was caused by the sinkhole, Brink said. Centurion business people and motorists have been warned to brace themselves for another bumpy ride after news that the City of Tshwane could not complete repairs of the problematic Jean Avenue sinkhole. Business owners who were negatively affected by the sinkhole convinced the high court in Pretoria to order the City to commence construction earlier this year, when the City appeared to be doing nothing. They were convinced the municipality was moving at a snail's pace after discovering the sinkhole in May last year.Popular eatery NewsCafe, situated close to the damaged road, was forced to close its doors after 17 years of operation due to the sinkhole. Owner Gerry Kanaris was one of the many frustrated business people who wanted the City to step up efforts to fix the sinkhole. Esme Janse van Rensburg, of Zania Hair Salon said she lost some of her talented stylists because they did not make good commission with fewer clients coming in. Mimmos manager George Vurgarelles said his restaurant, like most businesses near the sinkhole, had lost income significantly since last year. He said he had been running a series of promotional specials to keep customers coming, but that yielded little return. Asia House waitress Anesipho Boots said business was bad because waiters needed tips. Car guards Godfrey Moyo and Malembe Mulambo now take turns in duties at the shopping complex near the sinkhole. One works for two days before the other takes over. Jean Avenue was previously used by at least 40000 commuters during peak hours every day. These people supported local businesses and the nearby Zenex petrol station. The informal settlement of Mooiplaas has also been affected. Residents have to be moved as the area is prone to sinkholes and formal structures cant be built. Mayor Msimanga has promised to move residents to Olievenhoutbosch. This has proved to be problematic as the houses earmarked are being occupied illegally and residents of Olievenhoutbosch has threatened with mass action if the relocation takes place. .

title: Xolani Gwala's fight for life
oneLiner: A devastating cancer diagnosis almost destroyed veteran broadcaster Xolani Gwala’s life. Now he’s in remission and using his journey to help others.
summary:
9 Months ago, beloved 702 Breakfast Host Xolani Gwala shocked listeners and colleagues alike with the devastating news that he'd been diagnosed with Stage 4 colon cancer. Taking an indefinite leave of absence to begin the battle of his life. Since the news, he has undergone several operations and 6 cycles of chemotherapy which he describes as brutal. Last we he made an emotional and welcome return to radio, standing in for Joanne Josephs on her show. Now in remission but not yet out of the woods, the outpouring of joy from 702 listeners & colleagues illustrated just how beloved Xolani is. Tonight on Carte Blanche we revisit Xolani's brave battle with cancer over the past 9 months, his prognosis for the future and how this amazing story can inspire fellow cancer survivors

For the last nine months, veteran television and radio broadcaster Xolani Gwala has been in the fight of his life, battling colon cancer. Now he’s in remission and using his journey to help others. How has this beloved television and radio broadcaster Xolani Gwala been able to overcome the biggest fight of his life?
experts: Mr. Xolani Gwala Mr. Robert Marawa Dr. Ormondi Ogude Dr. Bheki Gwala

title: Train sabotage is crippling Cape Towns economy
oneLiner: only 8 trains on the central line to carry 200 000 people to work, its crippling the Western cape economy
summary:
This is just the latest in a sustained campaign to sabotage Cape Town’s rail system, in January the central line was closed for 6 weeks forcing 1000’s of rail commuters onto the roads. To date no one can work out who or why there is this sustained attack on the trains. Some say it’s to cripple the DA in the Western Cape, others say it’s disgruntled Union members. On the Cape Flats line it’s clear that copper thieves are the main culprits for train sabotage and Metro rail are now building a massive wall from Bontehewel to Netreg Heideveld linked to Nyanga which is costing R70 million rand. This is to separate the line from encroaching shacks and therefoe easy access for copper thieves. Copper thieves are well armed and organised syndicates that attack railway repair staff. They have to work under heavily armed security but no sooner they do a repair it is stolen. Copper thieves are even digging under vendors stalls to access the copper.

Cape Town’s Metro Rail is under siege. 33 carriages have been destroyed in the last 4 months alone costing R140 million rand in damages. Since 2015 149 carriages have been destroyed. The last attempt at burning the trains happen this Tuesday when a seat was set alight just after they had reopened platform 3 and 4 after a fire on 21st July destroyed 6 carriages and 160 meters of copper cable. Fortunately commuters caught the perpetrator. The impact of thhis sabatague is having a worse effect on the Western cape economy than the drought. Speculation is rife as to who could be behind this concerted campaign and the arrest this week of a man trying to set carriages alight in Cape Town station has given investigators some hope that it may lead them to who is behind this. Some say its a third force, others say its a way to win back the Western cape from the DA.
experts: Mr. Brett Heron Mr. Richard Walker Mr. Janine Myberg Ms. Leigh Jansen Mr. Sapho Wulana Mr. Emile O Brein Mr. JP Smith

title: Lewis Pugh and his biggest swim yet
summary: In 1875, Captain Matthew Webb became the first person to swim from Dover to Calais. Since then, some 1,800 people have swum across the English Channel. But no one has ever swum its entire length. Until this summer. On the 12th July extreme swimmer, Lewis Pugh donned his goggles, swimming cap and speedo and got into the water at Land’s End, Cornwall UK and started his biggest challenge yet. He is aiming to swim the full length of the English Channel, from Land’s End to Dover. This 560 km distance is the equivalent to 16 English Channel crossings and will take an estimated 50 days depending on tide and weather. In his words “ I am undertaking my toughest swim yet so that I can call …on all the governments of the world to strengthen our ocean protection.” Lewis Pugh’s mission is to clean up our oceans “ our world needs clean and healthy seas. And we are the only ones who can make that happen.” This swim will mark the beginning of a worldwide campaign to ensure that 30% of our oceans are fully protected by 2030. Since the start it’s been a riveting 13 days. Lewis is made for television: his pieces to camera; interviews; the visuals of the swim and the team work between the boat and his swim make great television- his encounters with the dolphins, sun fish and sharks and not so wonderful jelly fish, the visuals of the plastic pollution, the crew’s dancing on deck to keep Lewis motivated and the people from extreme swimmers to surfers to just people who like swimming who have joined Lewis on sections of his swim…. But it’s Lewis deeper insight into his mission that stays with you which is maybe why Prince Charles met up with him on Day 5 in St Agnes, Lewis wearing sneakers and shorts made for a much more intimate meeting than the usual Royal encounter.
caseStudies: Lewis Pugh Extreme Swimmer

title: Emfuleni Drowning in Sewage.
oneLiner: A total collapse in infrastructure and service delivery has the towns of Vereeniging and Vanderbijl Park drowning in sewage.
summary:
Community unrest and sabotage has stopped workers from entering the Sebokeng water treatment plant. The closure for several weeks has resulted in 150 Mega Liters of raw sewage flowing into the Rietspruit daily. The Rietspruit Waste Water Treatment Plant's effluent is also pumped into the Riet river.This then flows into the Vaal and the raw sewage has now reached the town of Parys. Everywhere you go in the district sewage pumps are overflowing. Not only is it flowing into the rivers but you find raw sewage in suburban streets and in residents properties.

The Emfuleni local municipality is one of three local municipalities comprising the Sedibeng District in Gauteng. Its the western most municipality in the district with the Vaal river at its southern border. In June Emfuleni was put under administration because of its inability to provide adequate service delivery and due to allegations of maladministration. Gauteng Premier David Makura has promised to rescue the embattled municipality. However it took a court order by the "Save the Vaal" civil organisation to move the province to intervention. Eskom and Rand Water have threatened to shut down services as the council owes millions.The towns of Vereeniging and Vanderbijl Park experience electricity cuts for up to three days per week and water pressure is being throttled. Low water pressure has been hindering surgeries at the Sebokeng hospital. The collapse in infrastructure maintenance has caused many of the sewage pumps to spill

title: DURBAN BOMB THREATS
oneLiner: A spate of bomb scares are terrorizing the people of Durban - are we dealing with terror attacks? Extortion? Or just simply very dangerous attention seeking?
summary:
Panic spreads through Durban as 10 bomb scares in three weeks in public shopping areas raise questions that police can’t seem to answer – who is behind it and what could they hope to achieve? The main theory for the motive behind the placing of incendiary devices in Durban seems to lean to wards Extortion rather than terrorism - Pay up or face the fire. But with targets getting bigger – are we dealing with a potential lonewolf with dangerous intentions as he becomes increasingly infamous.

- topical - not being addressed properly by authorities - panic and paranoia spreading

Researchers in the United Kingdom have successfully grown the world's first crop of barley using nothing but robot tractors and drones. The project's aim was to have no operators in the driving seats of the machines or have any agronomists set foot into the 1-hectare paddock.

This is cutting edge technology in agrculture.

title: "Give me Shelter"
oneLiner: Statistics show that Durban has approximately 4000 Homeless people living on the street or in Shelters. What is being done for these destitute citizens by the City claiming to be the Most Caring in
summary:
We take a real look at the lives behind the faces of destitute homeless folks in Durban. We spend the day with Homeless woman Serena Bather who wants to share her story with us. From riches to rags, she will show us where she once lived in an upmarket Durban suburb and then to her old haunts and places she slept on the streets, on the beach and under bridges. We go undercover into some of the worst shelters in SA and see how the Homeless are forced to live in filthy places they pay for per night for. Often exploited these folk have lost all hope of a better life and more importantly their dignity. We will see where little children are raised among drug lords and sex workers, born into a web they often never escape. We confront the Municipality and talk to NGOs about thier on going efforts to help these people from their marginalised situations to gain some sort of momentum to claw their way out from this horror of an existence.

Durban, touted by the Safer Cities wing of the Municipality as an International Tourism Mecca and "The most liveable and caring City in SA" has an ugly truth in plain sight for those who care to see it, as approximately 4000 homeless people live on the streets or in filthy Shelters, where they are exploited and often abused. Despite fantastic research on the Homeless in the City that was tabled, bought to council and passed in 2016 nothing has been done in 2 years. We investigate why promises to improve the lives of Durban's destitute have not been fulfilled and who is responsible for this total neglect of citizens and their basic human rights.

title: CB SPECIAL: The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela
oneLiner: This is a documentary, on the centenary of his birth, to celebrate and reveal new information about South Africa’s greatest icon.
summary:
On July 18th, Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela would have turned 100 years. This is a documentary, on the centenary of his birth, to celebrate and reveal new information about South Africa’s greatest icon. For the best part of 10 years the Nelson Mandela Foundation and South African National Archives have been collecting and assembling letters written by Nelson Mandela during his 27 years incarceration. Poignant, impassioned, gripping and always inspirational the letters – many of them never seen before by the public - provide new insight into how Mandela maintained his inner spirits while living in almost complete isolation and how he engaged with the outside world that became increasingly outraged by his plight as his imprisonment dragged into its fourth decade. A landmark book, *“The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela” - the first and only authorised and authenticated collection of correspondence spanning the 27 years Mandela was held as a political prisoner - will be released a week before Mandela’s Birthday. In perfect synchronicity our documentary Mandela 100 will reveal some of the most poignant, the most witty, the most dramatic of his letters.

For 27 years of Mandela’s life in prison his sole source of comfort, his only contact with his family and friends was the occasional visit and letters…letters he received and letters he wrote. From the very beginning Mandela was a prolific letter writer with both personal and official letters. Every letter was copied into an A4 hard covered notebook. These have been stored in boxes locked away in the State Archives. In celebration of Mandela’s 100th Birthday they are finally seeing the light of day.

title: HSCT THERAPY FOR MS
summary: HSCT or Hematopioetic Stem Cell Transplant, is to date the only scientifically proven treatment that STOPS underlying disease progression in all types of MS and restores normal immune self-tolerance and produces lasting curative symptomatic improvement for the majority of MS patients. It is not a new procedure as such, as it has been used to treat cancer since the 1960’s, but it is a relatively new treatment for MS. The term multiple sclerosis means ‘many scars’. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an unpredictable, often disabling disease of the central nervous system that disrupts the flow of information within the brain, and between the brain and body. MS symptoms vary widely and include blurred vision, weak limbs, tingling sensations, unsteadiness and fatigue. For some people, MS is characterised by periods of relapse and remission while, for others, it has a progressive pattern. For everyone with MS, it makes life unpredictable. With the treatment of HSCT for MS, comes the hope of stopping the progression of the disease and the opportunity of looking forward to a future. MS has no known cause/s as yet. There is no drug that can cure MS. HSCT as a treatment for MS, was discovered by chance by Dr Burt at North Western University, Chicago. He started HSCT treatment back in 1996. He noticed that the leukemia patients he was treating needed to be “re-vaccinated” because the protection from childhood diseases like the measles and mumps was being lost. The cells affected by transfusion treatments were losing the “memory” of these original childhood vaccinations. He started with trials in the lab to see if this treatment would be successful for autoimmune diseases and it worked. Then the FDA approved the procedure of adult stem cell therapy to be used on people suffering from Multiple Sclerosis. HSCT treatment involves transplanting stem cells, in the hopes that the new cells won’t have the properties that caused the body to attack itself and will create healthy new cells. Before the transplant, patients are given a high dose of an immunosuppressant regimen for six days. There is no ethical dilemma as the treatment uses adult stem cells extracted from the patients own blood, and no embryonic stem cells are involved.

title: Hard Hit Economy
oneLiner: Is the cost of daily living exhausting your resources? Well, you are not alone. Carte Blanche’s exclusive economic report explains why spiraling debt is gripping the nation.
summary:
Carte Blanche looks at the impact on markets and industries and the effects on struggling middle to higher income earners. The rapid and record increases in fuel prices, the impending rise of municipality rates, together with the VAT hike, have combined to hit the real estate industry hard. Not to mention the barriers put up by the banks with their reluctance to provide bond opportunities for middle income earners. So, housing sales are stagnant. To add to the economy’s woes, motorists are defaulting payments, risking repossessions and such luxuries as eating out have become unaffordable as consumers make cuts to their life style in a bid to make ends meet. Economist Trinity Ncube suggests that central factors creating the current economic crisis are the weak Rand, the rising price of oil and the political climate engendered by policies such as Land Expropriation Without Compensation. While the cost of living is rising inexorably, there has been little to no increase in income for the working class, particularly in the private sector. The outcome for consumers being, that they have lost about 25 to 30 percent in buying power. When compiling the report, Trinity focused on middle income earners (ranging between an income of R16500 to R35000). Especially striking is the observation that for people earning the low middle income of about R16500, then the effect of the recent price escalation is to have pushed these earners back into a poverty income range.

South African consumers have been hard hit in recent months and their future looks certain to get worse. A VAT increase in April, frequent fuel price hikes and rising electricity costs are taking their toll. Carte Blanche has an exclusive report, from economist Trinity Ncube, which reveals the knock on effects of these core increases. Earlier this year Carte Blanche forecast that people's buying power would decrease by 20%, but just three months later Trinity Ncube’s report shows that, in fact, consumers buying power has decreased by 25 to 30 percent. How are ordinary South African's coping with this extra burden on their pockets?

title: Health Care in Crisis
oneLiner: The Health Ombudsman says Health Care is in crisis, Minister Motsoaledi says its only distressed but doctors on the ground say hospitals have become a death trap.
summary:
South Africa's Public Health System is a country wide network of care facilities ranging from mobile and rural clinics to large academic hospitals in urban areas. The public sector is hugely under resourced. Bad management by provinces and corruption play a big role .While the state contributes about 40% of all expenditure on health, the public sector is under pressure to deliver services to about 80% of a growing population. The situation is compounded by health challenges such as HIV and TB and a shortage of medical personnel. Researching and interviewing the situation on the ground, we have uncovered some horror stories told by patients and doctors in public hospitals. Patients dying of septicemia, not being fed properly, patients booked for theater cancelled because theater nurses have exhausted their overtime.

Health Ombudsman Professor Makgoba recently stated that the Public Health Care System is in crisis. In a report tabled in parliament in June, the Office of the Health Standards Compliance told the parliamentary committee that only 5 of the 696 hospitals and clinics inspected passed the 80% criteria. 696 Hospitals is only a fifth of the 3 816 public health care facilities in South Africa. Bad management and negative attitude of staff is stated as part of the problem.

title: Ministry of Crime
oneLiner: For 2 years Mandy Wiener delved into what she has called the Ministry of Crime
summary: no holds barred interviews with the players

title: "Trafficked"
oneLiner: In 2018, some may consider the idea of Modern Day Slavery, a terrible myth; the reality is this sordid practice is not only real, but also happening in ever increasing waves in South Africa.
summary:
We look at the case of Miguel Louw abducted from outside his school. Human trafficking is on the increase in SA and Miguel is just one case of many children that get caught up in a trafficking Syndicate. His abductor is in custody. His mother and Uncle have agreed to talk to us. Zama was lured into a sex trafficking syndicate at the age of 12 and was rescued 6 years later from a Lodge in Durban. Her abductors received life imprisonment which is part of the legislation. Advocate Dawn Coleman comments on the Legislation and penalties for human trafficking. Nxo's little girl was abducted from church on New Year's day. She has not been seen for 6 months. Her father cries each day for his child. Col. Mbehle is the spokesperson for missing children SAPS. She will answer questions about the Police procedures and cols cases etc.

Modern Day Slavery, the illegal trade of human beings, is real‚ hidden in plain sight and tearing at the social fabric of the nation as the demand for cheap labour and sexual services keeps growing. Durban is a perfect source for the supply and demand of trafficked victims, both male and female. Termed Modern Day Slavery, the sordid practice which is growing daily. Children, women and men are simply taken, transported, sold and abused, with coercion, abduction, fraud and deception being the common denominators. Victims that are rescued from the hands of their cruel captors, often take a lifetime to heal and rehabilitate while more like them are tricked and trapped daily. Human trafficking is indiscriminate as victims both male and female are sourced from all socio economic and racial groups in SA.
caseStudies: Elizabeth Thoko Mandla Cele Goodness Thoko Dinesh Naidoo
experts: Ms. Advocate Dawn Coleman-Malinga Mrs. Gloria De Gee Mrs. Soraya Smith

title: Junior Doctors Need Life Support
summary:
The constant failure by government and provinces to adequately fund internship and community service placements for graduating health professionals represents a serious human resource challenge as well as ethical disquiet. The issue stems from a lack of funded posts and insufficient accredited hospitals to host and train medical graduates. Minister Motsoaledi blamed the lack of foresight and planning for the shortage of junior doctor posts. The national health department oversees the process, but it depends on provinces who runt the hospitals to create an fund the posts, Most of the unplaced applicants are foreign graduates hoping to join the SA workforce. Many hospitals are currently understaffed. In KZN Manguzi, Mosveld, Umphumulo, Stanger and Untunjabili are just a few facing doctor shortages affecting patient care and placing increasingly heavy burdens on the remaining staff. Why then are so many junior doctors forced to sit at home? Until they have completed their community year they are not employable as doctors in SA. The government has legislated that junior doctors do community service but now many are forced into unemployment and not able to complete their training.

Junior doctors have blamed the government's lack of planning for the emotional roller coaster they faced about starting their compulsory community service. Although most S.A born junior doctors have been placed in public hospitals, the future remains unclear for foreign graduates with permanent residency in SA. With the mid year application process opening soon , just under 200 junior doctors have still not been placed.

title: Bad Driving
oneLiner: South African roads are a dangerous place to be. We look at how we are contributing to this death trap.
summary:
South Africa is not for sissies. The country is rife with violence and danger and our roads are no exception. The average driver is quick to point fingers at taxi's, saying they are the cause of our bad reputation, but the fact is that we are all very bad drivers. It is relatively easy to get the initial drivers test and from there on you have a paper saying you can drive, even though you may not be very good at it. Our traffic laws are fairly comprehensive but there is very little enforcement and virtually no serious legal consequence, so of course people will take the change and send the text, answer the phone, skip the red light or speed along the highway. We simply have no discipline on the roads. Coupled with the fact that we have a serious shortage of Code 14 drivers in SA it means that inexperienced and sometimes unqualified people end up driving trucks on our roads. Some insurers have programmes that reward good driving (Like Discovery Drive Vitality). Anton Ossip will speak to the effectiveness of the programme (Specifically at Discovery) as well as what are some of the common transgressions. We will also take a look at how drivers qualify as so-called good drivers.

We have a lot of viewer contributions of bad driving. Showing people overtaking on solid lines, ignoring red lights, pushing in... even accidents. South African drivers rate amongst the worst in the world. In 2017 we lost 17,014 people on SA's roads and according to research 90% of the fatalities are as a result of human error/bad driving. Drivers are arrogant and disobey even the smallest of road rules like texting while driving on adhering to speed limits.
experts: Mr. Layton Beard Automobile Association of SA Mr. Anton Ossip CEO Discovery Insure Ms. Chantal Gray Managing Director Nosa Logistics Dr. Nicola Taylor Mr. Wayne Minaar

title: Peta's Angora video: Truth or fabrication?
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche: Angora goats are known for their exotic hair but in a recent video by an animal rights organisation that shocked the world disturbing visuals of goats in distres
summary:
According to Peta they visited 12 angora farms in the Karoo and “documented pervasive cruelty to animals at every single farm”. “Shearers threw angora goats; cut off swaths of their skin, and cut conscious animals’ throats. Workers picked up goats by the tails, likely breaking them. One farmer dumped rams into tanks of cleaning solution and shoved their heads into the liquid, which he admitted would poison them if they swallowed it.” They continue by saying: “workers punched holes in goats’ ears with pliers, causing the animals to scream. There is no doubt that the visuals are highly disturbing to watch, but look deeper and every single scene has been explained to us in detail by experts on what is standard acceptable procedures and not harmful to the animals in any way as Peta claimed. Par for the one scene where the adult goats are being handled roughly by shearers who were obviously in a hurry to finish, the rest of the scenes are not ‘cruel to animals’ as they claimed. Most consumers have no first hand knowledge of farming practices passed by the NSPCA and independent auditors. Farmers work with strict guidelines on sustainable practices and are controlled by independent organisations like Mohair SA to regulate and monitor farmers. Angora goats are highly sensitive animals and a farmer will go out of his way to ensure that his animal is treated in the best way as this is his ‘bread and butter’.

The video, produced by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or Peta, went viral on the 1st of May and since over 100 brands have threatened to stop using mohair in their clothing range. Peta is the largest animal rights organisation in the world with 6.5 million members and supporters. Their top video this month on the angora practices in South Africa, is headlined: “PETA has decimated the angora industry. Now let’s win against mohair!.” In 2015 they destroyed the angora rabbit fur industry in China and their next target was the mohair industry in South Africa. In this 4 minute video produced by Peta they claim “goats are thrown, cut and killed for mohair,” and are calling on a total ban of all mohair products from South Africa. The message resonated strongly as already international brands like Zara, Gap, H&M, Mango, Topshop, Banana Republic, Esprit, Old Navy, Athleta have agreed to take all mohair products off their 2020 winter range. This could spell the end of the mohair industry for South Africa, the potential loss 30 000 jobs and a R1.5 billion rand industry closing down. Peta promotes a total vegan lifestyle and say “animals are not ours to eat, wear, experiment on, use for entertainment or abuse in any way.” They are known to go to extreme lengths to create sensational news and often reported in the media as ‘getting their facts wrong.’ And on every news story where they feed on the emotions of the consumer, the ‘donate’ tab is in bold. Money speaks loudest and rumours has it that their biggest donors are from the oil companies. This has a twofold implication: promoting of synthetic fibres and secondly, an urban myth that the angora farms are smack back in the middle of the Karoo where fracking is said to take place. (our story will not cover these points as that will need far more investigation and possibly a follow up).

title: Low Cost Lessons for SAA
oneLiner: SAA has embarked on yet another cost-cutting exercise designed to return the airline to profit, but is it an old fashioned solution to a modern problem?
summary:
In explaining the national carrier's latest bid for a government guarantee, SAA's executive pointed out that unprofitable routes, inefficient planes and a bloated staff were among the reasons for its financial woes. The answer, apparently, would be to reduce the number of aircraft, cut unprofitable routes and limit frequency. In other words, downsize your way to profitability and, in the process, inconvenience your customer while providing a gap to your competitors. The question is: why does SAA find it so hard to make a profit on even the busiest of routes when other airlines, like Kulula locally and Ethiopian internationally are almost always in the black? That question becomes even more bothersome when you consider that you can fly from Jo'burg to Cape Town on Kulula for R900 return and from Jo'burg to Dublin on Ethiopian for R7000 - both substantially cheaper than SAA. Perhaps the lesson lies not in rampant downsizing, but in being more innovative. Why, in 2018 does SAA still serve meals on domestic routes? Why, in 2018, does SAA still have business class seats on domestic routes? Why, in 2018, are you unable to pre-pay for an economy class seat in a more comfortable part of the cabin on long-haul flights? These are some of the low cost innovations that other airlines have embraced. Each has the potential to add to the bottom line, and create an opportunity for growth rather than cuts.

Is cutting costs, aircraft and routes the secret to turning around an ailing, bail-out dependent airline? Efficiency is certainly one ingredient in the profitability recipe, but there are suggestions that SAA's backwardness is what's cooking its goose. And, we're going to fly from Dublin to Prague for less than a 1000 bucks to show you why.
caseStudies: Linden Birns MD, Plane Talking

title: Steinhoff, House of Cards
oneLiner: Beleaguered Steinhoff's web of complex accounting shenanigans came to light recently when the company revealed their situation as fragile and in desperate need of a short term solution.
summary:
On the 6th of December 2017, Steinhoff International CEO Markus Jooste announced his resignation amid the retail giants admission of irregularities in its financial accounts. The Steinhoff share price plummeted wiping R121 billion from its market capitalization. It wiped billions off the net worth of tycoons such as Christo Wiese and GT Ferreira, and of the pension funds of millions of ordinary South Africans. Jooste had built a house of cards. He would allegedly lend money to a company domiciled in Europe but never disclosed that the European company was run by a related party close to Jooste. Steinhoff would then charge interest on that loan, which would recognize in the income statement as revenue. For all intents and purposes, it was a fictitious debtor: that main debt would never be repaid and that debt would be classified as "cash and cash equivalents in Steinhoffs books. this resulted in operating cash flow not matching the profit it reports in its books. The bottom line: Steinhoff's revenue was artificially inflated, and so were the assets.

We ask Dr Christo WIese if and how Markus Jooste deceived him and the entire Steinhoff Board board comprising of accountants. How could he not have seen this happening? Steinhoff latest note to shareholders reflects a company heading towards liquidation. In a presentation to bankers in London recently, Steinhoff admitted that there are several very valuable businesses within the group but that the current position is fragile and the need for a solution in the short term is critical. The list of shareholders suing the company is starting to look as if they believe the company will be broken up or liquidated. Steinhoff is being sued by ex-chairman Christo Wiese for R59 billion and by prominent banker GT Ferreira for R1.5 billion. Tekkie Town has filed for a reversal of the Steinhoff acquisition claiming the sale was done on fraudulent terms. We will speak to experts trying to find answers on how it was possible for Markus Jooste to construct the scheme that saw the company plunge intoa scandal. Who was in on it? Whas Steinhoff's board deceived or party to the House of Cards.

title: Hook to Cook
summary:
Abalobe is an organisation that is enabling subsistence fishermen to get organised, access local markets, and keep track of fish stocks and their own finances on their smartphones. It also allows customers to learn more about the fish they are eating and about the life of the person who caught it through a QR code (two-dimensional barcode) which they access when their plate of fish is served. And the process gives fisheries researchers access to a host of local data. This app has value for fishermen, fishing co-operatives, monitors, fishing managers and seafood retailers. One of the biggest advantages of this app is that chefs are now offering a far wider range of fish on their menus - fish like Black bream, locally known as “Hottentot” is now being sold in top-end restaurants like Catharina’s on the Steenberg Wine Estate in Contantia. It’s taking the pressure off well-known fish and creating a market for fish that were previously seen as low-value. David Shoshola, a 3rd generation Lamberts Bay fisherman, says that it’s taken the pressure off the high value catches like crayfish. Crayfish licences are becoming extremely difficult to access and are closely linked with crime syndicates. David can now sell fish like Black bream - previously only marketable in the village for very little - at the same price as yellowtail. For the first time in years he doesn’t care that he doesn’t have a crayfish licence because he can sell fish throughout the year at a consistent price. The most important app for fishermen is the “dashboard”: here they log exactly what was caught, how many fish, how much it was sold for, weather conditions, who caught it and who bought it, what the cost of petrol was, and what they earned. This data has many spin offs.

Finally eating local fish can be done with a clean conscience without worrying whether the fish you are eating is having a disastrous impact on the ocean, or if it’s travelled across the continent to reach your plate. A series of Smartphone apps are changing artisanal fishermen’s lives, enabling them to sell fish to restaurants that is not only locally caught, but also fully traceable. This direct access to the restaurants is disrupting the supply chain and putting money directly into the pockets of subsistence fishermen. It’s making sustainably, traceable fish a reality in 22 restaurants across the Western Cape. Its a good news fishing story where fishermen are succeeding in an environment where most fishing stories are negative and its only the big players that are succeeding. Technology on smartphones is empowering the small guys

summary:
The church uses indoctrination and some very questionable teachings to convince members to basically leave every decision they make in life in the hands of the church elders. This has led to families breaking up, divorces and people handing over their life savings and properties to the church.

Christ in Me is a church based in Pretoria, with branches in places like Polokwane and Heidelberg as well. They preach a peculiar form of Christianity. title: Holy Wars
oneLiner: The unprecedented violent attack and murder of members of the Imam Husain Mosque in Verulum, has sent shock waves throughout religious communities in Durban.
summary:
This violent attack on a Mosque is unprecedented with many in the community saying it is definitely a terrorist attack bearing all the Hallmarks of ISIS and other extremist groups that are currently in South Arica. The Moulana Aftab categorically states that this attack is due to inciting of the Sunni sect of Muslims, who make up a huge majority of Muslims, against the far smaller Shia group. Hate speech and messages on social media referring to Shia's as being enemies of Islam, have been an ongoing threat to the members of the small Shia sect - they believe is due to some differences in their application of the religion. Besides the "Holy War" that seems to be playing out - Abbas Essop's family have been left fractured and desperate for answers. Abbas has now been martyred as in South Africa Islmaic rule - he died as he lived a hero, protecting members of his mosque. To add to the Extremist theories - after SAPS had swept the Mosque for evidence and clues and the Mosque left open - the Carte Blanche team were allowed in to film the scene of pools of congealed blood, gas canister and burnt library. Later theMosque was again shut down to the public and a bomb device discovered under the Imam's chair. The suggestion therefore has been made that the attackers wanted to blow up the whole Mosque. We are tstill tracking the story and are been given access to the family of the deceased who want this story of bloody murder, arson and hate to be brought to the public's attention.

Never in the History of South Africa has there been an act of such violence, perpetrated in a religious place of worship, such as that committed on Thursday 10th May at the Shia Imam Hussein Mosque in Verulum, Durban. Three men entered the mosque grounds posing as worshippers and proceeded to brutally attack 3 members of the Mosque in the grounds of the building. All three victims had their throats cut and bodies butchered, with 2 surviving and tragically a young father Abbas Essop succumbing to his horrific stab wounds on the way to hospital. The assailants proceeded to burn the library down which contained a collection of Holy Books including many translations of the Muslim Holy Book the Koran. After the police had "swept" the scene for evidence a canister of spray paint, a pair of glasses and a bomb device was found under the Moulana's chair in the pulpit.

title: Drought, what drought?
oneLiner: With a water crisis looming in Gauteng, why is one of the main sources of supply, the Katse dam, left to spill billions of liters of water daily into an already overflowing Vaaldam.
summary:
The Lesotho Highlands Water Project is an ongoing water supply project developed by the Governments of South Africa and Lesotho. It comprises of several large dams and tunnels in Lesotho and delivers water to the Gauteng's main water supply source, the Vaal River System. A treaty was signed in 1986. SA has been locked into this treaty where a prescribed minimum flow was to be released irrespective of the state of the dams downstream in SA. Hence in this lies the problem.

With recent rains, the drought of 2014 to 2017 seems forgotten by some. But according to the Gauteng Premier David Makura, the province faces huge challenges when it comes to water supply. Gauteng uses 11% of the country's water while contributing 38% to the national economy. There are fears that if the Gauteng experiences another drought soon it might run out of water.

title: On top of the world - Journeyman Pictures
summary: On Top Of The World Greenland’s melting season starts earlier and finishes later than it used to, bringing some major changes to the Arctic island. How are the locals dealing with the shift, and is there any upside? “If you were to melt the whole Greenland ice sheet here, we’re talking about around seven metres sea level rise”, says Thomas Juul-Pedersen, a senior scientist at the Greenland Climate Research Centre. “There’s always been a melting season, but that melting season seems to dramatically increase", he says. Since the 1950s, the island's average temperature has risen 1.5 degrees, bringing droughts and even tundra fires. Now vast swathes of sandy desert sit alongside rapidly melting ice. "It hurts the heart", says Inuit photographer Adam Lyberth, who has spent 35 years documenting the changing landscape. But while Greenland's shifting seasons present a huge worldwide threat, for some on the island the warmer summers are a welcome change. "Climate change takes many surprising ways", says Teunis Jansen, who notes that the first mackerel was caught in Greenland in 2011. To give an indication of the speed of Greenland's climate change, within just a few years there were 85,000 tonnes of the warm water fish. "It corresponds to about 20-24% of the national export of Greenland", says Jansen.

title: Digital Voices
oneLiner: Technology is bridging the gap for those without a voice, but plenty to say.
summary:
Voice loss can be caused by innumerable factors: stroke, motor vehicle accident, motor neurone disease (MND), cancer... Many children born with cerebral palsy never develop spoken language. Lacking an intelligible voice does not mean you have nothing to say, but the voiceless are amongst society's most vulnerable, unable to express likes and dislikes, to refuse consent, or to report the abuse and neglect that so many face. Even for those lucky enough to have access to AAC devices, the voices available are robotic, unemotional, impersonal...lacking all of the elements of age, gender, and character with which we broadcast our identities. It was this problem that Rupal Patel decided to tackle after witnessing two AAC users, one a middle-aged man and one a young girl, speaking to each other with exactly the same synthesised adult male voice. She decided that even those who have never developed language should be able to speak with their own voices, and VocaliD was born. VocaliD synthesises voices for text-to-speech devices using the sounds vocalised by the disabled AAC user, filtered through the voice of a donor of similar age and background, to create a voice that is appropriate and unique to each user. VocaliD is the only company providing this service, but there are people everywhere working to help the voiceless speak. At Chris Hani Baragwaneth Hospital, the MND clinic offers message banking for those who will lose their voices to the disease. At New Hope School, Pretoria, one learner is making use of a text-to-speech device that speaks Afrikaans, part of a CSIR project to provide AAC in all 11 South African languages. We will take a look into the wide world of AAC, and shed light on some of the spectacular ways in which technology can help those without a voice participate in a society in which vocal expression is so central.

Augmentative and Alternative Communication devices have existed for as long as there have been people who need help in expressing what those of us take for granted every day.From something as simple as a piece of paper and a pen or a colour-coded board, to cutting edge programming and electronics, the range is endless. But increasingly, tablets, eye gaze technology and voice synthesis is helping those without a voice to speak for themselves, in their own unique way...and without having to sound like Stephen Hawking or Google Maps.
