title: Taxi Drones
oneLiner: We get a glimpse into the future of urban travel where roads become obsolete, as driver-less taxis take to the heavens in crash-free, pollution-free sky-ways.
summary:
Airbus Industries is best known as one of the two biggest global aircraft manufacturers. Its most iconic contribution to modern aviation being the massive A380 superjet. But, behind closed doors at a facility on the outskirts of Munich, the company has a team dedicated to delivering groundbreaking design in the field of unmanned flight. The team is headed up by South African, Jana Rosenmann, a commerce and international relations expert. One of their civil functions (they also have a military mandate) is to develop pilot-less - or autonomous - passenger drones. In conjunction with other multi-national corporations, such as Audi, significant progress has already been made. Airbus also has units in other parts of the world working on similar concepts. Meanwhile, across town, at the headquarters of Lilium, similar strides are being made with an equally impressive team of engineers but on far smaller budgets. This aeronautical start-up has already attracted significant investment, and has tested a vertical take-off and landing, autonomous craft capable of travelling at 300km per hour. Carte Blanche would visit both facilities for a detailed look at the latest in autonomous flight technology being developed by a multinational powerhouse on the one hand, and a slick, modern upstart on the other. Both are bringing the future to within touching distance.

Germany is fast becoming the epicentre of future transport engineering. Munich, Frankfurt, Cologne... all are home to companies working on secret projects aimed at solving the mounting urban mobility crisis. Growing city populations, congested roads and pollution have caused a major re-think around how we transport people safely, economically and in massive numbers. One solution is tapping into drone technology to develop crash-proof taxis capable of ferrying people across cities in double-quick time. Carte Blanche visits Germany, the epicentre of modern European engineering, to see first hand the cutting edge concepts taking us closer to a roadless world.
experts: Mr. Arthur Bradshaw ATS System Specialist

title: "The man behind the Crown - King Goodwill Zwelethini
oneLiner: Controversial character or a powerful Father figure, Zulu King Goodwill Zwelethini commands a notable position in today's democracy - we find out first hand, about The Man behind the Crown.
summary:
In an exclusive interview, the Zulu Monarch, Goodwill Zwelethini will give us his take on the current affairs of our country and his personal life experiences. A man of Tradition – The King is a traditionalist and strongly upholds the Zulu customs handed down through the generations. He still supports and promotes “Virginity Testing” and Polygamy. He is a husband to 6 wives and has 27 biological children and one “adopted’ son – Ishwar Ramlutchman. Ramlutchman's position is unique in the Kingdom as he was ceremonially adopted into the Zulu nation and declared “Prince Ishwar Ramlutchman Mabheka Zulu” on Heritage Day in 2016. A Man of Faith and Unity - King Goodwill stands strongly for the unification of all South African’s, regardless of colour, race or religion. Although he is a Catholic Christian, he has embraced the Hindu faith, and hosted Diwali celebrations and prayed with leaders of the Muslim faith. The Farmer - He enjoys riding on his tractors and sharing conversations with his farmers as they go about planting and harvesting the organic food he is passionate for his people to share in. We have access to archival footage and photographs of the king and will pick up shots that demonstrate his personal interaction with his people such as, riding on a tractor with a farmer and the presenter. For the love of “his’ children – King Goodwill has a soft spot for children and believes that they are the key to the peaceful and productive future of South Africa.

Carte Blanche has been invited to an exclusive audience with the King, where he will share his personal story, his future hopes and his Kingdom’s current battles. He will share tales of his longing for his deceased mother’s bones, discovery of her remains and their reinterment. He will tell us about his spiritual faith, his fervent passion for agriculture and his fierce defence of the Ingonyama Trust for which he is the registered owner of 60% of the land in KwaZulu Natal. He will outline the reasons for his vehement opposition to the ANC government’s bid to introduce ‘Land expropriation without compensation’. 2018, is for the Leader, a special year as it is his 70th birthday and 47th year of his reign. He became the 8th Zulu king upon the death of his father, King Cyprian Bhekuzulu kaSolomon, in 1968. The Prophecy and the revelation - The sovereign ruler will reveal to us, for the first time, a prophecy that was made regarding his rule some years ago. We will learn of its relevance and bearing.

title: Bone chilling
oneLiner: A new report on the lion bone industry exposes just how the department is enabling the cruel killing of our lions for profit
summary:
Only 20 000 wild lions remain across the entire African continent. An estimated 8000 of those lions are unashamedly exploited for profit in a cruel and hidden multimillion dollar business right under our noses in the Free State and the North West province. Carte Blanche first exposed the canned hunting business to South Africans in 1997. Twenty years later that industry has given way to a darker, crueler industry - the trading of thousands of lion skeletons, by farmers, Chinese middlemen and exporters and enabled by the DEA, under the leadership of Edna Molewa. In 2017, the South African Government issued an export quota of 800 lion skeletons from captive bred lions, but our sources have told us that thousands more are being exported to Vietnam, China and Laos. By making the trade in lion bones legal, the illegal trade is made easier.

Hi profile good interviews, and hopefully good confrontations

title: Being Transgender
oneLiner: Being transgender - what does it mean, and what is it like to live
summary:
Life is tough for most of us - in one way or another. The struggle for identity, for belonging, for purpose and community is mired into every life journey. For those who live outside of social averages and accepted norms the struggle is measureless. ELLE, a young transgender woman faces a relentless battle for identity every day. Elle is one the fortunate ones. She comes from a tolerant family, who understood from very early on, that she was more girl than boy. She says that growing up, she was gender fluid, and had a supportive space within which to explore her identity. Elle is making her way as a successful model and is an activist in the trans space in South Africa. SIYA born male, is a trans woman who was thrown out of her home at an early age because she identified female. She moves from shelter to shelter and is often ejected through fear and ignorance. Siya is homeless and without family, but in spite of the daily onslaught on her personhood, she has achieved remarkable things. She has a degree in architecture and is studying towards her masters. It’s bittersweet, since Siya can’t get a job while her born identity mismatches her chosen gender fit. The admin precludes her. These are some of the difficult things trans gender people face in South Africa. We explore the lived experience of being trans up close and personal through the experiences of Elle and Siya and their immediate social group. We get a broader perspective from Jabu at Iranti – an advocacy organization working with trans rights in Africa and we talk to a psychologist about the particular complications of being trans in a hetero-normative world.

Being trans is a generally misunderstood lifestyle. It's current, it's edgy, it's curious and it's mostly kept under the covers - we blow the covers back!
caseStudies: Siya

title: Land Grabs
summary:
This past weekend Pretoria was marred by illegal land invasion as incidents in Olievenhoutbosch, East Lynne and the Blue hills caught the headlines. Land grabs in South Africa, particularly in Pretoria, were encouraged about two years ago led by the comments made at the time by EFF leader Julius Malema when he said that people must occupy land where they see it. In Mahube, Mamelodi residents were up in arms after EFF supports erected shacks next to their homes following their leader’s message in 2016. Although Land grabbing is not a new thing in South Africa, it is a strange coincidence that this passed weekend’s incidents come just 2 weeks after parliament’s promise to the masses that the “Land is coming”. On Saturday 10th of March, the Tshwane metro police were forced to use rubber bullets on land invaders. According to Freddie Pienaar, DA ward councilor in East Lynne, the squatters begin erecting shacks along Jan Coetzee and Lanham roads. Freddie believes this was a move that had been planned for sometime although he cannot confirm the instigators. He had to call the Police and Land invasion authorities to come rescue the situation. At the same time in Mnandi, Olievenhoutbosch, residents were also shocked to see people in their privately owned properties marking spaces with poles and saying it now their land. An initiative led by a certain Peter Sealelo, a community leader in Olievenhoutbosch, members of the community have went out to camp on privately owned land claiming that it is unused land that they are now claiming for themselves. A similar case of land grabbing occurred in Blue Hills.

In the past few days illegal land occupation took an escalating turn. This follows the ANC and the EFF’s radical stance in parliament on Land expropriation without compensation. Raising tensions and misinformation has fueled aggravated individuals on the ground putting people’s homes and safety on the line as private property is invaded.

Rumour has it that he has a gambling problem and is funding it through the sale of the land. Farmers have complained that he has tremendous influence in the area and even the SAPS Land Invasion Unit not been able to stop the land grab.

50 Small scale farmers in Tea Estate in the Inanda area, woke up one morning to find their farms invaded and people marking plots to start construction of informal dwellings. According to the invaders the local chief of the Qadi tribe,Induna MB Ngcobo, sold the land to invaders for R30 000 to R40 000 per plot. The farmers have title deeds to the 10 hectares of land that they own individually. According to the chief, title deeds do not authorize their ownership and that the land all the way to Umhlanga belongs to him and the tribe.

title: Leaky Legacy

summary:

"This department has a long history of instability and financial mismanagement‚ and Scopa has resolved to open a criminal case against the department because of the R2.9bn overdraft that the department took with the Reserve Bank. The Committee has also resolved to engage with the National Treasury on the overdraft‚" the committee said in a statement. The committee took officials to task for failing to answer questions adequately at a hearing on Tuesday. It also laid into Nomvula Mokonyane‚ who was shifted from water affairs to the communications ministry in Monday's cabinet reshuffle. "Scopa had a scheduled hearing this morning with the department on irregular‚ fruitless and wasteful expenditure. The Committee had to cut the hearing short due to the failure of the department's officials to respond to the questions posed by Committee members. The department was appearing before Scopa for the third time after failing to respond to questions at two previous hearings‚" the committee said. "Scopa is concerned that it is ordinary people who are affected by the instability and financial mismanagement in this department‚ because South Africa is a water-stressed country. In reality‚ Minister Nomvula Mokonyane has left a department that has completely collapsed. It is worrying that she is now a Minister of Communications at a time when the South African Broadcasting Corporation is recovering."

We have done extensive research and have documents to back up our assertions and a perfect hook for our story.

Debt ridden state owned enterprises are in shambles to say the least. Eskom, SAA, PRASA are some of the SOEs that were collapsed by state capture under Jacob Zuma. More than once the country was downgraded by Ratings Agencies relegating South Africa to junk status and loss of investor confidence. Most importantly free education and the National Health Insurance were introduced without a clear plan of where their funding will come from. These are some of the issues Ramaphosa will inherit from the Zuma presidency and with unemployment at 26.7 percent, the new president has a lot of remedying to do to regain economic confidence. As welcome as the change in leadership is, it certainly has an insurmountable task ahead, but is Cyril Ramaphosa a guarantee to a brighter economic future for South Africa. Carte Blanche finds out.

Corruption, state capture, struggling SOEs and economic downgrades are words that colour the Jacob Zuma presidential legacy. With Parliament electing Cyril Ramaphosa as state president and the country oozing with optimism, will the South African economy reclaim the stability it has missed in the past nine years?

title: Eastern Cape Water Crisis
oneLiner: With dams running dry and few alternative sources, cities and towns in the Eastern might reach "Day Zero" sooner than Cape Town.
summary:
In the Eastern Cape the Amatole district has been declared a disaster area with taps having run dry already. The Nelson Mandela municipality's combined dam capacity stands at 25.17%. It is possible that the Kouga dam will run dry in March leaving the metro dependent on the Nooitgedacht scheme which supplies only half the cities water. The scheme sources water from the Gariep dam through the Sundays River valley.the Nelson Mandela Bay municipality said nothing has been confirmed yet around "day zero. Local and national governments lack of coherent water supply policy has contributed to the current crisis. Failing and inadequate infrastructure and poor maintenance has largely contributed to the water crisis. The towns of Patensie and Hankey have used all of their water quota and taps will dry run soon. The Department of Water and Sanitation had in 2017 slashed the authorized maximum withdrawal for use by Hankey and Patensie by 25%

South Africa's cyclical and perennial droughts, along with ageing and inadequate infrastructure, poor maintenance, planning and capacity constraints at local and government level, are being blamed for 'Day Zero" when taps run dry.

title: The State's Legal War
oneLiner: What picture emerges from the litany of recent judgments going against the president, his top ministers and parliament? What does it say when our highest courts need to take matters in hand?
summary:
The state is by far the biggest litigant in our courts. Hundreds of cases are ongoing against national, provincial and local government departments and at any given time. But in the last year and a half, the highest levels of the state, such as the president and parliament, has been lambasted in certain high level cases about their behaviour and ordered to take steps to remedy it. The court’s have also taken the executive to task when it litigates “recklessly” with no chance of success. While briefly referencing cases such as the Al-Bashir matter and the nuclear procurement matter, we will unpack the following cases to illustrate how the state has been slammed by the country’s highest courts and the consequences for the state. In edit we will use a clever editing device to move from one case to the next. Links will also be cleverly scripted before the shoot to naturally flow from one point/court case into the next. We will look at the following cases in detail. 1. The review of the Public Protector’s State Capture report, ConCourt, December 2017 2. The Nkandla Judgment, ConCourt, April 2016, and the subsequent Impeachment Judgment, Concourt, December 2017 3. 3. The Sassa social grants case, Concourt, March 2017 and the inquiry currently underway 4. The NPA/Mxolisi Nxasana judgement, High Court, December 2017

What picture emerges from the litany of recent judgments going against the president, his top ministers and parliament? What does it say when our highest courts need to take matters in hand to force the top executive - President Jacob Zuma, his Cabinet, the National Authority of Parliament to do what they are actually just supposed to do being in those positions? Why is it necessary for any political party or labour union or civil society to go to court to ask judges to rule and make it a court order to see change? The last 18 months have seen several judgments going against decisions made by pres. Jacob Zuma, his top ministers and Parliament. In many of these cases, the courts have ordered the president, parliament and ministers to do their jobs - and often even ordered them to pay up for the legal costs too. We sketch the big picture of the cumulative effect of these judgments and look at the implications of such judgments being delivered against the state. With President Jacob Zuma's future seriously hanging in the balance and the President meeting with the the ANC's top six officials over his future this coming weekend, it adds to speculation that President Zuma could be removed as head of state. This is exactly where these judgments delivered against the state are even more significant - because they all happened under Zuma's watch and many were delivered directly against him or against decisions he acted on. We look at some of the major judgments in which the highest levels of the executive, like the Presidency and Parliament, has been lambasted in over the last 18 months and the consequences of these playing out at the moment. In many of these cases, the state has also launched appeal after appeal, driving up the costs even further. We will estimate the costs of these cases to the state, and ultimately to the taxpayer.

He became involved in illicit activities, and it was up to his coach Alex Heath and his father John Speelman to bring him back from the brink.

Skiing is not the sport of choice in South Africa for obvious reasons, but for Sive Speelman, it was an option as he grew up in rural eastern cape near South Africa’s only ski resort at Tiffendell, near the Drakensburg Mountains. Sive was in a Carte Blanche story on the resort back in 2008, and is now on the Winter Olympic team for 2018 in Pyeongchang, South Korea. He is the first black skier from South Africa. He qualified in 2014 for Sochi but was bitterly disappointed when SASCOC decided not to send him for monetary reasons. He is again on the team and has qualified and again, they may not send him, even though they have put a lot of money into developing him as a talent, and have sent him around the world.

title: Madswimmer and a new world record
summary: December 2017, 20 swimmers will attempt to do the fastest 100 km swim in one day. This has never been done before, if they succeed this will be a world record. And a once in a lifetime event. The Agulhas current, which flows down the South East coast of Mozambique, along the Transkei and Kwa Zulu Natal coast is one of the fastest and strongest flowing ocean currents in the world. It reaches a speed of 9.3 km per hour and 20 bold swimmers have been selected through swimming trials, (they needed to comply with a swim, speed criteria of over 3,25km/h over a long distance) will use this current to swim 100 km in one day – daylight hours. Daring: Besides the speed they are after, swimmers will be in shark waters with no shark protection to create awareness of shark and ray species that are on the verge of extinction. This is the latest adventure of the Madswimmer team in the pursuit of a second world record. Madswimmer is a registered, charity who do extreme open water swims to raise money for a variety of children’s charities and orphanages. Every swimmer carries his/her own expenses to take part in this swim, from travel, accommodation to anything related to their swim. They are also expected to raise money….and every rand raised supports children in need. .

title: Bush racing
oneLiner: It is known as bush riding - a brutal and inhumane sport organised by gangsters that forces retired racehorses to run themselves literally to death. Carte Blanche investigates.
summary:
It was the Wednesday before Easter Weekend. When most families were getting ready to celebrate this special time of the year, Michael Brand was in a state of anxiety. He bought a horse from Jenny Middleton who runs a rehoming centre for retired race horses in Phillip on the Cape Flats last Saturday. Max was a six year old mare in good shape and there was an immediate bond between the two. Michael was eager to fetch Max that Saturday. But then his plans went astray when he got a call from Jenny saying that Max was missing. The fence of the property was cut and both Max and another horse, named Wavin Flag was taken. Jenny’s immediate fear was that the horses were stolen for bush racing. With a large bush racing meeting scheduled for the Cape Flats over easter weekend, fears ran high that the horses had been stolen for illicit racing. Michael got onto social media and with the news shared on various platforms and the help of SAPS stock theft unit, a PI and drone surveillance footage Max and Wavin Flag was eventually found on Easter Friday in the dunes of Rocklands near Mitchells Plain. The recovery team was surrounded by a fairly hostile crowd of people leading to further speculation that the racing might have been linked to gangs who run the horses for bets, akin to cock fighting and dog figiting rings. When Michael saw Max his fears were confirmed. “Max could not even get into the horse box by himself, it took 10 of us to load him in,” he remembers. Back at the centre Jenny was waiting with a vet to attend to the animals. “They’d obviously been galloped into the ground” says Jenny as their mouths had wires through them and were bleeding and you could see straightaway that Max’s leg did not look good.” X Rays revealed that Max had sustained serious injuries, including fracturing his sesamoids beyond repair and due to the extent of his injuries the decision was made to euthanise him humanely.

Retired race horses are forced to run beyond their limits on tar roads, often around blocks of houses leading to severe animal cruelty and abuse. Controlled by gangs and suspected ringleaders the sport of bush racing has been difficult to crack down by law enforcement. The SPCA lacks the funds and so this inhumane sport continues to grow in the Western Cape amongst the coloured communities.

title: The mayor versus the minister
oneLiner: A battle is brewing between the mayor of Cape Town and the minister of Energy. Stand by to see how your city will be affected
summary: The mayor versus the minister This story began in November 2015 when the City of Cape Town decided they wanted to do things differently. Like all the metro’s Eskom has always supplied their current needs. The city wanted to diversify. With the advent of renewable energy – suddenly they had a choice. now they could get cheaper and cleaner electricity. The advantages are obvious, renewables are now cheaper per kilowatt hour and the city has a constitutional and statutory duty to find the cleanest and cheapest electricity to provide for its citizens. This is mandated across a range of legal provisions in the constitution, the local government and municipal systems act and the Electricity regulation act of 2006, so legally the city is on a sound footing. But, there is a catch. Any Independent power producer who wants to sell its electricity to the city has to be licensed by Nersa to do that. In itself that shouldn’t be an obstacle. But section 34 of the electricity Regulation act vests a range of powers in the minister of Energy, and Nersa would not give the go- ahead to the city, until the minister said so.

title: The Children's Flight
oneLiner: Volunteer pilots prepare for hundreds of children from all over Johannesburg -- to take to the sky for the first time and inspire a generation of children with the gift of flight.
summary:
Many people don’t think anything of hopping on a flight to Cape Town or Durban for the weekend. But for underprivileged children around Johannesburg, just getting to set foot on an airfield can be an awe-striking experience and a dream come true. The organizers behind The Children’s Flight aim to do just that with their annual event. Children from all parts of Johannesburg, all backgrounds, and all abilities are invited to the airport to experience their first flight. Felix Gosher and Michael Ferguson, the co-founders of the event, say it’s nearly tripled in size since last year (from 126 kids to nearly 400), and the response from the community has been truly remarkable. In this segment, we’ll spend a day in the life with two young people living in difficult circumstances -- 16 year old Doris in the mining township of Durban deep, whose mother has polio, and her family unable to pay her school fees; and 8 year old Chimdiebere, deaf since birth and living in Tembisa with a large family that often overlooks him, leaving him with rarely enough on the table to keep him from being hungry. Overcoming very difficult odds, they both excel in their studies, have dreams for professional careers (Doris as an astronaut and Chimdiebere as a policeman) and will be taking part in the Children’s Flight on 1 September. We’ll be with them the first time they set foot on an airplane and have an up close and personal look at how this experience inspires them in their personal lives to keep reaching for their dreams.

Working closely with the co-founders of the Children’s Flight, we’ll get access to various flights throughout the event, as well as coordinate having camera crew accompanying our young case studies as they take to the skies for the very first time.

Only 8000 can get dialysis. the other 42 000 are sent home to die. There are no kidneys for transplants. One way to fill the gap between need and supply would be to grow the organs another way — in animals. Scientists are now working to create designer pigs that could grow organs for human bodies. US scientists are the closest yet to creating genetically modified pigs with organs that can be safely transplanted into humans.

It was notable that all arguments from the ANC in Parliament on Tuesday were in defense of the ANC and not of Jacob Zuma. By not getting rid of Zuma the ANC are going to have a hard time at the election polls in 2019. On Wednesday the DA called for early elections and for Parliament to be dissolved. On the legal front in September there is an Impeachment case against Zuma and in October a Criminal case. The ANC clearly is a party divided trying everything in their power to cling onto it's legacy. They believe they can self-correct by announcing a judicial inquiry into the allegations of State Capture and with Zuma saying he will not stand again - but will he serve out his term until the 2019 elections?

This is President Jacob Zuma 8th vote of no confidence in his 8 years of Presidency. What set this one apart from previous motions was the massive civil society mobilization behind the call for Zuma to go and this was the first to be conducted in secret. title: Going high-tech to save a rare rabbit
oneLiner: going high-tech to save one of the world's rarest rabbits...
summary:
The Karoo. One of the most iconic landscapes in South Africa – a place of extremes, wide, open spaces and endless sunsets. Although the Karoo is well known for its seemingly barren environment, it’s home to an abundance of succulents and interesting wildlife species. One of these is the beautiful, and Critically Endangered, Riverine Rabbit. Sadly, the much-loved Karoo as we know it is in peril. It’s hard to imagine a South Africa without this backdrop, but threats such as climate change, mining, hydraulic fracturing (fracking), powerlines and the construction of dams are placing this special ecosystem at risk. The team will use a specially-trained dog and thermal imaging drone to help search out rabbits and work with the farmers to help protect this animal's threatened habitat. Because the remaining populations live in fragmented pockets of land around Loxton in the Karoo - any developments such as fracking and mining could spell the end for this rare mammal. We'd interview the expert involved with the dog handler, the drone suppliers and local farmers about this animal's future in this fragile eco-system.

The Riverine Rabbit is one of the rarest mammals on the planet, with some estimates putting the total population at less than 300 individuals remaining. Now a new project involving a specially-trained border collie with a GPS-enabled collar and a state-of-the-art thermal imaging drone is helping to try save this endangered animal.

title: Sardine Run 2017
oneLiner: The Sardine run is legendary off the KZN Coast line but for the last two years they have disappeared
summary:
Sardines support a whole informal economy along the KZN Coast line. Buyers like Seggie Pillay tail the fishermen and haggle for the best prices. But when the fish don’t run they too are affected as are the families that buy straight from their bakkies. Sardines are a high source of protein that poor people depend on. Sardines are a rapid growing fish, they spawn off the Agullus bank within a year of being born and then migrate along the coast of South Africa. But over the last 30 years their biomass has plummeted. Scientist are not entirely sure why. What they do know is that the ocean temperature is definitely warmer due to climate change and that narrow band of cold water has spread out and so the fish patterns have changed, they just aren’t coming inshore. There has been massive over fishing 70 and 80s by Spanish trawlers off our coast line when the stocks collapsed. When that was curbed the fish stocks recovered somewhat but the ongoing over fishing off our own coast line by domestic commercial fisheries saw the West Coast sardines collapse. Those boats then moved around to Mossel bay. The Department of Trade and Industry has been slow to reduce the total allowable catch as peoples livelihoods depend on the sardines. In 2015 the total allowable catch was 950 000 ton and in 2017 it’s down to 23 964 There is a massive local and international market for sardines much of which is consumed by the pet industry. But it’s not only people that are dependent on Sardines they we are competing with Penguins and Gannets. They too are a casualty of the plummet in sardine stock. For example the Penguin population off Port Elizabeth has dropped from 80 000 to 4000. In the past WWF Sustainable Seafood guide had sardines on their Green list and this year after two years of intensive research they have been moved to the Orange list which means they should be eaten with caution.

Goolam Isaac has been a fisherman for the last 40 years. Each year he relies on netting huge catches of sardines supporting his family for months on what they made during the sardine run. His father did the same before him. But for the last two years there have been no sardines at all. This year they have had 3 days of fish, this week two more days. They spend the whole of July driving up and down the coast hoping those bait balls will come into shore. Often spending more money on petrol than what they make from the catch. Each fisherman has a boat and about 40 people that pull in the nets so a lot of people depend on those fish coming in.

title: Shark cage diving
oneLiner: Shark cage diving is a multi-million rand industry keeping the town of Gansbaai on the map. We find out why for the first time in history are the shark nowhere to be seen.otry rthe
summary:
Gansbaai is the shark capital of the world for the Great Whites. With an estimated population of 1,500 sharks moving between the Cape waters and Mozambique, it was found that the majority of the sharks remained all year round in the Gansbaai waters. To study their movement in more detail, 38 Great White Sharks were tagged in 2012 with high tech satellite tags by a team of local and international marine biologists. They found the reason why so many Great White sharks are found around Gansbaai is due to the abundance of energy rich food readily available. Eight kilometres off the coast of Gansbaai a strip of sea between two small islands that forms the perfect breeding ground for seals and penguins, two key food sources of the Great White shark’s diet. Each year roughly 60 000 seal pups are born on Geyser Rock island and on Dyer Island the penguins are protected as part of ongoing research studies.

Shark cage diving attracts tourist from across the world to Gansbaai. Seen as the mecca of the Great White Sharks, Gansbaai is a unique spot for the Great Whites where food is readily available from the two small islands eight kilometres away. Sixteen years ago the first shark cage diving operator opened shop. Today there are eight operators running 3 boat trips every day. Until February this year shark cage diving generated in excess of R1 600 million every day. Recent sightings of a pair of Orcas and five dead sharks washed out on the beach has brought this industry almost to a halt. Studies have shown that the sharks now fear for their safety and have moved to safer waters. What does the future hold for Gansbaai and the shark cage diving boat operators and what has the economic impact been on every business, from the one man operator to the large operators who is have used this form of eco-tourism to fund valuable scientific and marine research.

title: Penny for your thoughts - Scoin

They are doing so knowingly, and despite numerous complaints on social media, radio stations etc the continue to operate with impunity. Our hidden camera footage, and the experts we will speak to, prove beyond doubt that this is nothing more than a cleverly packaged scam.

Our hidden camera footage reveals how brokers at three of the Scoin shops in Johannesburg blatantly mislead would be investors into believing that 1. They will have huge returns on investment if the buy collectable/commemorative coins, and that they 2. sell said coins at grossly over inflated prices and 3. that they promise to buy back the coins after a suitable period ie 5 years. Our case studies have all bought coins under the same sales pitch, and none of them have seen any return on investment. In fact they've all lost on their initial capital input and the coins are worth little more then the value of the precious metals they contain. A second hidden camera investigation where we accompanied a case study to Scoin's head office in Sandton shows a senior sales executive explaining to the case study that his coins are worth nowhere near what he paid for them and that despite years having passed they are now worth nothing more then the precious metals they contain, and also that despite their promises Scoin will not buy back the coins from them. It also shows a sales broker telling the case study that the he doesn't want to see him "get burned again" on the new platinum kruger rands that Scoin tried to sell us in the first hidden camera footage at the various shops.

title: 2 Dads, 3 Babies
oneLiner: Families come in all shapes and sizes, but what happens when the traditional notion of a nuclear family begins to shift as same sex parenting and surrogacy becomes more prevalent?
summary:
In “2 Dads, 3 Babies,” we’ll spend a day in the life of Christo Menelaou, who owns a construction business in Pretoria. A wedding ring on his finger indicates he’s happily married, and as we arrive home with him, we meet his partner -- Theo. No ordinary same sex couple, last year Christo and Theo fulfilled their quest to become parents with the help of surrogate. She just happened to deliver triplets: Joshua, and twins Zoe and Kate. As we spend a day with Menelaou family, we’ll see the human stories behind same sex parenting and surrogacy. Though same sex parents still face stigma in society, the tide is beginning to change. We’ll take a step back and explain the legal process that South Africa has in place for surrogacy and then speak with a researcher who's done extensive work looking at the changing notion of ‘family’ in South Africa and what that means to society. Recent studies have shown no significant difference between children raised in same sex homes and those raised in heterosexual ones. The findings are that as long as the core relationship between the parents is strong and healthy, children will thrive. The notion of family as a man, woman, and children is currently in a state of upheaval. And with that, we’ll meet two adults who are the product of same sex homes: brothers with 2 lesbian mothers who were born via invitro fertilization in the 80s -- Samuel, who is straight and now married to a woman, and his brother Ben, who is gay. Samuel now works for a gay rights advocacy group, doing work that he says comes naturally to him since he spent his formative years educating others and helping them shed their homophobia. Finally, we’ll return to the Menelaou family. Christo, Theo, Joshua, Kate, and Zoe are just starting out in this world. With research and case studies on their side for a bright future, will the rest of South Africa be there as well?

Christo and Theo Menelaou made international news when their surrogate delivered triplets in July 2016. Now Carte Blanche brings an exclusive update on the triplet’s progress, their first birthday, and delves into issues surrounding surrogacy and same sex parenting.

Where HH's motorcade of 60 did not move over for the presidents motorcade, the arrogance of HH seems to have become too much for the ruling party to stand for. Currently HH's lawyers can see no way for these trumped up treason charges to stand up in court, but treason is an unbeilable offence. So while they fight the state HH will remain behind bars in less than human conditions. Freedom of speech and police brutality are increasing in Zambia and this case is an extreme example. title: Cosplayers
oneLiner: Local cosplayers on the international stage - we meet the people taking dress up to the next level. -
summary: Cosplay, a contraction of the words costume play, is a performance art in which participants called cosplayers wear costumes and fashion accessories to represent a specific character. Cosplayers often interact to create a subculture and a broader use of the term "cosplay" applies to any costumed role-playing in venues apart from the stage. Favorite sources include manga and anime, comic books and cartoons, video games, and live-action films and television series. The rapid growth in the number of people cosplaying as a hobby since 1990s has made the phenomenon a significant aspect of popular culture in Japan and some other parts of Asia and in the Western world. Cosplay events are common features of fan conventions and there are also dedicated conventions and local and international competitions, as well as social networks, websites and other forms of media centered on cosplay activities. title: Life after death?
oneLiner: ....meet the world's leading researcher on life after death
summary:
A few years ago the first major study of life after death was concluded under Dr Sam Parnia. While at University of Southampton, Parnia was the principal investigator of the AWARE Study, This study which concluded in 2012 included 33 investigators across 15 medical centers in the UK, Austria and the USA and tested consciousness, memories and awareness during cardiac arrest. The accuracy of claims of visual and auditory awareness was examined using specific tests. One such test consisted in installing shelves, bearing a variety of images and facing the ceiling, hence not visible by hospital staff, in rooms where cardiac-arrest patients were more likely to occur. The results of the study were published in October 2014; both the launch and the study results were widely discussed in the media. In this insert we talk to Sam Parnai about this study, the results and life after death.

A question that affects all of humanity is: is there life after death? In this insert we explore what scientists say about this.

title: Fake news
oneLiner: ...South Africa is in the grip of a fake news epidemic.
summary:
It used be called propaganda in the pre-internet era. Deliberately misleading news reports to promote a certain cause or discredit a certain cause. And mainstream media sponsored by states were mainly used for this. On social media the phenomenon was slower in development but the last 3 years it has exploded. The term Fake News is fairly new and although used by analysts for a couple of years, it really came to the public’s attention during the US election in 2016. Interestingly a lot of the pro-Trump fake news were created in Europe and spread like wildfire over the internet. This was a fairly new development. Initially fake news on the internet was focused on the area of entertainment which is an extension of tabloid news which reported all kinds of made-up stories about celebrities, crime and science. Social media which began incorporating news feeds proved to be pivotal in the development of fake news in the political arena. Fake news now is all over and not always easy to spot. Although the jury is out about how deeply people are influenced by fake new on social media, but it is a significant phenomenon and it seems that South Africa is currently in the grip of a storm of fake news.

It is one of the biggest news issues world wide

But despite our extensive and well-funded public health care system, on which our government spends 12% of the national budget and 4% of GDP - our public healthcare sector is consistently rated below average by international health care monitor groups. In the past fifteen years the industry has been dominated by the irony of health workforce redundancy and vacancy freezes, shortages of medical staff, graduate unemployment and cuts in education and training provision. Arguably, recent trends have shown a slight reverse in this downward spiral, but overall, in this time frame - health outcomes have worsened. Our case study for this insert clearly highlights the shortcomings of the public health system (despite its proclaimed intension to ensure that every South African, irrespective of race, gender, geographic location and socio- economic status) and how it still fails those who so desperately rely on it in their most vulnerable state: the uneducated and the poor. title: Security Companies: Private protection or a Trojan Horse?

Far outnumbering the available personnel than the combined South African police and army. Studies have shown that South Africa had 2.57 private security personnel for every police employee. In South Africa, the high levels of crime and inability of the police to curb its upward trend, has lead many South African households to fork out thousands of rands every year to keep their assets safe. But are they? There is no doubt its a lucrative industry to be in. In fact, in SA it is in excess of R30 billion annually (as per surveys done in 2012). But are these private security companies contributing to combatting the insecurities it aims to address or are they exacerbating the problem and perpetuating the fear? We take a look at one such private security firm who is accused of facilitating break-ins, blocking paying clients' phones (preventing alarm signals to go through) and "scouting" potential targets before they get hit. All our case studies recounts the exact same modus operandi, indicates the same individual involved in the robberies and all of them lost a significant amount of stock and personal belongings.

Every month you pay a security company to guard you and your belongings. But can you trust them implicitly? Carte Blanche investigates three unrelated Johannesburg robberies that seem to have a lot more in common than meets the eye.

title: Migration
oneLiner: How many Malawians are in South Africa? Does anybody know?
summary:
In our story on human trafficking from Malawi last year, the Malawian High Commissioner in Pretoria said that she has heard figures of between 5 and 6 million malawians being in South Africa. The organisation Africa check has since published an article where they refute this claim - stating that the real number is less than 100 000. They base this on the official number supplied by STATS SA and also the number supplied by the UN, which in turn, is also based mostly on the Stats SA figures. The Africa Check article quotes 4 different experts saying that the 5-6 million figure given by the Malawian government is too high, yet not one of them supplies counter claims. In fact, they all say that no-one really knows, and that there are problems with the official numbers. The main problems are that the majority of foreign nationals enter the country illegally and the Stats SA figures are based on recorded entries at our border posts. Also, because they are in the country illegaly they are hesitant to admit their true nationalities on a census, or to even take part in such a process. Secondly, the xenophobic attacks of the past years also causes foreigners not to disclose their status. A further problem is that other statistics such as birth rates would also not be a true reflection, as the majority of malawians working in South Africa are male. We interview the same experts as Africa Check, and focus on the problems faced in calculating the figures. We also look at the impact these migrants have on our economy and in a very competitive jobs market. We ask why it is important to understand the magnitude of the influx, to better manage the threat of xenophobia

The seemigly uncontrolled influx of foreign nationals into South Africa has lead to the spates of xenophobic attacks in many parts of our country in recent years. Official figures supplied by Stats SA are based on the census and on the recorded figures at our ports of entry. But, while everybody seems to agree that these facts are wrong, no one actually seems to know how many of these people live and work in South Africa

title: Drones are the Uber moment for the Security industry
summary:
Copper thieves have been plaguing the Arcelormittal plant with over 30 incursions a month but since the introduction of drone security they have brought down the number of incidents to a couple, successfully catching the thieves. Drones circumnavigate the 25 km perimeter with thermal cameras sending back images to the control center. They have developed software that beeps when it detects something altering the security. If a suspicious person is spotted security is immediately dispatched while the drone hovers overhead keeping watch. (They will give us access to footage of people being caught using this technology.) Otto Werdmuller von Egg drones fly beyond the line of site and he says it’s the “Uber moment in security.” Otto discovered that security is a grudge spend for most companies and as soon as you have the problem under control companies cut back on the security spend so invariably security companies “create opportunities” but with this technology they are able to tackle the security issues more directly. The City of Cape is also using night drone security in the gang lands in conjunction with the shot spotter program. The other major break through with drones has been in the agricultural sector. Farmers are now using drones and associated software to monitor their crops - where they need water and what additional fertilizers are required. The drones using a sensor much like a park sensor on a car, criss-crosses a field only a meter or two off the ground carrying the near IR camera. It does this completely automatically and records all data onboard for analysis later. This software is being used extensively by the Sugar Cane industry. The information also assist farmers insure their crops more accurately as they have ongoing data assessing the health of their crops at a much more affordable rate.

It's the "Uber" moment in the security industry- using drones to patrol at night, fling out of line of sight. It is having a dramatic impact on copper and other theft. The other major development in the use of Drones for agricultural purposes, assisting farmers keep track of how their crops are fairing. Using drones alongside specialized software the aerial images allow farmers to manage water and fertilizing regimes for their crops.

title: Fake news and disclaimers
oneLiner: Social Media has been awash with fake and satirical articles lately – before you share news, make sure it comes from a real news source.
summary: Social media has been awash with fake and satirical articles lately but before you share news, make sure it comes from a real news source. Apart from looking like a fool when you share these stories as real news, you can be held legally liable for distributing damaging information. Nicholas Hall from Michalsons Law Firm said that in terms of our law of defamation, sharing, liking, or retweeting constitutes an act of publication. By sharing and liking a dubious Facebook post, like the “Two arrested over 80,000 ballot papers” article, you could face legal action for engaging in the “chain of publication”. The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) slated the fake report, and highlighted that it is an offence to make intentionally false statements with the aim of disrupting or influencing an election. The IEC opened a case with the SA Police Service to investigate the source of the false reports, and for referral for prosecution. The article received around 20,000 Facebook likes, which raises the question: Is it a legal risk to share or like fake reports? There is a risk if a person engages in “the chain of publication”. When a person likes or shares a comment, they are publishing that comment once again, especially in a Facebook and social media context, as it will appear on that person’s newsfeed. Who's behind these fake news stories, what is facebook/twitter/youtube/google doing to curb this and how can the public stop being duped into reposting and republishing such divisive material? summary:
Not all tracking is bad but it does have it's negatives; governments monitor data in order to protect us, or in non-democratic states sensor and monitor descent. They may want to find out where a terrorist cell is going to strike, but they may also want to silence detractors, for example, in North Korea. We are also tracked by corporates and data aggregators that use market intelligence to target us with audience specific ads. Criminals pursue us to steal our identity and commit crimes by hacking into any connected device, using malware such as Trojans, RATS, Key Loggers and alike. Cracks and Hacks for Games and software often come with additional payloads to make money. A look at the digital tracking industry reveals frightening and troubling trends, this is an opaque industry. Our online activity data is collected and aggregated into profiles that are sold on to third parties who will know who we are, where we are, what we are interested in and most likely predict what we will do in the future based on our past activities, all this without you knowing. Carte Blanche explores who is tracking who on line and why.

Every single day we go online we leave a digital footprint. These footprints make us vulnerable to millions of people that might harm us. The advances and conveniences that technology brings, also force us to trade off some of our liberties and privacy.

title: Eyes for the Blind
oneLiner: Tonight on Carte Blanche: Sight is something we all take for granted. But have you ever stopped to think what it must be like to live a world of darkness? John Webb has the story.
summary:
To the visually impaired every day is a challenge. Meet Theo. He lives in Paarl and works at the Maternity Hospital in Salt River. At 6h00 every morning Theo and his guide dog Chad, takes the train from Paarl station to Cape Town central during which he encounters many obstacles. He relies on Chad to guide him through the hordes of people to the correct platform and often the trains are switched or late, says Theo. Taxi’s and busses are the worst, he says. I have been told by Golden Arrow bus driver to purchase a ticket for Chad as he is passenger too. Most of the taxi drivers don’t allow my dog as they have an inherent distrust in dogs and some the passengers are scared of dogs. It does not matter how many times I have to tell them that he is a gentle dog and will not bite. Transport is a major problem for the visually impaired as Andre Neethling has told us. Andre and his trusted friend Emmie relies on taxis and often catches an Uber to work, as he is not on the main taxi line. On several occasions Uber drivers have left him standing in the rain and in the cold. They refuse to pick me up and still insist on charging a cancellation fee. The closest I get to lodge my complaint with Uber is via email, as they have never bothered picking up the phone to apologise personally. The best they are prepared to do is to apologise on email for the inconvenience and refund my money. Meet Michelle Botha. She holds a master’s degree in Gender Studies from UCT and works for the Institute of the Blind in Cape Town. Michelle’s positive attitude is inspiring and she does not let the hindrances of being blind disable her. But there have been times she says, where I have felt so despondent when people’s insensitive nature and ignorance has caused me great pain. Time and time again restaurant managers turn friends and I away because of my guide dog. It is so infuriating! I am a paying customer too. Is my money not worth it, she exclaims.

Our story will be told through the eyes of the visually impaired, their fears, their hopes and their challenges. What role does society play in aggravating their circumstances further and why are we allowing blatant discrimination against the visually impaired to continue? We will ask the questions to those who transgress and ask for comment from the wrongdoers

title: REGENESIS EXPOSED: FREE STATE HEALTH
oneLiner: Another controversial contract between the Free State Health Department and a service provider worth a max of R90 million for stem cell treatment, cancelled.
summary:
The National Health Department heard that we were investigating the contract and gave us a call because Health Minister, dr Aaron Motsoaledi was alarmed. We subsequently spoke to the Medicines Control Council who said that the Minister of Health immediately informed them and they sent two investigators immediately to go to the Regenesis Biotechnologies unit where dr Stander was treating patients with therapies including stem cell therapy. Dr Stander granted us an interview on the Monday, following the visit from the two MCC investigators. Dr Stander said the National Health Department was aware of the contract and what he was doing there and they have in fact visited the unit three days before and they've done an audit and investigation and all their findings were positive and they are in fact going to motivate to the provincial health department that he needed a larger space and larger theatre space because they could also see that the patients deserve it. But Prof Rees said the two investigators went there to investigate, they interviewed dr Stander whom he thinks, did not appreciate the fact that what he was doing there was in fact a clinical trial and that the therapy he was treating patients with is in fact regarded as a medicine and both of those fall under the Medicines Control Council and he had permission to do neither. Prof Rees said that dr Stander has never applied with the MCC to do any clinical trial, or to treat patients with muscoskeletal diseases with therapies including stem cell therapy. Stem cell therapy can only be used in blood-related diseases, such as leukemia, bone marrow transplants etc. - that is regarded as standard care because clinical trials to prove the success of the treatment had been done worldwide. No clinical trial have been done to prove the risks, pros and cons of stem cell treatment on muscoskeletal diseases and it is not regarded as standard care in SA. Dr Stander insisted he didn't need approval from the MCC.

Carte Blanche has been investigating healthcare in the Free State health department for more than three years. During those three years, we have uncovered widespread maladministration in healthcare in the Free State province. It was during a follow-up investigation that a contract between the FS Health Department and a company owned by a dr Wian Stander called Regenesis Biotechnologies was leaked to us. The contract states that Dr Stander was appointed to provide "cell based stem cell therapies for muscoskeletal diseases such as shoulder, knee and hip replacements, autoimmune diseases and other burdensome diseases AND therapeutic research. The contract is worth a maximum of R90 million over three years and the service provider will receive an amount not exceeding R30 000 per treatment per patient. The department also guarantees a thousand patients per year.

title: In defence of the penguins
oneLiner: May one wrong decision mean the extinction of the only penguin species found in africa?
summary:
Population numbers of the african penguin has dropped by 90% over the past 60 years and the figures still keep on declining. Many scientists reckon we may already have reached the tipping point where the species is caught in "the extinction curve". Currently the worldwide figures stand at 19000 breeding pairs in South Africa and another 4000 estimated in namibia. All of the breeding colonies have been declining for years except one - Stony Point in betts Bay. This colony accounts for about 13% of the total population. The penguins arrived here in the 1980's and started breeding on the edge of this stony outcrop, and as their numbers increased they slowly also started breeding on the 11 residential properties on Stony Point. The local municipality started managing the colony as a tourist attraction, but no real conservation work was done. As other colonies started collapsing Stony Point suddenly found itself being the most important breeding colony for this enigmatic species and Overstrand municipality started handing over the control to the provincial conservation body, Cape nature. During the process of handing over, the tourism facilities were upgraded, and it was also decided to fence the edge of stony point off from the residential properties protect the penguins from disturbances and threats by residents, their dogs, and also the otters and even a caracal that seemed to prey on the penguins. However, no official study was done on the impact the fence would have on this crucial breeding colony - although at the time only about 300 pairs nested between the houses, the properties represent almost 2/3's of the habitat available for the expanding colony. The fence was erected in Dec 2012, and now we revisit the colony to see what impact the fence has had - and how the colony is doing.

Lots of cute footage of penguins :) And some serious questions asked of the conservation body that has to save them from extinction.

On 16 August 2012, the South African Police Service opened fire on a crowd of striking mineworkers at Marikana. The fateful event left 34 mineworkers dead, 78 wounded and more than 250 people were arrested. And in 2015, the Farlam Commission recommended that a criminal investigation should be pursued against the police involved in the killings. Over the last four years protest action has increased in South Africa, from service delivery protests to the University protests related to the increase of Higher Tuition fees, police have been called in to assist and in some instances this has led to violence breaking out between police and protesters. In 2016, the SA Human Rights Commission made submissions to the UN Committee on Human Rights which in part highlighted “the high percentage of ... protests that turn violent, and the disproportionate use of force by the police to quell demonstrations.” It would seem that almost four years after Marikana, Public Order Policing hasn't improved as police turn to rubber bullets and tear gas to quell protests. Now almost four years to the day, Carte Blanche will track just what should have happened immediately after Marikana - in terms of effective police training. The insert will thus explore how the South African police has improved or changed its training protocols not only in public order police but for other instances where police are called in.

Widespread protest action and allegations of disproportionate use of force to quell demonstrations have kept the limelight on the police. Carte Blanche asks: Is the SAPS capable of dealing with a society in which often-violent civil unrest is an almost daily occurrence?

summary: In 2000 Kenneth Nkosana Makate came up with a Please Call Me concept when he was working for Vodacom. The product was launched in March 2001 with huge financial success. Makate’s plea for remuneration was ignored.Seven years later Makate took legal action. He instituted a claim against Vodacom in the Gauteng High Court which he lost. His luck turned when he met Chris Schoeman in 2011. Schoeman entered into a funding agreement with Makate for a 60/40% share in favour of Makate should he win.Schoeman appointed Stemela & Lubbe attorneys and three senior advocates who all agreed to work for half their fee. Investors Errol Elsdon, Tracey Roschard and Schoeman’s ex wife, Wilma came on board. Schoeman agreed to pay each a small percentage of the profit. When more funders came on board an addendum was signed for a 50/50% split between Schoeman and Makate.The funders paid R2.457,830.00 million towards legal costs with R521,214.77 still outstanding which Schoeman could not meet. Lubbe warned Makate that he would now be liable for the cost. This resulted in Makate cancelling the funding agreement with Schoeman on 7 January 2015. Makate kept his legal team on a contingency fee basis as he headed for the Constitutional Court. On 26 April 2016 the highest court in South Africa ruled in favour of Makate and ordered Vodacom to make a fair offer to his invention that has made Vodacom close to R10.5 billion.Before the dust could settle, Schoeman and the investors were back on the scene claiming that the funding agreement was never really cancelled but part of a ‘conspiracy’ of Lubbe to oust the investors. Lubbe calls his allegations a ‘blatant lie’. Makate is now heading for arbitration to settle whether his former financial backers are in fact entitlted to any compensation he will be recieving from Vodacom.

But as you know, the life line of any economy is an effect transport system. And it Cape Town this is being felt. This insert looks into the issues facing metro rail in cape town and its impact on workers who often now have to get jup at 4 am in order to make sure that they get to work in time. The issues are: criminal action (once we had the railway police which would travel on tains, this does not happen any more). We speak to one man who heroically saved the lives of commuters and who himself was thrown off the train. We look at the cable theft and also hear that a new law is being promulgated which will send offenders of cable theft to prison for a mononum of 5 years. We will look at the fight between the secutity company which tried to look after the safety of commuters and which were made redundant. But we will also look at the economy and why some people are being fired. Large companies can absorb people coming late, it’s the small SMO’s that suffer the most. Michael Bagraim, attorney, conducted research on the dilemma – and he got 650 responses from 3000 questionnaires that he sent out. It showed that the most vulnerable to the effects of train delays were the small smo’s , the life blood of economy. If a capetner came late, and affected then a crew of 5, then work would be lost for the whole day.

It was abandoned at that stage. In 1996 the new owners of the property, Anglo American conducted a R120-million geological study to see if the uranium could be productively mined. They determined the quality was not sufficient. In 1997 mining engineer Peter Skeat bought Afrikander Leases from Anglo and even he conducted the experiments and surveys to determine how he could profitably mine the uranium. While in this position, Skeat won the Department of Trade and Industry's TOP 300 companies award and twice, the JSE's top gold share award. Skeat's research basically confirmed the findings by Anglo American. Skeat was swindled out of his company by Brett Kebble and his collaborators (Skeat was vindicated after 6-year long court case and got about R40-m back after the court found in his favour agains Kebble & co.) Skeat's successor was Neal Froneman, who incurred a $1.8-billion loss at the Afrikaner Lease/Dominion property -- the history is well documented. Now Oakbay Resources acquired the Uranium Mine, using R1-bn of tax-payers' money, and a number of banks have contributed. We investigate who stands to lose how much now that the family seems to have abandoned their directorships and the mirage of Oakbay's market capitalisation, based on a share price that is manipulated and meaningless is exposed. The Guptas never paid for what is now named Shiva. The deposit is worthless, and will take billions to recapitalise if it is to ever go into commercial production. Even at current rand/dollar rate, it would require the price of uranium oxide to be four times higher than prevailing US$ world price.

Now he will be in South Africa, to demonstrate and teach us how to communicate with horses. Roberts believes that horses use a non-verbal language, which he terms "Equus," and that humans can use this language to communicate with horses. The moment a human has earned the horse’s trust is called Join-Up®. Equus is a silent language of gestures like signing for the deaf. It’s the Rosetta Stone for the student of horses, and to see Monty crack the code on the language of Equus with horses who have had a past or wild tendencies it’s extraordinary. Monty says he “didn’t create a set of methods, but only discovered what nature put in place long before humans domesticated horses 6000 years ago”. His father was horse trainer and a violent man, as a child, Monty worked with the horses, rejecting his father’s traditional and violent ways. In Monty’s word’s “Violence is never the answer. Violence is always for the violator and never for the victim. No one of us was born with the right to say 'You must, or I’ll hurt you’ to any other being, animal or human.” We will not only see Monty at work, calming and communicating undisciplined horses “During the shows he communicates with horses he has never met and horses that have problems either loading into a box of letting people near them . People were asked to submit details of horses and Monty’s crew selected a few. Its an entertaining show. ..but also go with him to visit the Shumbashaba kids near Diepsloot…these are children from the surrounding areas who are being taught horse skills, these kids are not only riders but also have won medals vaulting .

title: Is South Africa going Hungry?

summary: We are living in very uncertain times, but of all the challenges that currently face us in South Africa, the rising cost of food is one of the biggest. Due to a perfect storm of factors (including severe drought, unstable exchange rate, and a fragile agricultural sector), the price of all our major food products has been rocketing. Until recently, price increases have been largely absorbed by the retailers, but this is about to end and consumers are sure to get an extreme case of ‘sticker shock’. This will have an impact on all South Africans – but it will be a disproportionately heavy burden for the poor who already spend most of their income of food. In other foods, the issue of food security is a ticking time bomb that could engulf the country in a wave of hunger, social unrest, and even rebellion. In this incisive piece, we will investigate the issues affecting the rising price of food in South Africa; shedding light on what’s to come and how to prepare for the worst, through the use of personal narratives of ordinary middle class South Africans, ranging to the very poor, expert opinions and graphic treatments.

title: Nkandla: The Final Judgment
summary: Thursday was a day that changed the face of democratic South Africa - a victory for the Constitution and the rule of law. It also showed that nobody was above the law, even President Jacob Zuma. An important aspect was that the court had made declaratory orders that both Zuma and the National Assembly were in breach of their constitutional obligations. The court found it was duty-bound to rule on that. In a watershed unanimous judgment of the Constitutional Court on Thursday, the court found that President Jacob Zuma had acted inconsistently with the Constitution when he failed to comply with the Public Protector's remedial action on the upgrades to his Nkandla homestead. The court ruled that Zuma had to personally pay back the money for some of the upgrades, following a determination by the National Treasury. The Constitutional Court also found that the National Assembly erred when it dismissed Public Protector Thuli Madonsela's report. "The resolution by the National Assembly absolving the president from compliance with the Public Protector's remedial action is inconsistent with the Constitution, is invalid, and set aside," Chief Justice Mogoeng Mogoeng read from his unanimous judgment. Mogoeng said a draft order Zuma circulated eight days before the case was heard in the Constitutional Court showed he accepted that the Public Protector's remedial action was binding. Mogoeng said the president was enjoined to take definite steps to determine how much Zuma should pay for the swimming pool, cattle kraal, chicken run, visitors' centre, and amphitheatre built at Nkandla. "The president failed to uphold, defend, and respect the Constitution," he said. Only a court of law could have set aside the Public Protector's findings and remedial action.

title: Self-healing materials
oneLiner: a new generation of materials that have the ability to heal themselves if cracked or broken
summary: Scientists have developed aircraft wings that can detect and repair small-scale damage to their structure. Modern aircraft are made with carbon fibre-reinforced composites. These are high performance, lightweight and stiff making them an ideal material for aeroplanes or wind turbines. However, damage to the composite structure can be difficult to detect. The researchers added microcapsules to the composite. If the aircraft wing is damaged these microcapsules rupture and come into contact with a catalyst. A chemical reaction takes place which causes hardening (polymerisation) to 'glue' together any cracks. The Wass Research Group says that this can give up to 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength.Professor Wass was interviewed in an exclusive by the Independent on Sunday. In the interview he said he expected self-healing products to reach consumers in the “very near future” and said that inspiration came from the body's ability to heal itself by forming scabs.

title: City Powerless
oneLiner: If you are living in jozi, chances are that you are being billed a lot more for your electricity than you are actually using
summary: Ten years after they first admitted that they had billing problems, City Power recently went on record to say that it has been solved. But this is a lie - according to various legal firms, the Star Consumer Watch, and thousands of consumers. Wrong meter numbers, meters that are only ever estimated and never actually read and adjusted, and impossible consumption figures have lead to a chaos that is not about to be solved soon - and which is costing consumers millions of rands, and which leads to power and (illegal) water cuts by the council. Council has an approach of first pay the amount showing on your bill and then we will investigate your claim that it's wrong. This leads to the start of corruption from honest citizens - people who come to disconnect are simply bribed not to cut the power or water. At the same time this has also lead to various scams appearing - people who either work for city power or act as if they do, arrive at your gate and threaten to disconnect you unless you pay a bribe. We even have a case study of a guy who was phoned by someone from city power and told that they were mailing him his account and he had to pay R35 000 to bring it up to date - he received the account via email, paid the money and then realised a few days later that he was scammed. He went to City Power, phoned the guy's number from another official's desk, and they heard the phone ring in an empty cubicle down the passage. According to one lawyer we interviewed, the matter should really be taken to concourt - as an old bylaw seems to lie at the heart of the problem - this states that the burden of proof in cases against the municipality lies with the consumer - meaning that we all have to do our own daily readings with photographs. Many felt that virginity testing is a patriarchal tradition and that a woman’s right to an eduction should not be directly linked to her virginity. But on the other hand the cultural practice of virginity testing has been around for centuries and in KZN many girls have already pledged to be virgins and are undergoing virginity testing regularly. Mayor Mazibuko feels strongly that the bursary will inspired girls to stay virgins and therefore reduce the spread of HIV and teenage pregnancy cases. This story looks at two girls who received the bursary and have proudly pledged their virginity. We find out what their circumstance are, how they feel about doing regular virginity testing and getting the bursary. We also meet the elders from both villages who put the girls forward for the bursary and will be doing the regular testing. These elders are solely responsible to report on the girls virginity status to the municipality, every varsity holiday. We also speak to Nomboniso Gasa, an author and professor on politics and gender studies. She feels that the intentions behind the bursary are good, but is strongly apposed to a woman’s virginity being aligned to her right to an education. She is also very concerned about this bursary in relation to the high cases of sexual assault on woman in South Africa. At the end of the piece the audience will have made an emotional connection with the girls who have received the bursary. They will have heard both what makes this a genius idea and how this is a step backwards for woman’s rights in South Africa. And then they can make their own minds up.

title: Dying to be White
summary: Skin lightening products are big business internationally - in Asia they spend R18 Billion a year on skin lightening products. Before the early 1990s, there was a thriving trade in skin lighteners in South Africa, but Black Consciousness and the medical profession saw to it that they were banned in 1991. So why, when Prof Nonhlanla Khumalo of the Skin Institute at Groote Schuur tested 29 creams, 22 of them contained dangerously high levels of hydroquinone, mercury and corticosteroids? Two of these creams were stocked by pharmacies and the rest bought from informal traders. The creams are coming in from Europe – despite them being banned in the EU – and from North Africa and Asia. The cosmetic regulatory body is partially to blame for this as they don’t police the importation of products, and despite containing medicinal elements, they are not monitored by the Medicine Control Board. Many of these products are openly labelled and should be stopped by the port authorities. 35 % of South African woman admit to using skin lighteners. There was a dramatic increase since 1994 when more women were coming into the country from North Africa. 80% of the products tested by Prof Khumalo contained illegal or banned substances and many of the products combined more than one illegal product. The latest fad amoungst high profile celebrities like Kwaito queen Mashoza and Beyonce is going the intravenous route with an infusion of cocktail of Vit C and glutathione. Long term studies have not yet proved their safety or impact on the rest of the body.

title: Oscar Pistorius Probation: The process
oneLiner: In less than a week, Oscar Pistorius will be released under correctional supervision. He's served the ten months, as dictated by his sentence. But what is the process he had to undergo in prison?
summary: Almost all the media are incorrectly reporting that Oscar Pistorius will be released on parole. This, of course, is wrong. He is not being released on parole, but under correctional supervision and there is a big difference. According to the Criminal Procedures Act, when an offender is sentenced to five years or less, he or she only has to serve one sixth of the sentence behind bars. The other sixth of the sentence that would make up one third of the total sentence, could be served under correctional supervision - with conditions stipulated by the Department of Correctional Services.

title: Garnishee Orders
oneLiner: A victory for the poor
summary: Apartheid was dismantled in the early 90’s but it was replaced by another form of apartheid – the utter widespread exploitation of the poor through illegal debt recovery mechanisms. The chief culprit being the garnishee order. Despite major funded investigations by universities, work by the SA law reform society, widespread press, the government has done nothing to alleviate the suffering of the poor as they were exploited by banks, attorneys, furniture stores and debt collectors. Lets not fool ourselves that this is an phenomena that only affects one segment of the population (i.e. the poor) and not the normal Carte Blanche viewer. Industry bosses who are compelled by law to make these garnishee deductions watch in horror as their employees take home pay is virtually nill. Thousands of South African’s have to deduct from their domestic workers salaries. Productivity has to decrease because those exploited by illegal garnishee orders suffer. Strikes and demands for extra wages can also be tracked back to take home pay of employees. Lets not forget that the garnishee order is a very good system if 1) there has not been reckless lending and 2) if its done legally. Now the landscape is going to change and not through the government who sat on the sideline, aware of the situation but has done squiddly nothing. We tell the remarkable story of how this ended up in a marathon high court hearing. We hear first hand the breathless ways poor people were exploited and we hear the judges wrath as he listened to tales and tales of exploitation. The major hitters in this case were a dream team who all gave their services on spec – a top advocate, Webber Wentzel, Wendy Appelbaum and Clarke Gardener.

title: Identikit
oneLiner: Groundbreaking new identikit technology at UCT
summary: A fascinating look at the world of identikits, police artists, and controversies surrounding them, and how the University of cape Town Criminology department is working hand in hand with police whilst developing a new system which should greatly enhance the quality of identikits, by helping victims reconstruct faces of their attackers using friendly composite software. The controversies are that many people in the USA, and no doubt here have been convicted by wrong identikits. Hundred have been released from prison as a result. The big controversy here is of course the station strangler who was caught via his identikit drawing. It didn't resemble him at all and we can show this. But police have got it spot on as well, and we can look at how close the Facebook rapist identikit (which led to the suspect) was to the real person. The major controversy at the moment is of course the identikit which lead to the wrongful arrest of Zanokuhle Mbatha, accused of killing Befana soccer captain Senzo Meyiwa . The aggrieved man is now suing the police. The police artists are still using feature based identik, which is a difficult process. But they are beginning also to use composite technology but these faces are European and American. It’s against this background that UCT has developed composite programs with south African computer generated faces. I have seen it in action, it’s excellent. So we give John Webb the chance to see how he does when we get a person to so called attack him and he only sees his attacker for 5 seconds. He sits now with the UCT doctorate student and has to use the program identifying what his attacker looked like. We also sit with a conventional artist and John tries his luck at a feature based system which is choosing the right eyes, outline of face, nose, ears etc. Much more difficult.

title: "Shaiking" it up (Foetal Surgery in SA)
oneLiner: It has been two years since we watched baby Ford being born after lifesaving in utero surgery. Sadly many parents aren’t aware of or have access to these procedures. One SA doctor hopes to change th
summary: SUMMARY We first met Dr Samad Shaik in July 2012, when he successfully operated on Joel Ford, then a 32 week old foetus who had developed an extremely rare medical condition called chylothorax. Fluid had filled his chest cavity compressing the lungs and displacing the heart. Neither organ was able to grow properly and there was a chance the pressure would stop the heart from beating. Dr Shaik inserted a shunt that drained the fluid and two weeks later the little boy was born healthy. We were there. Today his dad “Hayden” describes Joel as a little “tiger” who celebrated his 2nd birthday in July this year. DR SHAIKS VISION But things could have been very different had their gynaecologist not introduced them to Dr Shaik – one of only a handful of foetal surgeons in the country. (He says he is the only Paediatric Surgeon in the country who has been performing some of these major surgeries. EXIT procedures without major surgery on placental support are being done in some hospitals – like the Nel case below.) According to Dr Shaik, many parents are advised to terminate pregnancies when potentially fatal conditions are detected in the womb. (He says this is especially true in the Cape). It’s a situation he hopes to change. He says many babies can be saved. He is advocating for the creation of at least two foetal surgery units to be established in Cape Town and possibly Johannesburg. Significantly he wants these units to be available to be set up at state hospitals, where ordinary South Africans can have access to this specialise surgery AND where young surgeons can be trained in the discipline. He hopes to be able to offer desperate parents a whole bunch of lifesaving procedures.
